documents.excerpt: Last week Jesus climbed into Peter’s boat after a night of catching nothing and told him to go back out to the deep water and let down the nets. Peter said, in effect, “This makes absolutely no sense to me, but because you say so, I’ll let down the nets.” The nets broke, the boats began to sink, Peter fell at Jesus’ feet, and Luke tells us they pulled their boats up on shore, left everything, and followed him.
excerpts: Last week Jesus climbed into Peter’s boat after a night of catching nothing and told him to go back out to the deep water and let down the nets. Peter said, in effect, “This makes absolutely no sense to me, but because you say so, I’ll let down the nets.” The nets broke, the boats began to sink, Peter fell at Jesus’ feet, and Luke tells us they pulled their boats up on shore, left everything, and followed him.

We read that and respond the way we think we should: “Amen. What faith. What devotion.” But Josh asks the church to imagine actually doing it. Peter has a business, employees who depend on a paycheck to feed their families, partners with families, and a family of his own. He grew up learning the trade to provide, and he leaves it.

The question Josh has been thinking about all week: “Peter, is he worth it? You left everything, man. Is he worth everything?” Following Jesus sounds great when he is filling the boat with fish. What happens when the boat is empty, when following Jesus costs you something, when obedience results in less fish instead of more?

documents.excerpt: If the church were asked by push notification, “How are you blessed?”, most would point to family, health, job, house, country, food on the table, money in the bank, and good friends. Those are blessings; James tells us every good and perfect gift comes from above, so thank God for them. But when Jesus describes the blessed life, he says poor, hungry, weeping, hated, rejected.
excerpts: If the church were asked by push notification, “How are you blessed?”, most would point to family, health, job, house, country, food on the table, money in the bank, and good friends. Those are blessings; James tells us every good and perfect gift comes from above, so thank God for them. But when Jesus describes the blessed life, he says poor, hungry, weeping, hated, rejected.

Josh is off social media, but he didn’t see a lot of people posting an eviction notice on Instagram with “#blessed,” or leave the doctor’s office after devastating news and decide it needed a gratitude post with Brandon Lake music. That isn’t how we use the word.

Usually “God has blessed me” means things are going the way I want them to right now, and we should thank God when they do. The problem is when they don’t. Most Christians don’t need a sermon on how to rejoice when God gives; we need constant reminders on how to rejoice when God takes.

If blessing means good circumstances, does God stop blessing when circumstances turn? If I’m blessed because the test came back negative, what do I tell the person with a positive test? If I’m blessed because my business succeeded, what do I tell the faithful Christian whose business failed? Our use of the word is flimsy.

excerpts: Who does Luke say Jesus is looking at? His disciples: people who belong to him. He is not giving everyone a four-point sermon on how to get into the kingdom: step one, become poor; step two, get hungry; step three, start crying; step four, make everybody hate you. That would be ridiculous.

This isn’t a gospel presentation; it is a perseverance presentation. Poverty doesn’t save you, hunger doesn’t save you, suffering doesn’t save you. Jesus is describing the blessing of people who already belong to the king.

Think how crucial that was for Peter, who had just walked away from everything. Jesus is discipling Peter into a kingdom mindset so he can launch the church. If Peter, walking away from the boat, still needed to change his thinking about what it means to be blessed, so do we.

excerpts: Josh returns to verse 20. Greek words typically have multiple meanings, at least five, which only becomes a problem when someone takes one and teaches it as the only definition. We hear “blessed” and think “happy,” and that is one meaning, but it is bigger than that. Jesus isn’t saying “happy are the poor” or speaking to the emotional state of people living in poverty.

We call people blessed by inspecting what surrounds them. Jesus determines blessing by looking at who possesses the person. We think of happiness as possessions, position, pleasure, and popularity; Jesus flips that upside down and says those things can never substitute for a relationship with God through Jesus Christ.

If blessing depends on what I have, I can lose it. The market can take money; disease and death can take health; people, or I, can ruin a reputation; failure can take success. But what if being blessed isn’t a gift God gives me? What if the blessing is God himself?

Over the years Christians realized they all shared a common ultimate hope in God and gave it a name: we will see him, know him, and enjoy his presence without sin, death, disease, separation, or anything standing between us and the one who made us.
The apostle John shares this vision throughout Revelation, especially chapters 21 and 22. Josh’s homework: go read both chapters, not to inform your eschatology, but to see King Jesus.
He shows one phrase he thinks summarizes the entire book: “They will see his face.” Who are “they”? Those who overcome by the word of their testimony and the blood of Jesus.

excerpts: Last week Josh asked who had been comforted by Jesus and who had been confronted by him. This week Jesus is going to confront our comforts.

Don’t miss the caution tape: you can spend your entire life asking God to give you stuff and never realize that he is the treasure. Bless the career, the marriage, the kids, the finances, the plans, the future, the church. We should pray for, desire, and believe God for these things. But what if he doesn’t? What if something you already thanked him for is taken, or following Jesus costs you something? Are you still singing? Is God still good? Is Jesus still enough? Are you still blessed?

But an empty bank account doesn’t earn someone heaven. Poverty isn’t a prerequisite for heaven, and wealth isn’t a fast pass to hell: Judas was broke, and Zacchaeus was rolling in it. documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 5, 2026 · King For All
documents.excerpt: Josh puts the four pairs on a T-chart and asks which side people would pick without being told what Jesus calls blessed. The right side: money instead of poverty, a full stomach instead of hunger, laughter instead of tears, respect instead of rejection. That sounds like the good life.
excerpts: Josh puts the four pairs on a T-chart and asks which side people would pick without being told what Jesus calls blessed. The right side: money instead of poverty, a full stomach instead of hunger, laughter instead of tears, respect instead of rejection. That sounds like the good life.

We are walking a tightrope between two value systems: a life built on what I can possess now, and a life built around the kingdom of God later. Not the candy squares. The “now” prizes power, comfort, success, and recognition; the “later” doesn’t require any of that to possess the good life.

The word “now” defines a temporary existence: blessed are you who hunger now, who weep now; woe to you who are well fed now, who laugh now. Jesus is teaching his disciples to evaluate their lives with eternity in view. The world says now is everything; Jesus says there’s a later.

Josh has seen many Christians robbed of joy here. If you forget the not-yet of Christianity, you will spend your entire life trying to make now feel like heaven, and only one event will turn now into heaven: when King Jesus splits the skies.

documents.excerpt: Hunger isn’t necessarily holiness, but it is a useful tool unto holiness. Hunger accomplishes something fullness never could: it reminds you that you need something, while fullness can make you forget.
excerpts: Hunger isn’t necessarily holiness, but it is a useful tool unto holiness. Hunger accomplishes something fullness never could: it reminds you that you need something, while fullness can make you forget.

Josh remembers a restaurant from growing up that served bread in flower pots, and asks the room whether they are top-bread or bottom-bread people. By the time the food arrives you have wrecked three pots of bread. He argues appetizers are the worst invention ever: food to warm up for food, at the price of a meal. His wife loves them, gets too full to eat her meal, boxes it to take home for lunch, and guess who ends up eating it.

Many of us do the same thing spiritually. We are full of entertainment, possessions, schedules, soccer leagues, and Netflix. We stuff our faces with the appetizers of this world and lose our appetite for God.
Remember the crowd reaching for Jesus because they needed what only he could give. The danger isn’t having nothing to give Jesus. The danger is becoming convinced Jesus has nothing you need.

documents.excerpt: Christianity isn’t misery. Josh is having fun and enjoying the Christian walk; this isn’t the Christian Oscars with an award for the most miserable-looking Christian. The Christian life has laughter and joy.
excerpts: Christianity isn’t misery. Josh is having fun and enjoying the Christian walk; this isn’t the Christian Oscars with an award for the most miserable-looking Christian. The Christian life has laughter and joy.

Laugh at what? Reading Luke from this side of the resurrection, how can we not hear these words in light of an empty tomb? It is like watching a movie when you already know how it ends: the conflict is real and the painful scenes still hit, but knowing the ending changes how you feel throughout. Christian, you know how this ends.

There will be funerals, goodbyes that come too soon, diagnoses, betrayals, and nights of questions without answers. Jesus never promised an easy life, but he did promise your tears have an expiration date. In light of eternity and his victory over the grave, how can we not laugh? Josh laughs at himself for worrying: “He empties graves, bro. Stop.”

documents.excerpt: Some walked in hurting, exhausted, at the end of the rope, grieving, looking around at lives that seem full while theirs feels empty. excerpts: For some, the question to wrestle with is different: what if this is all you get? What if now is as good as it gets? Josh reads verse 24 and calls it the second scariest verse in all Scripture. Any time you see “woe,” slam on the brakes; Jesus is warning us.

Don’t turn this verse into a civil war between rich and poor, or Jesus into a campaign surrogate for your preferred party. He isn’t giving an economic platform on capitalism versus socialism. Josh is grateful to live in America, blessed with extraordinary prosperity, maybe too much, which has enabled Christians and churches to give, send missionaries, feed people, build hospitals, fund ministries, respond to disasters, and carry the gospel worldwide. He suspects the church is winning that comparison with government, and invites a fact check.
Prosperity can be an incredible gift, but it can also be spiritually dangerous. The problem isn’t having things; the problem is when things have you.

documents.excerpt: Jesus tells a story in Luke 12 about a man whose land produces so much he runs out of storage, so he plans to tear down his barns, build bigger ones, and tell himself to take life easy: eat, drink, and be merry. excerpts: Jesus tells a story in Luke 12 about a man whose land produces so much he runs out of storage, so he plans to tear down his barns, build bigger ones, and tell himself to take life easy: eat, drink, and be merry. That sounds like the good life. But God said, “You fool, this very night your life will be demanded from you,” and Jesus says this is how it will be for whoever stores up things for themselves but is not rich toward God.

Covetousness is a nasty sin we don’t talk about much; we kind of forget the tenth one. It is an unquenchable thirst for more of something we think we need to be truly satisfied. The man’s issue wasn’t the barns or a lavish savings account; it was that the barns were never enough. He prepared for retirement but never considered a legacy or eternity.

Josh recommends a favorite song, a little old and Christian rap, by Beautiful Eulogy called “If.” Its question: what if God takes away the things I call blessings, the money, the career, the marriage, my spouse, my child, my health, or doesn’t fix what I’ve asked him to fix? Is he still good? Is he still enough?

excerpts: Josh invites the church to let Jesus open them up: What makes you feel secure? What could make your life better? What are you hungry for, afraid to lose, holding so tightly you refuse to let go? What is your hidden treasure? What do you truly desire?
If your definition of being blessed requires God to give you something, God isn’t your treasure; the life you want is your treasure, and you are using God as a means to get it.

It is a scary text, and everyone must examine themselves. If God took the comfort, the applause, the influence, the money; if he doesn’t remove the cancer, the relationship ends, or obedience thins the crowd, would you still worship? Would you still have a song? Or would you say, “God, after everything I’ve done for you, how could you do this to me?”

If losing the gift makes you believe God failed you or owes you more, it reveals that somewhere you stopped worshiping God as your treasure and started worshiping him because he gives you treasures. It is one thing to say Jesus is enough when the marriage is good, the kids are healthy, and the bills are paid; it is another when things start disappearing.

documents.excerpt: The king of heaven doesn’t only welcome the poor; he became poor. The one through whom everything was created entered his creation in the humblest circumstances. He knew hunger, tears, rejection, and homelessness, with no place to lay his head. Crowds praised him until they screamed “Crucify him”; his friends abandoned him; he was mocked, beaten, spit on, rejected, and hung on a cross.
excerpts: The king of heaven doesn’t only welcome the poor; he became poor. The one through whom everything was created entered his creation in the humblest circumstances. He knew hunger, tears, rejection, and homelessness, with no place to lay his head. Crowds praised him until they screamed “Crucify him”; his friends abandoned him; he was mocked, beaten, spit on, rejected, and hung on a cross.

On the cross Jesus doesn’t just show sacrifice; he makes atonement, a propitiation, and takes our place. Christ swaps positions with us, taking the rejection sinners deserve so that those united to him by faith are accepted before God. This exchange is the special boots you need to walk in the upside-down kingdom.

He became poor so that in him you could inherit a kingdom. He entered sorrow so that your tears would one day expire. He was rejected so that you could be welcomed. He bore our sin, guilt, greed, pride, idolatry, self-sufficiency, covetousness, worship of created things, need for human approval, and rebellion against the holy king. The judgment we deserved fell on Christ; Jesus bore our woe so sinners could say, “No matter what happens, we are blessed.”

Three days later the tomb was empty. Our hope isn’t that things will probably work out or life will get easier; it is a crucified and risen king. If you belong to him, the kingdom is yours because the king is yours: your portion, your treasure, your reward.

documents.excerpt: Josh opens with the irritation of unsolicited advice from someone who has never done your job: the person who has never raised children asking, “Have you tried telling them no?”, the YouTube viewer explaining to the mechanic what went wrong, the guest who opens the lid on your smoker and says the temperature seems low, and the WebMD search that ends with telling the doctor what’s wrong. It takes extreme patience when someone who has never done what you do starts telling you how to do it. That is where Simon Peter finds himself in Luke 5.

It takes extreme patience when someone who has never done what you do starts telling you how to do it. That is where Simon Peter finds himself in Luke 5.

This is week three of King For All. In week one, Luke showed that this king entered real history: not a fairy tale, but an account investigated with a historian’s skill and a doctor’s attention to detail, so that we might be certain. Last week, Mary taught faith, trusting that the child in her womb fulfilled God’s ancient promises.
Now the king has grown up and makes his way to the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus steps onto a fisherman’s boat, and that fisherman faces the single most important decision of his life.

excerpts: Josh reads verse 3. Jesus chose Peter’s boat, so the boat is now a pulpit and the shoreline an amphitheater; Jesus sits, as Jewish teachers commonly did, and teaches the crowd from the water.

The crowd is listening voluntarily, but Peter is a captive audience, an exhausted fisherman counting the minutes until the sermon is over. Josh says many are guilty of over-glorifying those who walked with Jesus: respect, sure, but not reverence. They had good days and bad days, just like us.

Peter probably believes he is doing Jesus a favor. But making something available to Jesus is not the same as surrendering everything to Jesus. Many people give Jesus access without giving him authority: he can enter the house when someone is sick, the conversation when the marriage struggles, the finances when money is tight; he can have an hour on Sunday as long as it doesn’t conflict with four hours of NFL; he can comfort at a funeral and give advice when needed. But giving Jesus access when you want to is not the same as giving him authority when he demands it.

excerpts: Josh reads Peter’s response in verse 5. The word translated “master” is used only by Luke and has a range of meanings that all speak of earthly authority: chief, commander, magistrate, governor, president. Peter’s response is respectful but not enthusiastic.

Josh imagines what Peter is thinking: the nets are wet because we just washed them; we fished during the best time of day, with the best equipment, the best guys, and the best spots; Jesus, the fish are sleeping. Peter is saying, in the most polite and professional way, “You’re the master when it comes to the kingdom of God, but I’m the fisherman.”
Even so, Peter submits to Jesus’ authority: “Because you say so, I will let down the net.” He doesn’t obey because it makes sense; none of this makes sense. He obeys because Jesus said it.

excerpts: Josh says this is an area he is trying to grow in. Peter had nets in his hands; sometimes Josh has a phone in his. When someone says something cruel, unfair, or untrue about him or someone he loves, he wants to fire back immediately, with the facts, a timeline, screenshots, and a calm, beautifully organized presentation of the evidence with neat bold headings. His instinct is to defend himself or someone he loves and to set the record straight.

Then he hears Jesus’ words to those who are listening: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you, turn the other cheek. Those commands make zero sense to him; everything in him wants vindication and the last word. Jesus tells him to pray and to bless.

That doesn’t mean becoming everyone’s punching bag or never correcting harmful behavior. But having a good argument doesn’t mean it is an argument worth having. Josh is learning to put his phone down and pray, and has deleted entire messages, possibly entire sermons, not because he was wrong but because Jesus spoke: “I guess I’ll just pray for you.” The master’s commands must always override our plans: because you say so.

excerpts: Josh reads verse 6. Water that showed no signs of life all night is suddenly bubbling; the ropes strain, the floats disappear, and the same net that came up empty is now too full to lift aboard. They signal their partners in the other boat, who come and fill both boats until both begin to sink. James and John come alongside, fish are flopping everywhere, the nets are tearing, and the boats are over capacity: an absolute joyous nightmare.

This wasn’t a better fishing day or a hot spot they’d never seen. These professionals knew the waters so well that this was not a matter of technique or timing. What they hadn’t considered was the person who knew the waters better than they did.

Peter is hesitating before Jesus’ authority while the fish do exactly what Jesus says. Jesus made the fish, the lake, and the water; the fish belonged to him before Peter ever pushed out. When the king of creation speaks, creation listens and obeys. Peter is still trying to determine who Jesus is, and the fish seem to know more than Peter at this point: a sermon from a goldfish.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 28, 2026 · King For All
documents.excerpt: Josh wants the church to see the difference between the Jesus of Scripture and the Jesus that modern Christianity is attempting to manufacture. Campaigns say “he gets us”; Josh thinks we need more campaigns making sure people get him. What if it is a different Jesus from Scripture?
excerpts: Josh wants the church to see the difference between the Jesus of Scripture and the Jesus that modern Christianity is attempting to manufacture. Campaigns say “he gets us”; Josh thinks we need more campaigns making sure people get him. What if it is a different Jesus from Scripture?

The church is creating a Jesus who never makes anyone uncomfortable, soft and cuddly, who affirms every instinct, approves every ambition, and shares every opinion we already hold. That is dumb, because if Jesus supports your opinion and mine, how can he truly support any opinion? We like our Jesus unconditionally supportive and frictionless, less like the Lord of heaven and earth and more like a life coach instructed by the CEO never to challenge a client.

Meanwhile here is Peter: “I’m a sinful man.” The Jesus of our invention might be more Instagram friendly and cause less controversy at the Thanksgiving table, but he can’t save, because that Jesus doesn’t exist.

The real Jesus comforts, and he also confronts; he welcomes sinners, and he demands they repent. Jesus didn’t just come full of grace; he came full of grace and truth. The light of his holiness exposes the darkness in all of us, and then the mercy in his eyes accepts our repentance and welcomes us home.

The miraculous catch sets the pattern for all of Christ’s ministry, the apostles’ ministry, and the ministry of his local church through the ages. documents.excerpt: Luke begins at the back end of one of Israel’s darkest periods. Herod is on the throne and Rome is in control. Herod is not David’s son reigning under God; he is a puppet king placed there by Caesar.
excerpts: Luke begins at the back end of one of Israel’s darkest periods. Herod is on the throne and Rome is in control. Herod is not David’s son reigning under God; he is a puppet king placed there by Caesar.

Herod was a brilliant builder who kept working on the temple until it was magnificent, but the men beautifying God’s house did not possess a heart surrendered to God. The people were crushed under taxes and bloodshed. Paranoid about losing power, he executed members of his own family, including his wife and three of his sons. Josh’s comparison: Herod makes Pharaoh look like a Sunday school teacher. Impressive from the outside, chaos on the inside, built on Rome’s success and on fear.

So God’s people look toward Jerusalem and see the wrong king on the throne, toward Rome and see a pagan power controlling the nation, and toward heaven and see four hundred years of silence. Malachi was the last prophetic voice Israel heard.

Josh makes the wait felt. People get uncomfortable when someone leaves them on read for an hour, and some treat four hours as a welfare check. Four hundred years is roughly fifteen generations. Travel back four hundred years from 2026 and the United States does not exist. No electricity, no automobiles, no airplanes, no internet, no phone reporting every tragic event everywhere all at once.

documents.excerpt: Then one day Zechariah was serving as a priest and his name was selected by lot to enter the holy place and burn incense before God. Not another day in the office. A career opportunity of a lifetime.
excerpts: Then one day Zechariah was serving as a priest and his name was selected by lot to enter the holy place and burn incense before God. Not another day in the office. A career opportunity of a lifetime.

Josh puts numbers on it. Probably around 18,000 priests in Israel, 24 priestly divisions, so Zechariah’s division of Abijah may have held around 750. The Super Bowl of priesthood. Most priests would serve a lifetime and never be selected to play in the big game. Zechariah won the priestly Powerball.

He would enter the holy place alone. Outside, the people would pray. Inside, he would place incense on the altar and the smoke would rise, a visible representation of the prayers of God’s people ascending before him.
The tension he carried in: new heights in the priesthood, unanswered prayers in his personal life.

documents.excerpt: Josh refuses to give Zechariah a bad name. Yes, Zechariah struggled with unbelief, and that is not good. But who hasn’t? He was a faithful priest. Luke calls him righteous and blameless, and he is also an old man who has carried disappointment for a lot of years.
excerpts: Josh refuses to give Zechariah a bad name. Yes, Zechariah struggled with unbelief, and that is not good. But who hasn’t? He was a faithful priest. Luke calls him righteous and blameless, and he is also an old man who has carried disappointment for a lot of years.

When you have held disappointment that long, hope starts to feel risky. Opening up to the possibility of something better also opens you up to being hurt. So in that fear, people stop asking, stop believing, and stop hoping, because it is safer not to. Nothing happened before, so why would it happen now? That is where Zechariah is.
Josh’s reading: Zechariah believes God will do what he said he would. What Zechariah does not believe is that God will do it through his wife Elizabeth. That is where the issue is.

Surveying Luke 1, there are two songs, Mary’s and Zechariah’s, and two very different paths to them. There is the path that sings now, and there is the unbelief God must discipline until it sings. Which path are you on?

That is the journey of the day. Zechariah received the promise and lost his voice. Mary received the promise, believed the Lord, and found a song. Unbelief left a priest speechless. Faith taught the young woman to sing.
documents.title: Two songs, two paths — Just As He Promised

documents.excerpt: Some take their desires, attempt to convert them into divine promises, and then get angry with God when he fails to do the thing he never promised he would do.
excerpts: Some take their desires, attempt to convert them into divine promises, and then get angry with God when he fails to do the thing he never promised he would do.

God did not promise every Christian a spouse. Josh gets the frustration and hopes people meet that person, because marriage can be an amazing blessing. But that is not God’s path for everyone. Singleness has value: a single person can reach people with the gospel that a married person never could, at least not until the kids are raised. Ministering in some remote place would mean taking a family into harm’s way or leaving them.

He did not promise that every married couple would have a child. He did not promise that every sick person would receive immediate healing. He did not promise that every dream would come true if we just believe hard enough. He did not promise comfort, uninterrupted success, or complete freedom from suffering.

When you attempt to make your preferences into prophecy, you are sitting on a throne that only God sits on. Faith is not confidence that God will eventually do what you want him to do. Faith is confidence that God will accomplish everything he has actually promised in Christ.

Some walked in and all they can see is the army surrounding them. The medical diagnosis. The financial pressure. The conflict in the home. The child who is drifting. The marriage that feels cold. The grief that will not leave. The temptation that keeps lingering. The criticism. Everything that is wrong.

documents.excerpt: Josh loves what Elizabeth says to Mary. Blessed are you among women. Why, really, is Mary blessed? The word blessed is overused and wrongly used by Christians. We say we are blessed when the biopsy comes back negative, but we were blessed when we went in for it.
excerpts: Josh loves what Elizabeth says to Mary. Blessed are you among women. Why, really, is Mary blessed? The word blessed is overused and wrongly used by Christians. We say we are blessed when the biopsy comes back negative, but we were blessed when we went in for it.

Mary is not blessed because of her circumstances. She is young. She is pregnant before becoming Joseph’s wife. She has no way of rationally explaining her pregnancy. Her only explanation is that she is carrying the Messiah, which has its own social and cultural implications. She faces public shame and the possibility of losing Joseph. This will not be a run-of-the-mill pregnancy. One day, as a mother, she will kneel at the foot of the cross as her son pours out his blood to save sinners, in his early thirties.

Yet Elizabeth calls her blessed. Why? Because despite everything coming her way, what she knows and what she does not know, what once could only be witnessed in the holy place is now growing inside her. He is Immanuel. God with us.

Paul asks Timothy to come quickly: Demas, in love with this world, has deserted him for Thessalonica; Crescens has gone to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me.

excerpts: The church will hear from steadfast Luke for twelve weeks. Josh prays that by the end of the series some of that Luke character grows up in this place.

In Colossians Paul calls him our dear friend Luke the doctor. Educated, intelligent, observant, Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke and Acts—more New Testament words than any other author, even though Paul wrote more books.

Before he was a great writer he was a faithful man, a fellow worker. In Acts the narrator shifts from they to we: Luke was on the ship, on the road, in the city, waiting out the storm, not an ivory-tower embellisher of another man’s journeys.

Jesus came to seek and save the lost. He lived the righteous life we could not, went to the cross willingly, and laid down his life of his own accord. He could have called for divine backup, but he did not. He stood in the place of the guilty, and on the third day God raised that pierced body. More than five hundred saw him at one time. The risen Christ restored Peter and commissioned him to feed his sheep.
Forgiveness and eternal life are offered to everyone who turns from sin and trusts Jesus. The church is certain God sent his Son, Jesus accomplished salvation, the gift of God is eternal life, death will not have the final word, everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, and every knee will bow.

The defensive spirit instinctively builds a case. Context can matter, but a defensive spirit uses context to avoid confession; a broken spirit cares more about making things right than proving it was right.
The blaming spirit passes responsibility like a hot potato: Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent, and Saul blamed the people. David could have blamed Bathsheba, leadership loneliness, throne pressure, or supposedly unmet needs, but instead says, ’I have sinned.’
The minimizing spirit reduces guilt through ’everyone makes mistakes,’ comparison, or ’only once.’ Responsibility cannot be accepted while simultaneously being reduced.
documents.title: Wrong directions: defense, blame, and minimization — Crushed Joy

excerpts: Elijah states the principle: the sin one makes peace with today can become the sin that masters tomorrow; the useful question is where present compromises are leading.

Private choices form desires. Kept boundaries strengthen the next boundary, while moved boundaries make later movement easier; affairs begin with messages, hidden conversations, repeated looks, and welcomed attention.
Quoting John Owen, Elijah urges believers to be killing sin rather than accommodating, renaming, negotiating with, or keeping it publicly manageable.
James describes desire’s progression through temptation and conception to mature sin and death; therefore the church must evaluate not only a compromise’s small beginning but its end.

Application: identify the small compromise, moved boundary, dismissed conviction, or fed appetite; bring it to the Lord and to those harmed, trusting God’s promise to forgive and purify confessing sinners.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · July 27, 2026 · By Faith
documents.excerpt: Josh opens with a common objection to Christianity: its commands can look like an exhausting list of prohibitions and an impossible demand for perfection. His rapid examples include "Don’t have sex outside of marriage," "Don’t love money," "Love your enemies," "Love strangers," and "Honor marriage."
excerpts: Josh opens with a common objection to Christianity: its commands can look like an exhausting list of prohibitions and an impossible demand for perfection. His rapid examples include "Don’t have sex outside of marriage," "Don’t love money," "Love your enemies," "Love strangers," and "Honor marriage."
The gospel is not merely that Christ teaches better behavior; Christ gives new hearts so that forgiven sinners begin to love what he loves, finding joy and freedom in obedience.
God does not simply hand saved people a kingdom handbook: "He puts his spirit within them," gives them power, changes their desires, and enables a new life.
Josh says, "He writes his law on their hearts," so the order is grace and inward renewal before the commands that follow.

documents.excerpt: Kingdoms, presidents, elections, friends, churches, bodies, memories, and wealth change, but Jesus Christ remains the same forever.
excerpts: Kingdoms, presidents, elections, friends, churches, bodies, memories, and wealth change, but Jesus Christ remains the same forever.
The Jesus who sat by the fire and "forgave Peter for denying him still forgives today."
The Jesus who told the dying thief he would be "in paradise that day" still welcomes sinners, even as Josh notes that the thief had no time for baptism or a polished doctrinal statement.
The Jesus who appeared behind locked doors to "doubting Thomas" still turns doubt into belief.
The Jesus who "called Lazarus from the grave" still gives life to the dead.
His promise remains: "All whom the Father gives me will come to me and whoever comes to me I will never drive away." Because Jesus does not change, neither do his promises.

excerpts: Josh argues that prosperity teaching cannot survive Hebrews 11 because victory belongs both to those who live by faith and those who die by faith.
Victory over suffering occurs when God delivers, as with Daniel and the three Hebrews.
Victory through suffering occurs when God does not remove pain but glorifies himself within it, as in Job, Paul, and Stephen.
Faith can change circumstances, but it does not guarantee that God will do so.

documents.excerpt: Elijah thanks the Father for who he is and for the opportunity to participate in kingdom work.
excerpts: Elijah thanks the Father for who he is and for the opportunity to participate in kingdom work.
He prays for those exhausted by long days, heaven’s apparent silence, and weariness, asking that they find rest and strength in God.

Because Jesus has promised to return and make all things new, he asks that the church view the world not as pessimists but as “divine optimists,” trusting the enthroned King of kings and Lord of lords.
He entrusts seasons of suffering, doubt, success, and harvest to God’s plan and purpose, ending: “Help us to worship while we wait. It’s in your name. Amen.”

excerpts: Josh recalls attending a Jessica Simpson concert as a high-school freshman, entering an onstage singing contest despite not knowing her songs, winning the crowd’s approval, and receiving unusual backstage access.
After the other contestants leave, he meets Simpson’s family and is seated onstage, where she kisses and serenades him; he later jokes that she was a shadow of a better woman, Kristen.
The experience briefly transformed his social confidence, but the imposing security guard’s warning made clear that no one entered the protected area without authorization.
Josh uses the comic story to introduce the far more serious confidence Hebrews gives ordinary believers to enter God’s presence.

excerpts: Believers enter a place they could never claim for themselves because Jesus has unlocked it. Unlike an old covenant high priest who entered alone, Christ leaves the way open and is himself the door through whom people come to God.

Josh asks the church to remember the sentence, “Jesus unlocked the new and living way.” It is new because the old covenant is obsolete in its light, and living because Christ has an indestructible life and always lives to intercede.
When Christ’s flesh was torn and his life sacrificed, God tore the temple curtain. That event signified open access for all who believe.
Believers may therefore enter boldly rather than fearfully; Josh joins this confidence to the assurance that perfect love drives out fear and identifies Jesus as perfect love.

excerpts: Josh asks the Father for help building deep fellowship and community in a selfish, discontented world, praying for the Spirit to flood hearts and draw the congregation into one ecclesia—one assembly, purpose, and body.
He asks that the church move, speak, serve, and sing together, making Christ’s name greater than every brand, mission, and institutional name.
Pointing to the cross displayed above the church’s name on the building, he calls that placement a deliberate proclamation that Christ stands above the church’s brand, name, mission, and purpose.
The prayer ends by asking God to make service compelling again and to help the church stop like the Samaritan, meet needs, and change the way people see the church.

excerpts: Josh explores apparently risky biblical comparisons: Jesus’ arrival carries a thief’s surprise without a thief’s character, while shepherd, slave, father, king, and husband imagery each illuminates one aspect of God and leaves others in shadow.

Because no human word, picture, or experience fits God perfectly, hearers must ask what part of each comparison is intended and what part is not.
God’s condescension in using human language reflects the love that brought him down to humanity’s level.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 8, 2026 · By Faith
documents.excerpt: God renames Abram and Sarai, promises that Sarah will become the mother of nations, and says she will bear Abraham a son. Abraham falls facedown laughing at the thought that he could father a son at one hundred and Sarah could bear one at ninety.
excerpts: God renames Abram and Sarai, promises that Sarah will become the mother of nations, and says she will bear Abraham a son. Abraham falls facedown laughing at the thought that he could father a son at one hundred and Sarah could bear one at ninety.
Sarah later laughs too. Josh treats their ages as Scripture’s deliberate emphasis: however long people lived, this birth was still humanly impossible and therefore had to be an act of God.
He briefly applies Sarah’s response to husbands, warning that a husband’s example gives his wife cues that matter.

God renames Abram and Sarai, promises that Sarah will become the mother of nations, and says she will bear Abraham a son. Abraham falls facedown laughing at the thought that he could father a son at one hundred and Sarah could bear one at ninety.
Sarah later laughs too. Josh treats their ages as Scripture’s deliberate emphasis: however long people lived, this birth was still humanly impossible and therefore had to be an act of God.
He briefly applies Sarah’s response to husbands, warning that a husband’s example gives his wife cues that matter.

Stop counting the harvest and remain useful
Josh tells exhausted believers that obedience does not count only when outcomes can be measured or seen. God asks faithfulness in the field, not control of the harvest.
They may never know what prayers prevented or healed, what kindness softened, what consistency taught a child or spouse, or what one invitation, sermon, coffee, text, hug, conversation, pair of shoes, or act of integrity accomplished twenty years later.
The goal is not spectacular performance but consistent usefulness. Mature Christians let God decide where fruit falls and stay too busy abiding in Jesus to obsess over yield, trusting that God sees love, service, and perseverance.

The memory fits Next Gen Sunday: Christian faith is not generational slang that others wait to see disappear. It is shared and passed on like a relay baton because the difficult race carries eternal rewards.

The old message did not need a polished messenger. Steve had obeyed God’s call, stepped beyond his comfort, developed his gifts, and declared a Word that cannot fall short even when its speaker feels shaky.

The old office was neither self-appointed nor open to volunteers. God selected fallible men from Aaron’s family in Levi’s tribe, giving them real authority and responsibility among Israel.

excerpts: Steve reads Hebrews 5:3 and 8–10. Traditional priests needed sacrifices for their own sins as well as the people’s, while the Son learned obedience through suffering, became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey, and was designated high priest in Melchizedek’s order.
Sinful priests could offer only temporary help. Repeated animal sacrifices covered sin without finishing the work; Jesus did not merely bring a sacrifice but became the sacrifice and washed sin away.

Steve clarifies that being ‘made perfect’ does not imply that Jesus was formerly sinful. His already-perfect obedience was completed in action and suffering at the cross. Children’s promises to do chores illustrate the difference between verbal agreement and costly follow-through, down to taking out trash that spills coffee grounds and cleaning up after the dog.
Christ’s death and resurrection completed the work. His once-for-all, everlasting priesthood means mercy and grace do not expire and sacrifice need not be repeated.

Steve quotes Jesus’ final cry, ‘It is finished,’ then Hebrews 10:12: after offering one sacrifice for sins for all time, Jesus sat at God’s right hand. Standing Levitical priests could not rest because their work continued; Jesus’ seated posture declares payment complete.

excerpts: Beginning Hebrews 3:1, Josh pauses over ‘therefore’ and reaches back to the prior week: Jesus suffered temptation and is able to help the tempted, so believers should ask for that help more often.
Hebrews dignifies Christians as holy brothers and sisters who share a heavenly calling and commands them to fix their thoughts on Jesus, acknowledged together as apostle and high priest.

excerpts: Apostasy usually begins not with a dramatic farewell to Jesus but with one small thing becoming more important than him. documents.excerpt: After joking that he nearly left without preaching, Josh tells hearers with a “sword of the Spirit” to turn to Hebrews 2 and says its opening picture is meant to be seen whether or not someone considers himself a visual learner.
excerpts: After joking that he nearly left without preaching, Josh tells hearers with a “sword of the Spirit” to turn to Hebrews 2 and says its opening picture is meant to be seen whether or not someone considers himself a visual learner.

He recalls Hebrews 1:1: God spoke to the ancestors through the prophets in many times and ways. Even with the Old Testament’s pictures, types, shadows, and near-savior figures pointing toward Christ, the eternally significant message can still be ignored, dismissed, or forgotten.
Hebrews 2:1 therefore commands the church to pay the most careful attention to what it has heard so that it does not drift away.

excerpts: Returning to Hebrews 2:2–3a, Josh says “violation” or “transgression” concerns sins of commission, while “disobedience” suggests sins of omission. Sin includes both doing what God forbids and failing to do what God commands.
Avoiding robbery does not fulfill the command to love one’s neighbor, and refusing to curse an enemy is not the same as praying for that enemy. Omission can therefore be as troubling as commission.

A rapid church quiz illustrates the categories: David’s adultery with Bathsheba is commission; Jonah’s flight from Nineveh is active commission rooted in resistance to mercy; Adam’s passivity while Eve is deceived is omission; and Moses striking the rock instead of speaking to it is commission.

Grace does not eliminate the Lord’s discipline. Jesus’ warning that much is required from those given much leads Josh to summarize: commission does what God hates, omission fails to do what God loves, and Hebrews 2 says both are judged. Neglect is especially dangerous because it can destroy while a person feels safe.

excerpts: Josh says that if believers do not even know their gifts, he is failing them.
Josh compares physical birth certificates with the absence of a “new life certificate” listing spiritual gifts. Discovery requires action, and most believers likely possess several gifts.

He urges hearers to take the church’s available gifts assessment and then ask an elder or pastor for help interpreting and deploying the result. He names prophecy, service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leadership, mercy, wisdom, discernment, faith, healing, miracles, tongues, helps, and administration.

The participation numbers trouble him: only two of ten who begin the assessment finish, and only half of those find a use in the body. Even allowing other ways to discover gifts, Josh says that if the assessment were the only route, only forty people in the church would be using their gifts; the pattern pictures widespread drift.

The modern church drifts not only when people skip Sunday but when they refuse daily church life and participation. Families that do not teach children to value the body deprive others of God’s gifts. The Spirit gives, Scripture governs, and the church is built; gifts serve and strengthen salvation rather than distracting from it.

By Faith
God has spoken in his preeminent Son—will the hearer listen?
Josh welcomes the congregation to Hebrews and returns to the letter’s opening declaration that God has spoken in his Son.
Because Christ is preeminent, the unresolved question is not whether he speaks but whether the hearer will listen.
Josh prays, thanking God for his word and for the Father’s love of the Son. The recording ends while that prayer is still going.

documents.excerpt: Josh thinks creation is as disgusted with dead religion as Jesus is. Everything was made through him and for him.
excerpts: Josh thinks creation is as disgusted with dead religion as Jesus is. Everything was made through him and for him.

The Magi were led by the star to Jesus. When they stepped into Jerusalem—the city that should have known God—the light disappeared. After they heard the king, the star went ahead again until it stopped over the child.

The Lord was protecting the child from Herod, the new Pharaoh throwing babies in the river. When they left Jerusalem the light appeared again. Josh hears creation preaching light versus darkness: you can stand in the most religious place on earth and still be in the dark. The star led them out of a city of darkness into Jesus’ presence.

Nothing changes until the light of Christ shines. We do not come into the light because we figured it out. The light came for us. When he shines, what used to own you loses its grip. Josh quotes the hymn: the things of earth grow strangely dim in the light of his glory and grace.
The greatest evidence of being born again is not a prayer, an aisle, or a thing in a place. It is that you no longer love the darkness you once lived in. That is the fruit.

documents.excerpt: Jesus says those who live by the truth—the doer of the truth. Josh says the modern church hates this: not those who listen every week, keep a podcast, agree, or give a loud amen, but those who do the truth.
excerpts: Jesus says those who live by the truth—the doer of the truth. Josh says the modern church hates this: not those who listen every week, keep a podcast, agree, or give a loud amen, but those who do the truth.
Truth here is the opposite of evil. The evildoer acts from falsehood; the Christian acts according to the truth.

The sinner believes the lie that God will not punish, that there is no God, no judgment, no hell, and lives like it. The Christian believes God will punish those who reject his Son and reward those who earnestly seek him, that judgment leads into eternity, that hell and heaven are actual places—and more important than streets of gold is the presence of God himself. They live as if those things were true.

documents.excerpt: In Matthew 5 Jesus describes the flock: one flock, one shepherd; those who love him and keep his commandments. You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden.
excerpts: In Matthew 5 Jesus describes the flock: one flock, one shepherd; those who love him and keep his commandments. You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden.
Josh sees a problem: many claiming to be sheep have sharp teeth. They have traded the city on a hill for king of the hill—the childhood snow-pile game of shoving others down.

The church stops trying to shine his light and tries to win the fight, the argument, the comparison. When that game takes hold, the lamp goes under a bowl. A city on a hill invites people up; king of the hill shoves people down.
Those who exalt themselves will be humbled; those who humble themselves will be exalted. The city Jesus names shines so they see God. King of the hill wants to be the only one standing.
Jesus told the Pharisees they could look bright and clean outside and be filled with darkness inside. The church is not called to compete with the world. We are the light of the world.

documents.excerpt: Stop pointing at everyone else’s darkness. Look inward: where are you more concerned about being right than pursuing righteousness, comparing instead of confessing, performing instead of repenting?
excerpts: Stop pointing at everyone else’s darkness. Look inward: where are you more concerned about being right than pursuing righteousness, comparing instead of confessing, performing instead of repenting?
There is only one reason a person rejects Christ: they love their sin more. They do not want to come near because he shines light on sin, and sinners love sin.

It is not that the gospel is complicated, that they have not heard enough sermons, that they cannot find a church that fits, or that the teaching is bad. Sinners hate the light and prefer evil. They hate the truth, the church, Scripture, and Christians.

Jesus tells the disciples the world cannot hate them, but it hates him because he testifies that its works are evil. Believers are Christ’s ambassadors, so that burden of being hated fell first on the apostles and now on the church.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 27, 2026 · Born Again
documents.excerpt: The difference is not perfection; it is direction. One runs from the light; the other runs to it.
excerpts: The difference is not perfection; it is direction. One runs from the light; the other runs to it.
Josh says people are not here for the show or the comfort. Most are here because the light is on. When it comes on, there are no shadows, hiding places, or pretending—only authenticity.

If you have something to protect, this is a bad place to be. The light of Christ does not negotiate with darkness. If you are his, his light will reveal it and reject it. That is why some leave: not because the light is untrue, but because it is too bright. They want shade.

If you belong to him, you love the light. You start to see what is happening in you is not you—that is God. That is where assurance, confidence, and joy come from: I am not who I was; I did not do this. We come not to hide but to be seen by him and by others, fully known and fully loved.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 20, 2026 · Born Again
documents.excerpt: Two reasons the verse is misunderstood: lazy definitions, and lack of exposure to the full counsel of God.
excerpts: Two reasons the verse is misunderstood: lazy definitions, and lack of exposure to the full counsel of God.

Any sermon worth hearing must present two things: since God is love, present him as love; since Jesus is the Lamb of God, present him as the atonement for sin. Parting from those does not make a minister creative; it makes him foolish.
The Spirit directs, but he will not send you down a path separate from the core doctrines of the faith.

Josh reads John’s epistle: whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. God showed his love by sending his Son that we might live through him. This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 20, 2026 · Born Again
documents.excerpt: He had been trained by pop songs and sitcoms. What culture calls love is shallow, hollow, fragile—love you cannot feel safe in. Put biblical love next to it and the culture does not admire it; it criticizes it as unhealthy, unstable, controlling, too much.
excerpts: He had been trained by pop songs and sitcoms. What culture calls love is shallow, hollow, fragile—love you cannot feel safe in. Put biblical love next to it and the culture does not admire it; it criticizes it as unhealthy, unstable, controlling, too much.

English is awful here. Love has become purely emotional: you fall in and fall out. If it rises and falls on how happy someone makes you, you are not loving them. You are loving yourself, using them to do it.
He is not above this. There have been seasons with no peace in the home, because if love is built on feelings, peace is always fleeting.

Worldly love has expectations of the other; biblical love has expectations of self. If it is the other person’s job to keep you happy, they cannot be themselves, so we pull an Adam and Eve and hide. In marriage you cannot hide. Weaknesses show, love is tested, we defend and blame, and the marriage becomes a storm instead of a shelter.

documents.excerpt: The Hebrews had a word beyond emotion: hesed—loving-kindness, steadfast love based on promises, not feelings. A hesed marriage says, I’ve seen the worst of you, and I’m not going anywhere. Then you can be fully known. When emotion is gone, commitment remains.
excerpts: The Hebrews had a word beyond emotion: hesed—loving-kindness, steadfast love based on promises, not feelings. A hesed marriage says, I’ve seen the worst of you, and I’m not going anywhere. Then you can be fully known. When emotion is gone, commitment remains.

He credits God for teaching Kristen to love like that, and her obedience for their joy. She could have left. He never cheated in the flesh, but the Sermon on the Mount made clear that what he was doing was unfaithfulness in the heart. She loved him at his worst. He witnessed the undeserved initiating love of God in his bride.

The church uses the same word for barbecue and a spouse. Kristen used to smile when she was annoying him and say, Love me. One time he answered, I’m committed to you. Worldly love prioritizes romance; biblical love prioritizes promises.
He is giving this view into the marriage so that when they talk about God’s love it will seem as awesome as it actually is.

excerpts: If there is no hunger for righteousness, no thirst to look more like Jesus, no growing discomfort with the world’s empty promises, you do not believe in the way Scripture describes belief. God defines belief through his Word.

John 3:16 does not only say God loved the world; it tells who receives that love: whoever believes. Whoever is wide open, but it is not careless universalism. It includes anyone who believes and excludes anyone who refuses.
You can wreck your life with sin; if you believe in Jesus, you’re in. You can be moral, polished, churchgoing; if you will not trust Christ, you’re out. The line is faith in Christ.

Whoever covers all kinds of people and various levels of faith—strong, weak, mustard-seed small. Jesus says he sees it and it is enough; together we can move mountains. Come, and he will never cast you out. That is sovereign saving hesed. Are you in the whoever? The promise stays open until the trumpet blows.

documents.excerpt: John 3:16 says God loved you enough to give his Son; Romans 8 says he loves you enough to put his Spirit in you. The question is not only do you believe that, but is there life in you that proves it. When the Spirit moves in, a war breaks out.
excerpts: John 3:16 says God loved you enough to give his Son; Romans 8 says he loves you enough to put his Spirit in you. The question is not only do you believe that, but is there life in you that proves it. When the Spirit moves in, a war breaks out.

Spurgeon said the first week he came to Christ the new life had to fight for its existence. Then he heard a sermon from Romans 7—O wretched man that I am—where the preacher said Paul was not a Christian when he cried that. Josh calls that bogus. Apart from grace Paul would still be chucking rocks. The Spirit is moving in Romans 7.

If someone says struggle means you are not a Christian, tell them that is how you know you are. We used to follow sin; now there is tension, conviction, a war. Dead people do not fight. The love of God does not produce perfect people; it produces new people who fight, repent, and get back up.

You know this love is yours not because life is flawless, but because your heart is no longer at peace with sin. The cross proves God is for you; the war in you proves God is in you. Grab the armor of God and sprint in with songs of praise.

excerpts: Days earlier Jesus began north from Judea to Galilee. The direct route was through Samaria; Jews went around. Jesus went straight through, not lost, not convenient—pursuing this woman, crossing every boundary.

The scene has happened before. Jacob meets Rachel at a well in Genesis 29, sees her, loves her. In John 4 the greater Jacob sits at a well again. Rachel was beautiful, honored, desired. This woman comes ashamed, rejected, discarded.

She asks if he is greater than their father Jacob. Josh hears the real question: Jacob loved Rachel because she was beautiful; would he ever love a woman like me? That is our question: can God love someone like me?

excerpts: One of a dozen parallels Josh sees between John and Revelation: those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans—repent, or I will fight them with the sword of my mouth.
Nicodemus and Nicolaitan are virtually identical in Greek: the people’s victory. If Nicodemus represents the Pharisees, note the Lord’s hatred of that teaching.

The born-again Christian’s anthem is victory to God even at my expense. Pharisees and Nicolaitans are about the victory of the people. Two extremes: Pharisees legalism, adding rules, making grace too expensive; Nicolaitans license, ignoring rules, making grace too cheap. One says do more so God will accept you; the other says do whatever you want because he already has. Both wrong. The gospel: you are accepted in Christ; now walk by the Spirit.

Pharisees stand outside the temple and say clean yourself before you come in. Nicolaitans stand inside and say it does not matter how you live once you are in. One locks the door from outside; the other defiles the house from within. Christ, the true temple, does neither: he cleanses you to bring you in, then dwells in you to make you holy.

Matthew 26 is not only leading to the cross. It is interpreting the cross. Three scenes, each with coordinates and conflict: Bethany, worship versus waste; the upper room, faithfulness versus betrayal; Gethsemane, submission versus resistance.

Jesus seals a better covenant with the Son’s blood, not an animal. Before the cross death was the end; because of it, death is a doorway. Slow down at the table. Hold that promise of drinking it new in the Father’s kingdom.

Sixty-six books, forty-plus authors, three continents, three languages, about 1,500 years, yet one story: garden gone wrong, a cross, a garden made right. Tolkien, Rowling, Lewis display patterns first in God’s Word. You can even witness God in a non-believer’s creativity.

The transfiguration teaches that Jesus is glorified when we deny ourselves, take up the cross, and follow. The world says save yourself; the Christian says surrender. Cross before crown. That is why they must not tell yet: no glory apart from the cross. A temple on the mountain next week is not the way. Look at 70 AD.

Coming down, they still puzzle over Elijah and Malachi 4. Some think Elijah will be a Revelation 11 witness; others think John the Baptist fulfilled it. Either way, Jesus was promised by Moses and preceded by Elijah. He fulfills law and prophets.

Head belief in Jesus without fruit. He did not ask forgiveness. He apologized, told God he deserved hell, and asked God to help his parents and sister past his murder. God had other plans. Examine hearts. Repent hidden sin. Release unforgiveness. Recommit, or come to faith now. You are not promised tomorrow. Living sacrifice, not conforming to the world. Examine yourselves before communion. 1 Corinthians 11. The ground is level at the cross. All have sinned. George prays for humility, repentance, reverence, eyes for the lost as image-bearers, and that everything would honor Jesus’ name. Amen.

excerpts: 1 Peter 4: you spent enough time doing what pagans choose. They are surprised you do not join reckless living and heap abuse on you. They will give account to him who judges the living and the dead.

The church has failed to be honest about how hard holiness is. As the gospel wins souls it also exposes an anti-God segment Scripture calls the world: not a passive you-do-you force but an active recruiter led by Satan, seeking to devour.
1 John 2: do not love the world. Cravings, lust of the eyes, boasting come from the world. The world passes away; whoever does the will of God lives forever.

Last week Peter called us aliens. Being different is hard. Josh and Kristen watched a Netflix comedy about an alien trying to fit in, watching Grey’s Anatomy to learn doctoring, missing sarcasm. Resident aliens struggle in a fallen world. Alien speaks to future hope. Another title speaks more to holiness: stone.

documents.excerpt: 1 Peter 1:13: therefore, with minds alert and fully sober. Josh says the ESV is better here: preparing your minds for action. Greek: girding up your loins. Robes hiked into the belt. Modern: roll up sleeves, lace boots, get your head in the game.
excerpts: 1 Peter 1:13: therefore, with minds alert and fully sober. Josh says the ESV is better here: preparing your minds for action. Greek: girding up your loins. Robes hiked into the belt. Modern: roll up sleeves, lace boots, get your head in the game.

Fully sober is not only about drink. Paul: take thoughts captive. Peter: sober-minded. Josh’s paraphrase: do not be ignorant of your surroundings. Observe everything, admire nothing. Christ’s return should make us cool and collected. Many get lost in end-times studies and lose their cool. Peter’s eschatology: the end of all things is near; therefore be alert and sober so you may pray. Above all, even above eschatology, love each other deeply, because love covers a multitude of sins.

Sober also means knowing Satan prowls like a roaring lion. Resist, stand firm; fellow believers worldwide suffer the same. Satan loves to kill alertness with boredom. Lazy Christians have no outward-facing ministry, only an echo chamber. Chirp, little dirt under the nails.

True salvation results in obedience, not perfection, but a progressive bend.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 23, 2026 · Forging Faith
documents.excerpt: Today they start a two-week miniseries called Forging Faith. The hardest part will be not making it longer. They will probably come back to 1 Peter. For now they dip a toe into chapter 1: faith can be purified through trials. Christians do not just survive. They thrive. Faith can grow stronger than imagined. The visual is the forge: roar, smoke, heat, sparks, metal struck again and again. Fire reveals impurities. The hammer shapes. Repeated blows strengthen. Steel is not forged in comfort, and neither is faith.

excerpts: Josh loves Peter: a normal guy with a loud mouth. Paul was a Pharisee of Pharisees; Peter is a fisherman with dirty nails who never went to college. Favorite biblical authors: Peter and John.

Acts 4: when they saw the courage of Peter and John and realized they were unschooled ordinary men, they were astonished and took note they had been with Jesus. Unschooled is not unintelligent. Jobs, Gates, Zuckerberg, Jim Carrey. Education matters, but it is one metric. If Josh went to seminary now he would probably be more frustrated than blessed; God let him learn on the job. Peter illustrates 1 Corinthians 1: not many wise, influential, or noble; God chose the foolish to shame the wise so no one boasts. Boast in the Lord.

excerpts: Peter was married; children unknown. Owner-operator of a fishing business with Andrew, who worked with John the Baptist, Jesus’ cousin, preparing the way. Handpicked as apostle. Three years of meals, travel. If he had questions in Joshua he could just ask Jesus. Hard to need seminary after the Master’s feet.

Eyewitness to the healing ministry, and he could ask the meaning later. Imagine Jesus explaining Isaiah 53, then displaying it. Matthew: evening, demon-possessed brought, he drove out spirits and healed all the sick to fulfill Isaiah: he took up our infirmities. He heals because he is the suffering servant. Shriveled hand healed because a nail-pierced hand leads to healing. Healing ministry points to Calvary.

Inner circle: Peter, James, John. Transfiguration: greater Moses, new covenant, Moses and Elijah from heaven. Peter met Moses and Elijah while hanging out with Jesus. He was there for betrayal, arrest, trial, crucifixion, resurrection, ascension. The angel tells Mary: go tell Peter. Pentecost sermon, reversal of Babel, 3,000 saved. He gave his life as a pastor; his words still preach.

documents.excerpt: Chapter 5: writing from Babylon. They just finished Ezekiel; Josh did not see Peter in ancient Babylon. A town named Babylon in Egypt has no evidence Peter went. Timing: early to mid-60s, before Nero’s persecution. Early Christians spoke in code. Rome is Babylon in Revelation 17 and 18: temple-destroying kingdoms. Paul the missionary, Peter the pastor after him. First letter about a year before Paul’s martyrdom; Peter soon laid down his life.

Paul the missionary, Peter the pastor after him. First letter about a year before Paul’s martyrdom; Peter soon laid down his life.

Fiery trials are something most of us know nothing about. Some emperors dipped political prisoners in oil, impaled them, set them on fire. Genocide was part of the Roman system. Peter pastors a church that probably smelled burning bodies and wondered who was next. Think twice about raising complaints in church. He mentions suffering at least fifteen times with eight Greek words. They suffered for wanting to live godly lives. Keep being good witnesses, especially to persecutors. Suffering leads to glory.

documents.excerpt: 1 Peter 3: do not repay evil with evil; repay with blessing so you may inherit a blessing. Suffering is the path to glory. Why do bad things happen to good people? Christians who fire back no one is good make Josh cringe. True, only God is good, but that does not declare the gospel. Stop invalidating a question Scripture validates. Read Job. Read the Psalms: how long, Lord? Hear Jesus on Golgotha: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
excerpts: 1 Peter 3: do not repay evil with evil; repay with blessing so you may inherit a blessing. Suffering is the path to glory. Why do bad things happen to good people? Christians who fire back no one is good make Josh cringe. True, only God is good, but that does not declare the gospel. Stop invalidating a question Scripture validates. Read Job. Read the Psalms: how long, Lord? Hear Jesus on Golgotha: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

Suffering does not prove who God is. It proves what the world is. Ripple of Genesis 3. We live in the rundown neighborhood outside Eden. The gospel’s radical claim: God entered the suffering. He sent his only begotten Son, the only truly innocent one, who suffered in our place to save sinners. Substitution. Josh cannot explain why some things happen. He knows God is with us, justice will be done, death will be destroyed. The story will have pain. It will not end in pain.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 23, 2026 · Forging Faith
documents.excerpt: Two: when you know who loves you. Before the world, God knew we would rebel and prepared a plan to redeem us. He is not the author of evil. He made us knowing we would, then took on flesh as the suffering servant, died, and could not be contained in a grave. The invitation: join me in suffering like a good soldier. God does not know how to fail. Keep your eyes on Jesus. The crown of life awaits those who endure.
excerpts: Two: when you know who loves you. Before the world, God knew we would rebel and prepared a plan to redeem us. He is not the author of evil. He made us knowing we would, then took on flesh as the suffering servant, died, and could not be contained in a grave. The invitation: join me in suffering like a good soldier. God does not know how to fail. Keep your eyes on Jesus. The crown of life awaits those who endure.

Three: when we meditate on our future. Three of the most amazing verses: new birth, living hope, imperishable inheritance, shielded until the last time. Peter erupts in praise at mercy. Religion says look how good we are; the gospel says look how evil I am, but God has been merciful. You cannot understand the gospel until you realize the greatest injustice is your sin against a holy God. Romans 9: Jacob I loved, Esau I hated. Mercy on whom I have mercy. It does not depend on human desire or effort. Mercy piled on mercy. After Easter they will discuss regeneration.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 23, 2026 · Forging Faith
documents.excerpt: Four: when hope is all that remains. Hope says it will be worth it; present affliction is weightless next to eternal glory. Viktor Frankl in Auschwitz: fight and become the monster; give up and die with hope; cling to this-world restoration and collapse when family and career are gone. Those who endured anchored hope beyond this world. Trials do not just hurt us. They reveal us. Many put hope in better instead of heaven. Better waits and strives. Heaven is already chosen, already with the Lord, treasure not here, already united to Christ. The world says live your best life now. The gospel says you have not seen anything yet.

Heaven is already chosen, already with the Lord, treasure not here, already united to Christ. The world says live your best life now. The gospel says you have not seen anything yet.

Five: when we know he guards us. The power of God guards us, not our strength. Independence Day: the little ones got shields too. Until we see Jesus face to face. Ephesians: sealed with the Spirit, deposit guaranteeing inheritance. Hard to focus on bumps when you are headed home. 2 Corinthians 4: treasure in jars of clay, hard pressed but not crushed, light momentary troubles achieving eternal glory, eyes on what is unseen.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 23, 2026 · Forging Faith
documents.excerpt: Six: as he prepares us for glory. Rejoice though you suffer grief so faith, worth more than gold, may prove genuine. Welcome to the Jesus way, where joy and grief unite as the song of the redeemed. After his sister died at 39, church was the last place he wanted to be. Family at the altar. Weeping and smiling, singing, a mess, confident and crushed. An eastern goldsmith keeps metal in the furnace until he sees his face in it. The Lord keeps us until we reflect Jesus. Stop staring at the trial. Look at the promises.
excerpts: Six: as he prepares us for glory. Rejoice though you suffer grief so faith, worth more than gold, may prove genuine. Welcome to the Jesus way, where joy and grief unite as the song of the redeemed. After his sister died at 39, church was the last place he wanted to be. Family at the altar. Weeping and smiling, singing, a mess, confident and crushed. An eastern goldsmith keeps metal in the furnace until he sees his face in it. The Lord keeps us until we reflect Jesus. Stop staring at the trial. Look at the promises.

Seven: in the fire. Job, with God’s approval: he knows the way that I take; when he has tested me I will come forth as gold. Oldest book in Scripture talking Peter’s language. Born for glory, inheritance locked, guarded, purified. We will be ready. Do not settle into wait and see.

Eight: present enjoyment of glory. Though you have not seen him you love him. Three ways first-century believers enjoyed glory now: love Jesus, trust Jesus, rejoice in Jesus. Unlike Thomas we cannot see the wounds and say my Lord and my God. Since the ascension the Spirit has poured God’s love into our hearts. If you want to suffer well, learn to sing. If you love yourself more than Jesus, the fire will burn you alive. If you love him more, it purifies. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. Joy is rooted in Christ, not in smiling at circumstances. Abraham learned on the mountain. The three Hebrews learned in the furnace. Paul learned sufficient grace with a thorn. Inexpressible joy: words fail.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 23, 2026 · Forging Faith
documents.excerpt: You are being forged for more than escape. Forged for re-entry. Peter does not tell them how to get out. He reminds them who they are: chosen, born again, kept, guarded, heirs, refined. Unspeakable joy now, not someday. The fire is not transporting you to heaven. It is transforming you with heaven. Coming out shining. Black velvet for the jewel of grace.
excerpts: You are being forged for more than escape. Forged for re-entry. Peter does not tell them how to get out. He reminds them who they are: chosen, born again, kept, guarded, heirs, refined. Unspeakable joy now, not someday. The fire is not transporting you to heaven. It is transforming you with heaven. Coming out shining. Black velvet for the jewel of grace.

When you forgive in suffering, that is a glimpse of heaven. When you rejoice despite loss, heaven. When you love an unseen Christ with unashamed obedience, heaven coming down. The world expects bitterness, fear, collapse. Trials producing worship, peace, kindness do not belong to this world. Inheritance imperishable. Angels long to look into what you have. Stop living like you are barely hanging on.

Spurgeon: little faith will take your soul to heaven, but great faith will bring heaven to your soul. Not just rescued, refined. One day Christ will be revealed. Meanwhile he intends to reveal himself through ambassadors, children, co-heirs. If called to suffer, suffer like Jesus. If called to die, die like Jesus. If called to live, live like Jesus. Amen.

Prayer: hard to comprehend that angels long to look into what I see. Thank you for taking on flesh, living the life I could not, dying the death I deserve, walking out of the grave. I cannot see you, but I love you, trust you, and wait for you.

documents.excerpt: Josh loves singing with them. He is a better husband because of Jesus. Addiction from 12 to 32; baptized at nine, rebellious at 12, faithful late 20s. Could fall any moment. Eyes on Jesus. Asks for strength, patience, rest; he never left even in rebellion. Wants a postcard; God already breathed out a letter. Word fills, directs, reminds, awakens, calms. Crazy Christians, but he has to be near them. Outpouring: serve, sing, tell someone Jesus loves them.
excerpts: Josh loves singing with them. He is a better husband because of Jesus. Addiction from 12 to 32; baptized at nine, rebellious at 12, faithful late 20s. Could fall any moment. Eyes on Jesus. Asks for strength, patience, rest; he never left even in rebellion. Wants a postcard; God already breathed out a letter. Word fills, directs, reminds, awakens, calms. Crazy Christians, but he has to be near them. Outpouring: serve, sing, tell someone Jesus loves them.

Church is not a chore. If it feels like one, consider whether you have received what you say. Mercy does not give what we deserve; grace gives more. Forgiveness, adoption, peace, eternal life, living hope, Spirit. Nobody guilt-trips a cancer survivor to their party. Fast-food churches every half hour so you can keep idols. This is the Lord’s Day, the first day, every Sunday Easter. Inspect the empty tomb together. Tell the coach Sundays are out. Less than one percent go pro. Do not make room for him; save him a seat.

Perseverance of the saints. Storms cannot take them off the rock. Names written with a Sharpie. John 10: no one snatches them. When you fall you slip from one hand to another. Romans 5: while we were sinners. People who walked away: they went out because they were not of us. Judas never loved Jesus; Peter restored by the fire, Judas by temple religion. Confess Jesus is Lord and believe he was raised: you are his. Grief over sin is evidence. Spend less time on leavers, more praising the one who will not let go.

documents.excerpt: Someone told him he was not saved because he does not think the rapture is biblical. Junior-high Left Behind. The Bible never describes a secret separate coming. One visible climactic event. Matthew 24 this generation: not talking past the disciples to baby boomers. Flee to the mountains, pregnant women—destruction of the temple; Christians were in the mountains. 1 Thessalonians 4 loud command; how watch the dead rise if secretly raptured? 2 Thessalonians 2 man of sin. Christians do not escape; they rise to greet the King. No two-stage return from the first century to the 1800s. Do not call a believer a heretic for thinking the church goes through tribulation. In this world you will have trouble. Paul stoned. Path to glory is suffering. Last trumpet at the end.
