documents.excerpt: Gideon asks God to put dew only on a wool fleece with the ground dry, and God does it; he wrings out a bowlful of water. Then, “Don’t be angry with me,” an important line (why would he be angry, Gideon?), he asks for the reverse: dry fleece, wet ground. Talk about dragging your feet. That night God does it.
excerpts: Gideon asks God to put dew only on a wool fleece with the ground dry, and God does it; he wrings out a bowlful of water. Then, “Don’t be angry with me,” an important line (why would he be angry, Gideon?), he asks for the reverse: dry fleece, wet ground. Talk about dragging your feet. That night God does it.

We’ve modernized the fleece test. Josh has watched people move their families across the country because of one, putting conditions on God in their pride: if I get a text from this person at this time, we’re moving; if the weather changes, I’ll break up with him. Stop asking for signs and start reading his word. Are you equally yoked or not? You don’t need the weather to tell you.

Gideon’s fleece was a sign of distrust, not a model for determining God’s will; it reveals unbelief, not faith. We have it not so you put a fleece on your doorstep this afternoon, but to see how gracious God is: patient, not angry, stooping down to reassure his trembling servant, “I am here with you.”

Considering God’s holiness, one truth keeps coming to him: you are so much worse than you think you are. No effort can fix your position before Almighty God. He is holy; you are not; his perfect justice demands punishment.

But the gospel says Jesus, fully God and fully man, lived the life we couldn’t, died the death we deserve, and rose again in victory. The Creator’s message is simple: repent and believe; turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ.

If you know deep in your bones he is calling you, you have just experienced God’s most marvelous wonder, the miracle of repentance happening in hearts right now, which floods your life with forgiveness, shalom, and eternal life. It isn’t the end of the journey but the beginning of something new. It won’t be easy, but no matter where life takes you, he will be with you to the very end.

excerpts: Josh prays that he cannot get over the picture of God sitting and waiting while Gideon prepares an offering in the kitchen, a waiting God and patient Savior, and that it brings him peace.

He prays that anyone putting off following Jesus would see that picture, stop dragging their feet, and run to him to experience mercy, grace, and the greatest wonder the world has seen: that God gave his Son to save sinners. God is waiting because he desires that no one should perish, and Josh prays that everyone from a 10-year-old to an 80-year-old would gather around the promise of eternal life through him, the way, the truth, and the life.

documents.excerpt: In Josh’s opinion, the seeker-friendly movement is the greatest widespread church tragedy in modern Christianity. In the 80s and 90s influential leaders decided the church should be designed and tailored for the unbeliever: “We want to be a church where the unchurched want to be.” It sounds great and catchy.
excerpts: In Josh’s opinion, the seeker-friendly movement is the greatest widespread church tragedy in modern Christianity. In the 80s and 90s influential leaders decided the church should be designed and tailored for the unbeliever: “We want to be a church where the unchurched want to be.” It sounds great and catchy.

But unchurched people at least respect believers with convictions. Ditching values Christians have held for thousands of years in the name of tolerance makes you a lot of things, but his church isn’t one of them.
Church is for the believer: believers come, hear, receive an education in the gospel, then preach it in the streets, and those who hear come join the church. That is how it has always worked.

If you aren’t a believer, you are welcome; you drink the same coffee, and we pray you encounter the risen Christ. But we will never tailor our services to make you comfortable. That doesn’t make us rude; it makes us people of conviction. Our services are built to bring glory to God.

documents.excerpt: Praise God, Judges is a hopeful book, even if it doesn’t look like it on the surface: it teaches that human failure will never stop God’s plans.
excerpts: Praise God, Judges is a hopeful book, even if it doesn’t look like it on the surface: it teaches that human failure will never stop God’s plans.

The historian Josephus says Jabin had an infantry of 300,000, a cavalry of 10,000, and over 3,000 chariots; he was locked and loaded. Israel had no army; they’d be lucky to gather a few farmers on a Saturday with sticks and ox goads. But as last week showed, God doesn’t need an army, just a few good men, or in today’s text, a couple of women.

Judges reminds every believer that God hears the cries of his people. Even when we sin, God is still merciful; when you cry out, he will hear, act, and deliver you in his time and for his purpose. So we need to cry out like David, not because of our circumstances, but because something needs to happen in here: “Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.”

excerpts: Look at how God responds to the cries of his people: Deborah, a prophet, the wife of Lapidoth, was leading Israel and held court under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel, where the Israelites came to have their disputes decided.

Her name means honeybee: she will sting the enemy but is a sweet treat for the people of God. God raising up Deborah was an act of grace but also a slap in the face, because the men were passive. Josh doesn’t want to hear a passive man’s opinion on complementarian views. Israel was a male-dominated society that wanted strong male leadership, and he points to Isaiah 3: “Youths oppress my people, women rule over them.” Putting a woman judge over them was God treating them like little children, which is how they were acting.

She is the celebrity of the story, and many modern Christians would rewrite it as “Lapidoth, Deborah’s husband,” but it literally reads that Deborah is a woman of Lapidoth. excerpts: Josh loves that verse 4 calls Deborah the wife of Lapidoth. She is the celebrity of the story, and many modern Christians would rewrite it as “Lapidoth, Deborah’s husband,” but it literally reads that Deborah is a woman of Lapidoth. Feminists everywhere are convulsing, but Josh calls it healthy and biblical: she was proud to be her husband’s wife and didn’t need to rise above her position in the home.

In Ephesians 5 husbands are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the church, and wives to respect their husbands. Deborah is extremely talented, smart, and well recognized, but doesn’t let her status in the community confuse her status in the home.

Some women are far more gifted than their husbands (“Don’t look at him right now. It’ll make it awkward.”). You may find great success in your career, but don’t let it distract you from your duties in the home; you are called to love and respect your husband and give yourself to the home’s needs and priorities.

Some try to use Deborah to advance a feminist agenda, but Josh says they don’t have a leg to stand on. Deborah was gifted by God, as women can be just like men, and being gifted, she still maintained respect for her husband.

excerpts: Before ministry, around 2006 or 2007, Josh lived with his dad, who had just planted the church in Anthem School, while going to GCC. He was a punk: bitter, rebellious, angry, a womanizer, addicted to nicotine and pornography. He knew that parable from Jesus all too well; he knew how to clean things up and look acceptable, but he had never trusted Jesus or experienced the miracle of repentance.

He was opinionated about everything, especially his dad’s hiring choices in youth ministry. His dad always fired back with a line he’d stored up: “Well, I know the perfect guy for the job, but he’s not willing.” He meant Josh, who answered with a word of eternal torment followed by no.

Josh should have said yes. That summer, as an intern taking students to CIY in Colorado, on day three his heart was opened by the Lord to ministry through prayer. He came home with a massive calling, ready to love people and baptize them, and the job was gone. For a while he served that ministry as a volunteer when he knew the Lord wanted him to lead.

Before ministry, around 2006 or 2007, Josh lived with his dad, who had just planted the church in Anthem School, while going to GCC. He was a punk: bitter, rebellious, angry, a womanizer, addicted to nicotine and pornography. He knew that parable from Jesus all too well; he knew how to clean things up and look acceptable, but he had never trusted Jesus or experienced the miracle of repentance.
He was opinionated about everything, especially his dad’s hiring choices in youth ministry. His dad always fired back with a line he’d stored up: “Well, I know the perfect guy for the job, but he’s not willing.” He meant Josh, who answered with a word of eternal torment followed by no.
Josh should have said yes. That summer, as an intern taking students to CIY in Colorado, on day three his heart was opened by the Lord to ministry through prayer. In verse 18 Jael goes out to meet him: “Come, my lord, come right in. Don’t be afraid.” She covers him with a blanket, and he thinks he has survived. excerpts: Sisera flees to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the double agent, since Heber’s family had an alliance with Jabin. In verse 18 Jael goes out to meet him: “Come, my lord, come right in. Don’t be afraid.” She covers him with a blanket, and he thinks he has survived. In that culture no one but her husband would enter a wife’s tent, but she rolls out the red carpet, or does she?

He asks for water and she gives him milk. Josh jokes about craving lukewarm, fermented, chunky goat’s milk after a hot day. Church pop quiz: what does a baby do after milk? Sleep; milk has tryptophan, which the body uses to produce melatonin.

Before he sleeps, Sisera tells her to stand in the doorway and say no if anyone asks whether a man is inside. That is when Josh thinks a light bulb goes off for Jael: married to a double agent, she knows the game. Sisera fleeing means Israel won and the Canaanites lost power; protecting him would put her in trouble, and his pursuers won’t stop. Sisera falls asleep thinking he is in good hands, not knowing Deborah said God promised a woman would take his life.

excerpts: Someone is always offended, morally outraged that Jael showed hospitality, broke her promise to guard the door, and killed a defenseless man in cold blood. Josh says calm down. First, no one in that day would walk into another man’s wife’s tent, so she had every reason to believe she was in danger and that Sisera might wake and want his way with her.

And Deborah wrote a poem about her: “Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women.” Some are screaming injustice while Deborah is singing her praise, so we should wrestle with it.

You are a Christian who has sat under the teaching of Jesus and the apostles; Jael has not. Remember the 20 years Jabin and Sisera brutally mistreated God’s people. If Sisera had recovered and the Canaanites won, hundreds of Jewish girls would have been captured and raped; Deborah’s poem speaks of dividing the spoils, a woman or two for each man. Jael not only helped deliver Israel but protected those women from unspeakable brutality.
Heber and Jael played both sides for decades, and suddenly the house of Heber stood next to the people of God. The Lord really can use anyone.

documents.excerpt: “But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Josh asks the church to travel with him from the tent in the Valley of Jezreel to the empty tomb in Jerusalem.
excerpts: “But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Josh asks the church to travel with him from the tent in the Valley of Jezreel to the empty tomb in Jerusalem.

Some are living under the oppression of a king called sin, an unholy trinity selling enslavement packaged as freedom. Now the deception is clear and you want to be free, but feel powerless. Like Jael, Josh wants to show you where your powerful enemy is: “Come, look.” That is your sin lying dead, your condemnation with a tent peg driven through its skull.

Jesus said it in a word, tetelestai: it is finished. The sins you were enslaved to can be forgiven; run to God in the name of Jesus Christ and trust him alone. Believer, your sin isn’t wandering in the desert, waiting to return when you least expect it. Whatever broke your heart or controlled your life is no more; your sins aren’t wounded or napping, they are gone.
When Jesus said tetelestai, he was like a judge handing down a decision for your soul: not guilty. There is no court of appeals; no one can overturn it or accuse you. It’s done.

He prays for anyone trying to fill their lives with things that promise joy, meaning, and purpose: he tried them all, and none came close to what Christ gives, life eternal through faith in Jesus. He thanks God for a church that declares what is true in a culture that demands it shut up.

He confesses the years he didn’t give God his life and was afraid to go at it alone with him, and now says, “It’s just me and you. Me and you against the world. Use me however you want, whenever you want, whatever the cost.”

documents.excerpt: Things were not going well in Israel at the end of last week’s passage: the Israelites forsook the Lord, served the Baals, and aroused his anger.
excerpts: Things were not going well in Israel at the end of last week’s passage: the Israelites forsook the Lord, served the Baals, and aroused his anger.

Canaanite theology differs sharply from Christian theology. A Christian reads Genesis 1 and 2 and understands sex is God’s gift to be shared between a man and a woman in marriage, not a divine act we mimic. God sits on his throne acting in history; he isn’t in some cosmic bedroom with a goddess bride. We are made in his image, but we are not like him and he is not like us.

Baal was the god of storm and fertility, of crops, livestock, and family, with a female counterpart, Ashtoreth. Canaanites believed the land’s fertility depended on the sexual relationship between Baal and Ashtoreth, and they didn’t leave it to Baal: they tried to spur him on with prostitution as worship at the Baal shrines, the very places Yahweh wanted Israel to break down. In paganism the gods must be spurred forward; in biblical faith we are taught to trust God.

Healthy churches aren’t measured by members, campuses, or services, but by Christians who live godly lives, not just say godly things or look Christian, and who are bold enough to speak up when godless culture creeps into the body. documents.excerpt: Josh can’t help but see the Lord’s patience. They kind of failed the test, yet God keeps testing; three times it says Yahweh tested them, to see whether his ways still mattered to them.
excerpts: Josh can’t help but see the Lord’s patience. They kind of failed the test, yet God keeps testing; three times it says Yahweh tested them, to see whether his ways still mattered to them.

Watching the Lord’s anger carried out in controlled, measured discipline time and again is the most comforting thing to a believer who knows how messy they are. We can only join Jeremiah: because of the Lord’s great love we are not consumed. God has great compassion for his people, but he is angry at their sins.

excerpts: Yes. God’s humor is reflected in Scripture, creation, and human nature. In Psalm 2 the one enthroned in heaven laughs: a divine mockery of human arrogance, pride, and rebellion.

Jesus uses exaggeration about rightly judging others. The church screams “judge not,” but Jesus says judge rightly: why look at the speck in someone else’s eye and ignore the plank in your own? It’s holy humor to picture a guy with a 2x4 sticking out of his eye worried about your speck.

Elijah the prophet, not the worship pastor, taunted Baal’s worshipers that maybe Baal couldn’t burn the altar because he was using the bathroom or taking a nap. In creation, look at an axolotl. And there’s the gift of contagious human laughter.

God’s humor isn’t crude; it has a purpose. It humbles the proud and lifts the lowly, and it shows in his reversals: the last become first, the weak become strong, the blind see, the crucified Christ becomes the risen Lord. It is holy, redemptive, and filled with joy.

excerpts: People think the Christian life is boring. Josh is having a fantastic time following Jesus. He has been praying that the Lord would restore the joy of his salvation and of his calling, and God is helping him despite some of the hardest years of his life. Since he took the lead pastor role in 2021, it has been one blow after another; maybe one day he can tell the story.

Walking it out, he is relearning that the Lord gives and the Lord takes; he came in with nothing and will leave the same. He has a divine optimism from the Holy Spirit that no circumstance could shake his faith to live as Christ and die as gain. He can’t lose; God has made it impossible for him to walk in defeat.

If you think the Christian life is boring, your eyes aren’t set on Jesus; you’ve gotten distracted. The Father loved Josh while he was still a sinner, then gave him power to beat the sin he was under: “Here’s my Spirit. Go bury that addiction.” When he failed again, the gospel hadn’t changed: “I love you still. Go bury it.” One day it was gone, not just the act but the desire, and he was like a child thrown in the air by his daddy: can we do that again? The rest of the world lives in chains, but the Lord is teaching his children to slip chains, all because of Jesus.
We all deserve Ehud’s left-handed secret message, yet because of God’s great love we got the gospel message from Jesus.

The Romans and the religious establishment thought he was dead and it was over. But when they rolled the stone in place, Jesus reached for a weapon no one thought he had and shoved that dagger into the heart of death. He killed death, walked out, and led his people to victory: where, O death, is your victory? Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

The period of the judges shows God loves sending salvation from unexpected sources. Jesus’ victory was so surprising that Roman soldiers were in awe: surely this was the Son of God. So Paul preaches Christ crucified, a stumbling block and foolishness to some, but to those God has called, the power and wisdom of God.

excerpts: Ehud’s story ends on a sad note; get used to that in this series. His encounter with the oversized king may have encouraged people for a while, but it couldn’t change their hearts. Still slaves to sin, they once again did evil.

That’s why, whether for rebellious Israelites 1,200 years before Jesus or carefully curated Christians 2,000 years after he was raised, it never gets old hearing about the one who purchased our freedom. No lefty with a dagger can free us from what held us captive, but one with nail marks has secured the victory. Yahweh has sent his Redeemer, Jesus, who freed us from our sins by his blood.

excerpts: The only way this story ends badly for you is if you go on after this message with business as usual and back to your old ways. Your ways will never be enough; they are filthy rags.

The empty tomb proves there is life after death. Humanity has had plenty of time to drop Jesus’ body in the street to prove him a liar and never did. No body means eternity. It is either foolishness to you or the power and wisdom of God that saves.

He was patient then and is patient now, but a day is coming when the Lord will close all of time, and you don’t want to see him riding on the clouds unless your name is in the book of life. Repent and believe the good news. If you believe God raised Jesus from the dead and are ready to say out loud that you want him as Lord, the baptism waters are ready. What are you waiting for?

documents.excerpt: Some love Jesus but feel God can’t use them; the last verse is for them.
excerpts: Some love Jesus but feel God can’t use them; the last verse is for them.

Scholars can string out one verse: was Shamgar named after the Canaanite goddess Anath, or just raised in Galilee? It doesn’t matter whether he was an Israelite; ask Cyrus if God can use anyone. Focus on what he did: he killed 600 bad guys with an eight-foot pole. He too saved Israel.
We know nothing about Shamgar, yet he saved God’s people. That is why Josh sings: his God uses unknowns with ox goads, and if he can use Shamgar, he can use Josh.

documents.excerpt: Are you willing to be used by God and content with the gifts he has given you? If you don’t get a sword but an eight-foot ox goad, are you wielding it with courage and joy like it’s the best sword ever?
excerpts: Are you willing to be used by God and content with the gifts he has given you? If you don’t get a sword but an eight-foot ox goad, are you wielding it with courage and joy like it’s the best sword ever?

Many Christians are waiting for God to give them something when God is waiting for them to use what they already have. If nothing else, he has given you a story, a testimony. Are you using it, or afraid to go to battle with it?

Ask him for help and step out in faith: love your neighbor, serve in a ministry, meet a need through Crossroads Cares, volunteer at the care center, share Christ with a coworker or family member, start a Bible study with your kids. God doesn’t need you to be extraordinary, just willing. He uses lefties, oddballs, and anyone. If Judges 3 shows anything, it’s that all you need is his Spirit.

documents.excerpt: Josh recalls the church singing, with the instruments turned down, “Come fill me again with your Spirit.” People aren’t killing people with eight-foot poles anymore, but temptations to look like, love, and befriend the world are alive, so he asks for the Spirit’s guidance, conviction, and discernment to know God’s voice from the deceiver’s.
excerpts: Josh recalls the church singing, with the instruments turned down, “Come fill me again with your Spirit.” People aren’t killing people with eight-foot poles anymore, but temptations to look like, love, and befriend the world are alive, so he asks for the Spirit’s guidance, conviction, and discernment to know God’s voice from the deceiver’s.

He prays for just one person to say, “If God can use an unknown dude with an eight-foot pole, he can use me.” Not everyone is gifted to sing like Elijah and Michaela, but God has given different gifts to use together for his glory. He asks for one who has been masking a gift or holding back a story out of shame. We aren’t ashamed of where we came from: when Josh says he is an addict turned preacher, it is to God’s glory. Raise up more.

excerpts: Ten weeks into Ephesians, Paul transitions to an extensive layout of God’s blueprint for Christian households, a discussion that continues well into chapter 6. First Josh recalls a key phrase Chris covered last week from the back half of verse 18: “Be filled with the spirit.”

The exact instant you surrender to Jesus as Lord and call out to him as Savior, you receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. How people respond varies; many believers still meander around with training wheels and diapers because they haven’t developed godly habits. God gives the gift, but having the Spirit is different from being filled with the Spirit. It takes effort, prayer, submission, and obedience.

Jesus makes clear in the parable of the talents that how we use what God gives matters. Jesus will return; we don’t know when, but the call is the same: don’t waste the gift. Use your gifts, talents, resources, and every opportunity to do good and build up the church. Keep watch, don’t cause others to stumble, but don’t be afraid to take risks. Walk in faith, not fear, and be faithful in small things.

excerpts: Josh asks veterans to stand and thanks them; he’ll never forget what his salvation cost or what his freedom cost. Then: have you ever been outranked by a dummy? How many are smarter than their boss?

We don’t submit because the person is smarter than us, or even because they’re a good or bad boss. We submit because they hold authority. The military calls it mutiny when the low-ranked no longer wish to be under obedience. Without levels of authority a military is weak, and society and the church weaken the same way. It’s a hot mess.

Yes, men have God-given authority in the home, but why? To bless God, your wife, your kids, your church, and your community. Godly men don’t ask for a blessing because they know they are tasked with being the blessing.

The man is called the head and the woman the helper; things go wrong when the helper becomes a hater. Point out what he does well, build rapport, then throw out an idea.
excerpts: “Josh, he won’t lead.” There are ways to help him without tearing him down; nagging won’t get the job done. Try a loving nudge: offer an idea, help him, but let him lead. The man is called the head and the woman the helper; things go wrong when the helper becomes a hater. Point out what he does well, build rapport, then throw out an idea.

Many women hear that the man should lead and assume they should do nothing and can’t have a vision for the home. That isn’t healthy, and waiting around will make you a hater, not a helper. Call a meeting with paper and pen, develop a vision for your home together for five, ten, twenty years and retirement, pray over it, and ask him to lead you there.
We talk about passive men, but passive women exist too. Empower him; don’t harm him. A Christian wife’s careful, thoughtful words can change the trajectory of a home and revolutionize her man.

Let him lead
“Josh, he won’t lead.” There are ways to help him without tearing him down; nagging won’t get the job done. Try a loving nudge: offer an idea, help him, but let him lead. The man is called the head and the woman the helper; things go wrong when the helper becomes a hater. Point out what he does well, build rapport, then throw out an idea.
Many women hear that the man should lead and assume they should do nothing and can’t have a vision for the home. That isn’t healthy, and waiting around will make you a hater, not a helper. Call a meeting with paper and pen, develop a vision for your home together for five, ten, twenty years and retirement, pray over it, and ask him to lead you there.
We talk about passive men, but passive women exist too. Empower him; don’t harm him. A Christian wife’s careful, thoughtful words can change the trajectory of a home and revolutionize her man.

excerpts: Chris warns that the next few minutes will be uncomfortable for some, and he won’t pull any punches, because Scripture doesn’t pull punches.

Here’s the context: when we are running after immoral, impure things and we are greedy, we become idolaters, and the Bible tells the rest of us not to partner with them. Idolatry means putting something else in the place of God and worshiping it.

Don’t mistake this for sin we are truly repenting of, praying about, and fighting to get out of our lives. Idolatry means we have purposely crafted it and set it up in our lives, and it has taken the place of God because we won’t remove it.

Do you decide that’s not what Scripture is saying, point out that others are doing it too, or say, “What I’m doing may not be right, but it’s not as bad as what the person over there is doing”?
excerpts: Do you make excuses for doing something Scripture clearly tells you to stop? When a message calls it sin, or someone who truly cares about you calls it out, do you get mad? Do you decide that’s not what Scripture is saying, point out that others are doing it too, or say, “What I’m doing may not be right, but it’s not as bad as what the person over there is doing”?

When convicted by Scripture, a sermon, or a loving brother or sister in Christ, instead of getting mad or defending yourself, ask why you feel convicted. Is the Holy Spirit convicting you of something you need to change? Then read God’s word on the subject of your conviction and devour it, pray that the Lord would reveal whether it’s an idol you need to destroy, and if it is, destroy it. Kill it.

excerpts: Your life might be great living together and your relationship might be awesome, but you’re outside of God’s design for your life.

Chris asks how many have told a lie to parents, at work, or to a spouse to keep from getting in trouble, and how many got away with it. He has, more times than he cares to admit. But just because he got away with it and the outcome he wanted happened, that didn’t make his lie okay. If you’re having sex outside of marriage, and maybe even living together, that’s not God’s design, and no human reasoning can change that.

His challenge to those living together: get married, or, though it can seem insurmountable, one of you move out until you decide what you actually want to do is get married. When you’re ready to live together, get married.

excerpts: Chris addresses an idea he has heard from multiple people: words aren’t containers. A word is like a puzzle piece whose significance comes from how it fits with other words, context, and speaker intent. He grants that language has nuance; English is a lazy language that reuses words, like “bank” for money or the side of a river.

But when it comes to coarse language, obscenities, and crude jokes, no matter what other pieces you throw at it, it’s not okay for a believer. He says “I hate you” to someone up front in several tones, as sweetly as he can, but the word is still hate and still carries a connotation. There are much worse obscenities he could say in no way that would make anyone okay with it; he wouldn’t have a job in five minutes.
Words matter and have meaning, or we wouldn’t need dictionaries. Telling someone you love that their hair is “round” or that they have a nice chair on their head makes no sense.

excerpts: With everything exposed to the light, Paul reminds us how to live. How do we live wisely and understand the Lord’s will? Someone in the room held up a Bible: that’s right. Chris reads 2 Timothy 3:15–17 and urges anyone who doesn’t know it to memorize it.
He has no amazing new thing to wow everyone. He’ll say what they’ve heard a million times, because some need to hear it a million and one: you live wisely by reading and studying the Bible.

It couldn’t be easier to access on our phones, but our phones seem more important to us than our Bible. We panic when the phone is lost, broken, or out of battery. Do we have the same reaction when we haven’t read God’s word in a day, a week, a month? Is this service the only time you see what’s in God’s word because it’s on the screen? If you are not regularly in the pages of Scripture, you are unwise and foolish.

Chris cites a study he saw but forgot to note the source of: reading the Bible one to three times a week changes your life statistically the same as never reading it. He has no amazing new thing to wow everyone. He’ll say what they’ve heard a million times, because some need to hear it a million and one: you live wisely by reading and studying the Bible.

excerpts: The placement is interesting: Paul has just talked about living in the light and confirms what we all know, drunk people do stupid things.

Chris confesses he has never been drunk; all his poor decisions he made perfectly sober, which probably makes it worse. He isn’t holier than thou: he hates the taste of alcohol and can’t stand being out of control, even on strong pain medication. Being around drunk people irritates him, and he can’t count how many times he’s heard, “I would never have done that if I was sober.”
Hence Paul’s warning. We don’t make good decisions when we’re drunk. Instead, we should be filled with the Spirit.

excerpts: After all the talk of what not to do, sexual immorality, greed, drunkenness, idolatry, darkness, foolishness, we hear what brings love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control: be filled with the Spirit, speak psalms, hymns, and songs, sing to the Lord, and always give thanks.

Chris knows they covered tough things: sexual immorality to bring into the light, mouths to clean up, idols to kill, and darkness in his own life to expose. But when you let the Spirit fill you, every day should look like today, when we speak hope, love, joy, and peace, pray for each other, and praise God at the top of our lungs. Why does it look different the other six days of the week? It shouldn’t.

Call a brother or sister and speak hope and life into them. Don’t know what to say? Paul just told you: speak a psalm or hymn and pray it over them. Sing your lungs out in the car or the shower; if you’re praising the Lord in the car, you won’t be cussing out the driver who cut you off.

And thank him. Whatever is going on in your life, you can be thankful to God for sending Jesus to die on the cross so you can have eternity with him. Life is hard, but in eternity we will have all the fruit of the Spirit without even trying, and all the hard stuff will be gone. Go kill those idols and make every single day Sunday.

excerpts: Josh welcomes guests and wishes a happy Father’s Day to the men who don’t just fill a spot on the couch but see their role as fathers as part of their Christian duty. May the dedicated Christian fathers go down as heroes, remembered for keeping the faith and acting like men.

Don’t let the world reduce a father’s role to provider. Josh honors men who protect the hearts entrusted to them, joyfully embrace their role as priests in their homes, and lift high the name of Jesus; they don’t just talk about Jesus, they walk with him while their kids watch. These men deserve a steak and a beer, if you’re into that kind of thing.

He asks who loves Jesus because a man sitting here loved Jesus first, and invites those whose man is no longer with us to pray, thanking the Lord for the men who loved Jesus and taught us to love him too.

excerpts: Paul mentions people who have lost all sensitivity and given themselves over to sensuality to indulge in every kind of impurity: people enslaved to their desires. This person can’t say no to porn. Some 60% of active churchgoers struggle with pornography, which is why Josh talks about it.

What is sometimes taught improperly is that the desire itself isn’t inherently bad; it is how you are meeting it that hardens your heart. Your desire is for your wife, but you satisfy it with a stranger; your desire is for your husband, but you satisfy it with a screen. And the desire isn’t only for your satisfaction but for your spouse; sex is more about giving than receiving.

The old attitude says, “There’s a desire; I must feed it now.” The new attitude says, “I know this desire and why I have it. I know what God says. I’m to serve my wife with this; it builds my family, our intimacy, and makes the marriage bed holy. Get behind me, Satan. Help me, Jesus. I’ll wait until my wife and I can satisfy it together.”

Maybe that isn’t your thing. Maybe you are a glutton, a liar, a cheater, a thief, covetous, a gossip, or just lazy, going on 40 and still playing World of Warcraft in your mom’s basement. Whatever it is, call it to mind and hang on to it.

Christians don’t sit around inventing new ways to think about things; we want to know what God thinks. documents.excerpt: Paul says the unsaved person is futile in their thinking: empty thinking with no meaning behind it. If they don’t know God, how can they understand the world he created, themselves whom he created, or those around them?
excerpts: Paul says the unsaved person is futile in their thinking: empty thinking with no meaning behind it. If they don’t know God, how can they understand the world he created, themselves whom he created, or those around them?

Romans 1 explains how this went down; Josh invites the church to read the whole chapter. He reads from verse 21: although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened; claiming to be wise they became fools, and God gave them over to the sinful desires of their hearts; they exchanged the truth about God for a lie. The assumption of all Scripture is that God exists; there are no apologists in Scripture.

Futile thinking leads to nothing. They have innovative ways of thinking that sound really good, but without godly thinking they are meandering in the dark, fools who think they are wise. That is what people look like apart from God, and Satan loves to blindfold them from the truth in Jesus.

The unsaved man is dead because of spiritual ignorance; the Christian is alive because of what they learned about Jesus. Truth and life are connected, which is why Jesus says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Life flows in after truth flows through: believe God’s truth and you receive God’s life. Unbelievers are in a terrible position: they have given themselves over to sin and can’t even feel it anymore.

documents.excerpt: Paul insists we not live like people who don’t know God, yet we do. With that sin still in mind, have you tried to hold it in one hand and your faith in the other?
excerpts: Paul insists we not live like people who don’t know God, yet we do. With that sin still in mind, have you tried to hold it in one hand and your faith in the other?

Here is what we do: pick a church with a soft preacher so we never hear about our sin; have zero Bible study time so we don’t encounter it; avoid accountability and godly men who would call things out; dismiss loving correction as “judging me”; skip life groups because close Christian community might bring things into the light.

How many Christians pull from Adam’s playbook in the garden and go into hiding instead of facing it head-on? We suppress the truth because we don’t want to be found out. We know we are sinners; we just don’t want others to know, and sometimes we know they know and don’t want to know they know. Our ego, image, and reputation can’t take the hit.
The tragedy is that the longer you live like this, the more distance you create between you and God, and the worse it gets. Be careful: there may come a day you don’t even feel it anymore.

documents.excerpt: Another thing we do is bury consequences. We hate thinking our sin could affect others and pretend our struggle comes with no consequences. But there is a simple rule: cause and effect.
excerpts: Another thing we do is bury consequences. We hate thinking our sin could affect others and pretend our struggle comes with no consequences. But there is a simple rule: cause and effect.

“Josh, I never wanted this life: two kids, two cars, two jobs, two divorces.” Josh knows life is hard and may not have gone as you wanted, but you only create kids one way; your smart bed didn’t force you against your will, and if it did, you might want to lawyer up. We experience consequences and play the victim card, then look up and ask, “Where’s God in all this?” Where is God in the consequences of your actions? Probably waiting for you to own it, accept the consequences, repent, and stop sinning against yourself, your family, and most of all him.

When the human heart is alienated from God, it craves sin. God could be right next to you and you couldn’t see him, because your heart is hardened, your understanding darkened, and your senses deadened by sin.

In other words: “I want this.” “But it isn’t good for you.” “Says who? I’ll determine what’s good for me.” “Stop, think about your family, your children, your marriage.” “I don’t care. The heart wants what the heart wants.” But the heart can lead you straight to hell. That is sensuality: no discipline, no self-control, no self-denial.

Jesus makes clear that liars won’t inherit the kingdom. In Revelation 22 he says outside are the dogs, those who practice magic arts, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Jesus calls liars dogs.

Paul’s instruction is specific to truth-telling in the body of Christ: we can’t build up the church the way we are supposed to if we lie to each other, whether telling lies or living lies. The first lie in the early church came in Acts 5, with Ananias and Sapphira. They died not only because they lied but because their lie harmed the body they had committed to. They wanted to look good for a big pledge, then pocketed the proceeds when they sold, and God made an example of them.

We belong to each other in Christ; our actions affect each other, and we share, work together, and meet needs as one. The church can’t function if we are shady with each other. We must speak the truth in love.

documents.excerpt: Christians control their anger, not the other way around. It isn’t a sin to have anger; it is a sin to let anger have you. God’s holy anger is part of his judgment against sin and is good; Jesus turned over the tables in the temple because he was angry at their unrighteousness. But holy anger is hard for us: we feel rightly that something is unjust, then act on it, and emotions tainted by sin ruin everything. God’s holy anger is part of his judgment against sin and is good; Jesus turned over the tables in the temple because he was angry at their unrighteousness. But holy anger is hard for us: we feel rightly that something is unjust, then act on it, and emotions tainted by sin ruin everything. We also lack God’s view of the whole timeline; we only see right now, and that causes us to lose control.

A woman defended her temper: “I explode and then it’s all over with.” Her friend replied, “So does a shotgun, but look at the damage it leaves behind.” Just because you can’t see the damage doesn’t mean it isn’t there.

It is possible to be angry and not sin. But if we do sin, we must make it right as quickly as possible: go directly to the person and stomp it out, because if the fire of anger isn’t put out with loving forgiveness, it can spread and destroy everything the Lord has built around you. That is why Paul says in verse 27, “Do not give the devil a foothold.” Take Solomon’s advice in Proverbs 15: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” In the spirit of speaking the truth in love, some of us would benefit from practicing gentle answers in the mirror.

documents.excerpt: Verse 28 echoes one of the Ten Commandments: “Thou shalt not steal.” When God gave it to Moses, he meant it. Stop stealing.
excerpts: Verse 28 echoes one of the Ten Commandments: “Thou shalt not steal.” When God gave it to Moses, he meant it. Stop stealing.

You would expect the application to be “work so you aren’t tempted to steal,” but Paul raises the bar: we work so we can give to others. The default setting of the unsaved is selfishness; the default setting of the believer is generosity. If we steal, we hurt others; so we are commanded to work so we can bless others. A lazy Christian robs himself, others, and God. If you can’t work, the church should care for you; if you can, make sure you are contributing to the life, mission, and ministry of the church.

What parent wakes up hoping for one of those days when the kids scream, drop-kick each other, and pull each other’s hair out? Conflict in the house is no fun, and neither is conflict in the believer. documents.excerpt: There is nuance, and the church should give itself a little grace. The numbers haven’t stayed flat because the front door isn’t being used; new people are coming and neighbors are being invited, frequently. excerpts: There is nuance, and the church should give itself a little grace. The numbers haven’t stayed flat because the front door isn’t being used; new people are coming and neighbors are being invited, frequently. But the back door is overused, people are sneaking out, and it comes out a wash.

Josh believes the biggest obstacle to growth this last year has been maturity. It isn’t subpar preaching, loud music, a building that is a shopping mall, or being non-denominational rebels. It is people who join this body with no interest in growing up: infants who divide over secondary issues, who expect paid professionals to carry out all the ministry, who need to be bottle-fed and shown which way to go at every moment.

Josh apologizes for swinging, but the message is confrontational. Some of this is outside the church’s control: people who aren’t interested in holy lives avoid biblical teaching, truth takes a back seat to grace when holiness doesn’t matter, and those who don’t love sacrificially love to scurry. Today will force self-evaluation in everyone; he has wrestled with it all week. How can you come once a month, never serve, never give, and call yourself a disciple? He commanded us to love one another as he loved us; if we disobey that command and say we love him, how does it add up?

documents.excerpt: One way this shows up is when people report that someone has left: they didn’t like this, “You were bald, now you have hair,” whatever it is, and Josh should reach out and bring them back. Why? You had the relationship with them, and you were there through their departure. Go get them.
excerpts: One way this shows up is when people report that someone has left: they didn’t like this, “You were bald, now you have hair,” whatever it is, and Josh should reach out and bring them back. Why? You had the relationship with them, and you were there through their departure. Go get them.

The immaturity of believers is one of the most discouraging parts of ministry. Have you seen a grown-up throw a fit like a child, rolling on the ground because his toy got taken or Daddy spoke too firmly? In high school, if somebody ticked Josh off he stopped talking to them and found other friends. You come to church thinking it won’t be like high school, and then people disagree and go down the street instead of working through it like mature adults, dodging you in the supermarket. “Josh, you should do this.” “No, that’s not us.” “Okay, I’m leaving.” “Okay, bye.”

The irony is that the church these immature believers split from will one day be brought under one roof by our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ. If we are going to have unity, why not have it now? From what Josh knows of his king, you will answer for breaking unity 18 times over secondary issues. If he is preaching heresy and a false gospel, split; if he just doesn’t align with your preferences, that is an unacceptable reason. And if you slip out the back door without a word to an elder or Josh, you are in error and will give an account for acting like an infant.

The church needs to grow up, and if that means a season of pruning, so be it. The all-talk-no-walk model is not his design for his church. Today not Josh but Paul is coming after our poor attitudes, our lazy efforts, and most of all our immaturity.

documents.excerpt: Josh warned this day was coming in the series. We have dealt with doctrine: we know who he is, who we are in Christ, what we are called to be, what to believe, and what has been done on our behalf. Now Paul wants us to know our duty and responsibility. Believers have spiritual wealth, not to hoard but to share.
excerpts: Josh warned this day was coming in the series. We have dealt with doctrine: we know who he is, who we are in Christ, what we are called to be, what to believe, and what has been done on our behalf. Now Paul wants us to know our duty and responsibility. Believers have spiritual wealth, not to hoard but to share.

The key word in the first three chapters of Ephesians is riches; the key word in the back half is walk. You can tell a lot about someone by how they walk, and Paul makes clear that Christians walk in unity, purity, harmony, and victory.

Paul’s pattern is first doctrine, then duty, and the connection point is the word “therefore.” Romans has the same pattern: the first 11 chapters are doctrinal, and in chapter 12 he gets personal and practical: “Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice.” Based on everything said so far, present your life to God.

If you don’t know, you can’t do. This is how the Spirit works: we hear, we are convicted, and we change course. What you believe determines how you behave. We are called by grace, raised from the dead, reconciled to God and each other, and share Christ’s victory over Satan, sin, and death, and we must know these riches to walk according to them. So, church, it is time to get stepping.

documents.excerpt: “As a prisoner for the Lord, then, I urge you to live a life worthy of the calling you have received.” First we notice the costly nature of the Christian walk. Paul knows he is a prisoner of Rome, but he makes clear it is for the Lord.
excerpts: “As a prisoner for the Lord, then, I urge you to live a life worthy of the calling you have received.” First we notice the costly nature of the Christian walk. Paul knows he is a prisoner of Rome, but he makes clear it is for the Lord.

This is one of the first areas where we need to grow up. We cry out, “Why did this have to happen to me? What did I do to deserve this?” Imagine adopting the mindset that no matter my circumstances, it is for the Lord. Optimism for a believer who understands the gospel is relentless. Paul saw everything through the gospel: he is a prisoner not because Rome wants him there but because the Lord has him there for a purpose. That is how Paul learned contentment, with a vertical, kingdom perspective instead of an earthly one.

documents.excerpt: All we need are the graces Paul lists, starting with humility. If you are convinced you have it, you probably don’t. Someone truly humble is haunted by the reality that they might be the worst one, not the best one.
excerpts: All we need are the graces Paul lists, starting with humility. If you are convinced you have it, you probably don’t. Someone truly humble is haunted by the reality that they might be the worst one, not the best one.

You can’t get the gospel and be prideful; they are oil and water. Even a basic understanding of what God has done makes you humble, because your most righteous acts are like filthy rags to God. He saw your hopeless condition and made a way back from the dead through faith in Jesus Christ, when you weren’t even interested. He finished it and drew you to himself. You didn’t see how good God was and run to him; he saw how terrible you were and saved you. There is nothing to boast about.

True Christian humility puts God first, everyone else second, and yourself last. How much you give financially makes no difference to Josh if it is joyful and sacrificial, but if you don’t give at all, or not sacrificially, you have some growing up to do. Humility shows up in service and sacrifice.

Paul says this to the Romans too, in the Romans 12 parallel: do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but with sober judgment. There is a balance: we shouldn’t think too highly of ourselves, but not too little either, because God went to great lengths to save and redeem you, and shame has no right to hang around.

excerpts: Patience literally means long-tempered: the ability to endure discomfort without fighting back. It can’t be separated from love; Paul tells the Corinthians, “Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud.”

Noah is a wonderful example of long temper and loving patience. God told him to build a ship in the desert, miles from water, and he worked 120 years. Some of us have two months of hardship and fall apart; Noah endured 120 years while people mocked him and called him a fool. He loved them and told them of the coming judgment rather than spitefully withholding it. No one believed him, but he told them.

To this day the rainbow is a sign reminding us that God is the ultimate promise keeper. How ironic, Josh says, that the sexual rebellion in our world chose the rainbow, the symbol reminding us that God hates sin, to boast about their sin.

We need to shift how we handle this culturally and start hitting our knees for these people. A Jonah mentality toward sinners, “They don’t deserve your mercy, they deserve your wrath, I’m not going over there,” is not a worthy Christian walk. Rebellious people don’t need our campaigns of shame; they need our campaign of the gospel. Go tell them; as Paul will show, that is your job too, not just Josh’s.

documents.excerpt: We are tasked with keeping unity, not creating it. The Holy Spirit creates it. We can notice its beauty, preserve it, protect it, and fight for it, but we don’t create it. And this unity isn’t only in this church or denomination but among all Christians of different races, nationalities, languages, and economic classes.
excerpts: We are tasked with keeping unity, not creating it. The Holy Spirit creates it. We can notice its beauty, preserve it, protect it, and fight for it, but we don’t create it. And this unity isn’t only in this church or denomination but among all Christians of different races, nationalities, languages, and economic classes.

Most of man’s systematic efforts to create unity have failed and only created more permanent separation. History also shows that one church doesn’t work, because large faith institutions grow corrupt over time. Whether many small institutions or one large one, we don’t create unity; our job is to notice, promote, and celebrate it, walking by the Spirit and bringing light to it.

Some today say the key to unity is getting rid of certain people: “If we just get rid of the fundamentalists, we don’t need doctrine, we need love,” those Christians who take the word as literal and infallible. Notice the hypocrisy: they are name-calling in order to create unity.

Paul didn’t bring up spiritual unity until he spent three chapters unpacking the foundation of our new life and riches in Christ. Unity not built on truth will crumble. Bash us for loving the word of God, but it is the word that reminds us daily not to draw lines between brothers and sisters, call them names, or poke fun at their traditions or lack of tradition. Unity built on tolerance crumbles; unity built on truth lasts.

excerpts: Being one body doesn’t excuse a believer from having a local church home. “I don’t need to be a member of a church; we’re all the church,” says the one who doesn’t give and comes seven times a year so he can stay home and watch football.

You can have unity with believers in Asia, and Josh has unity with brothers and sisters in China, but you can’t have community with them. You need a place to worship, serve, and grow. You are born with natural talents and born again with spiritual gifts, and every Christian needs a place to use their gifts to bless God and others.

“Josh, you don’t get it, I’m a super introvert.” So is he; people drain him. But it has taken a long time, and he is still a work in progress, and Jesus is teaching him: let them drain you, because Jesus will fill him back up when he rests in him at night and wakes hearing his word. Josh used to make the same excuse, until he realized the reason we like our personal time is that we are the only person we are actually skilled at loving.

Jesus commands us to love others, and failing to do so proves we have never experienced God’s love ourselves. Jesus didn’t need anything we had, yet he stepped down and got involved anyway; we drained him of life and he let it happen. That is how Christians live and love: “I have been crucified with Christ and I no longer live.” Have at me.

Non-believers may think only miserable Christians long for home, but he has an amazing wife, two wonderful kids, a beautiful home, and a ministry the church makes an incredible joy, and he still wants to go home.
excerpts: Are you ready for the day Christ’s bride is presented? Josh longs to go home. Non-believers may think only miserable Christians long for home, but he has an amazing wife, two wonderful kids, a beautiful home, and a ministry the church makes an incredible joy, and he still wants to go home.

He is tired of seeing people lose their way, of streets paved in gay pride when he knows streets will be made of gold, of people following every social media influencer with a lot of likes when there is only one worth following. He wants to feast with his Savior and Lord. He wants his kids to see and know the heavenly Father he keeps failing to mimic, his wife to be loved as she deserves instead of being stuck with an idiot like him, and his brothers and sisters to sing together and worship in spirit and truth. He is tired of war, death, disease, fighting, and division, and without the Lord he would be a mess.

This morning Josh was blessed by a hymn from the mid-1800s: “Stand up, stand up for Jesus, the strife will not be long; this day the noise of battle, the next the victor’s song.” He wants the church to know and depend on Jesus like that. He has nothing else to offer but a way to Jesus: call on his name today and let his Spirit fill you. There is nothing better than walking with Jesus.

We are children in the same family, set out to love and serve the same Father, and we should be able to walk in unity. Earthly families make compromises to walk in unity at home; God’s heavenly family must make allowances for one another too. excerpts: Paul moves from what we have in common to how Christians look different: unity in the Spirit, but also variety. “But to each one of us grace has been given as Christ apportioned it.” When he ascended on high he took many captives and gave gifts to his people; he who descended is the very one who ascended higher than all the heavens, in order to fill the whole universe.

God’s purpose in salvation wasn’t only to save you and give you eternal life but to fill you with himself. The whole point of Christ’s work was that he might fill the whole universe. He wants you to experience him walking with you through life and to be empowered and equipped to love the world as he does. Paul has been praying for us to know the power at work in us, and spiritual gifts are how we grab that power and do good works that glorify God.

Josh understands the hesitation: people have come up to him in the lobby announcing, “I am a prophet sent by God to warn you.” Of what? That he must stop selling bagels. God’s people need to eat too.

Twelve first-century apostles were set apart to know Jesus and be eyewitnesses of his life and ministry, and none of the twelve are with us, so in a sense the office of apostle concluded in the first century. What continues is the gift: a missionary pioneering work or a church planter reaching a city without access to the gospel. The church’s founding pastor had the apostolic gift.

We all need to participate in that kind of ministry, but exercising a gift differs from assigning a title. Josh doesn’t have this gift. If someone here discovers it, the elders and Josh would help launch them into a first ministry where the gospel is desperately needed, though Anthem doesn’t need more churches.

documents.excerpt: Over the next minutes there is freedom: tables throughout, prayer walls in the back, benches up front for anyone who wants to fall to their knees, and anyone alone is invited to pray with Josh’s family or join any family circle. Paul tells Timothy to entrust these truths to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others, and to guard what has been entrusted to his care like the most precious thing he has, turning away from godless chatter and what is falsely called knowledge.

For a long time God’s plan was a mystery, but it isn’t a secret anymore. He has pulled back the curtain. We are lavished with spiritual blessings in Christ, so live up to the calling and share those blessings with others.

excerpts: Josh has kept Paul’s situation in front of the church throughout the series: Paul is writing from prison. Acts 28 shows he wasn’t in a traditional cell. Luke, his travel companion, says that when they got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself with a soldier to guard him: house arrest under constant surveillance.

This worked out beautifully. Paul had peace of mind, quiet, space, time, and freedom to write letters like Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon, and he could have visitors. Some scholars Josh read this week think this house in Rome was where Philemon met Paul, heard the gospel, and gave his life to Christ.

We hear imprisonment and think dungeon, but his imprisonment in Rome looked more like a schoolhouse for the gospel, a hub for teaching and preaching. To which we all say, “Praise God. What they intended for evil, God meant for good.”

The discouragement of a prayer ministry is great; stick with it.

excerpts: Our Father in heaven, from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name, is the uncaused causer of all things. All things were made through him and for him. He is the great original: as the young people would put it, God is the OG.

He created us with distinction, beauty, dignity, value, and worth. The Godhead held a divine meeting before time and said, “Let us make man in our own image.” It isn’t what you do or what you believe that gives you dignity and value; it is who made you. God is the original artist, and because he is beautiful, so are you. Psalm 139 says, “I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made.”

What is the difference between an image bearer and a child of God? Faith in Christ. Not everyone is a child of God. That line is used by weak-minded Christians to push universal salvation and let people keep their idols and keep living in sin. We aren’t born into God’s family; we are adopted into it. We are born children of wrath, which is why Jesus says we must be born again.

documents.excerpt: Paul prays that out of his glorious riches God would strengthen them with power through his Spirit in their inner being. For charismatic brothers and sisters, it helps to ask what kind of power. Healing power? Fire from heaven on their enemies? Tongues to reach neighbors who speak the same language they do? No.
excerpts: Paul prays that out of his glorious riches God would strengthen them with power through his Spirit in their inner being. For charismatic brothers and sisters, it helps to ask what kind of power. Healing power? Fire from heaven on their enemies? Tongues to reach neighbors who speak the same language they do? No.

Paul is talking to discouraged people. He prays for the kind of power that keeps them from being crushed by the weight of discouragement. Jesus says “take heart,” and Paul prays the Lord would give them the power to take heart. Their newfound faith has brought persecution and challenges, and the discouragement is piling up.

Paul isn’t praying for their circumstances to improve. There is nothing wrong with wanting things to get better or asking God to heal someone and trusting him whether you get it or not. But Paul’s prayer is more like, “God, would you strengthen me so I can endure this? Would you give me what I need to suffer well for your name?” I want to walk with you through this in a way where you are glorified on the other side, and whatever story you are writing, even the final chapter of my life, becomes a testimony of your grace and goodness. It isn’t about circumstances; it is about the power you need to walk by faith.

documents.excerpt: Spiritual power isn’t only given to upper-class Christians. His power is in every Christian who submits to God’s word and walks by the Spirit.
excerpts: Spiritual power isn’t only given to upper-class Christians. His power is in every Christian who submits to God’s word and walks by the Spirit.

Josh and his wife recently bought a Lumen, a breathalyzer-like device that measures your metabolism. (If you ever see him holding a device to his mouth, it isn’t a vape.) He didn’t need a device to tell him his metabolism is slow. They loved it: cooking together, counting macros, being told when to eat and work out. But it still took time, and he still isn’t at his desired results. That isn’t the device’s fault; it is the device holder’s. He isn’t willing to make the sacrifices, and he can’t stop eating chocolate cake.

Improving physical health takes time and sacrifice, and so does growing spiritually. There is nothing wrong with the device; it is the device holder. We need to discipline our minds, strengthen our resolve, take in the right amount, and exert the right amount. And the stronger we get as believers, the less what is going on around us matters.

documents.excerpt: One of the strongest men in this church can barely physically walk into the building. He is in tears, broken over his sin; that is all he and Josh bond over. They don’t talk baseball or the Pacers reaching the NBA Finals for the first time in 25 years. excerpts: One of the strongest men in this church can barely physically walk into the building. He is in tears, broken over his sin; that is all he and Josh bond over. They don’t talk baseball or the Pacers reaching the NBA Finals for the first time in 25 years. Josh sees his faith and his brokenness over what God has done for him: “I did this, but Christ did this.”

Scripture says the outer man is perishing and the inner man is being strengthened, which is why the strongest man in the church can barely walk in on his own. Paul expands on this in 2 Corinthians: “Therefore we do not lose heart. Though outwardly we are wasting away, yet inwardly we are being renewed day by day,” fixing our eyes not on what is seen but on what is unseen, since what is unseen is eternal.

Paul isn’t trying to minimize your problems; he is trying to magnify your power, because we get exhausted when we fix our eyes on what is seen. Social media has trained the culture to live from the outside in instead of the inside out, and that is why believers become troubled, discouraged, anxious, and depressed. So we pray for one another to be strengthened in our inner being and live from the inside out. Work out what God has worked in. Do not lose heart.

documents.excerpt: Paul’s third request is that we grasp how wide and long and high and deep is the love of Christ, and know this love that surpasses knowledge. “Grasp” isn’t just understanding; it is such a firm grip that you can explain it, live it, and share it, moving from a one-dimensional to a four-dimensional perspective: width, length, depth, and height.
excerpts: Paul’s third request is that we grasp how wide and long and high and deep is the love of Christ, and know this love that surpasses knowledge. “Grasp” isn’t just understanding; it is such a firm grip that you can explain it, live it, and share it, moving from a one-dimensional to a four-dimensional perspective: width, length, depth, and height.

It seems like a contradiction but isn’t; it is profound. Paul prays we would know personally the love of Christ, while there is no way to fully know it because it surpasses knowledge. We are so rich in Christ that even AI can’t calculate those riches. It is wide enough to include all people, long enough to reach through all of time, deep enough to rescue the most desperate, lost sinner in the darkest pit, and high enough to lift us to heaven and seat us on the throne.

Christian, take heart: you have access to unlimited resources in Christ. If you pray for spiritual strength and depth, you will grasp it, and like Paul you will begin to boast, “I can do this through him who gives me strength.”

It is wide enough to include all people, long enough to reach through all of time, deep enough to rescue the most desperate, lost sinner in the darkest pit, and high enough to lift us to heaven and seat us on the throne.
Christian, take heart: you have access to unlimited resources in Christ. If you pray for spiritual strength and depth, you will grasp it, and like Paul you will begin to boast, “I can do this through him who gives me strength.”

excerpts: If you are losing heart, discouraged, defeated, tired, and weary, look now to him. Paul does for the believers in Ephesus what we should do for one another here: he points them back to God.

“Josh, I can’t carry this. I can’t do this anymore. It’s just one thing after another. I’m done.” You might be right; you can’t do it. But God is able. He is more than able, abundantly more than able, exceeding abundantly more than able. Some of you are doing great, and Josh rejoices with you, but you might be cruising into a storm. When you pull up to it, write this down: God is able.

Abraham believed God was able when he was a hundred years old, and was willing to give up Isaac because he knew God could do immeasurably more than he could ask or imagine. The three Hebrew boys declared publicly, “If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it”; even if God chose not to, they knew it wasn’t because he couldn’t.

Paul tells basically everyone in Asia Minor that God is able. Jesus proves it by willingly clinging to the cross and gloriously walking out of the tomb, and he wants people to believe it: he asked the blind men, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” “Yes, Lord.” Church, do you believe God is able?

To those with little faith: Josh loves you, but maybe this is why you live without power, because you don’t believe he is able. What is your alternative, doing it yourself? Josh has tried that, and Jesus’ words in John 15 are true: “I am the vine; you are the branches. If you remain in me and I in you, you will bear much fruit; apart from me you can do nothing.” We wander off, remain in our sin instead of in him, and wonder why his power doesn’t mark our lives. If you live for yourself, he won’t share his power; if you live for him, he will, and it will strengthen you.

He closes with a shout: now to him who is able. excerpts: Ephesians 3 ends with Paul on his knees praying that God’s people would be strengthened from within, that Christ would dwell in their hearts by faith, and that they would know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. He closes with a shout: now to him who is able. Able to do what we ask, but not just what we ask: what we think; not just what we think: more than we think; immeasurably more than all we ask or even imagine.

This isn’t about your power, resources, abilities, limitations, weaknesses, or even your past. It is only and forever about the one true living God who sits on the throne of the universe with all power in his hands. Seek first God’s kingdom, and all these things will be given to you as well.

We all have days when we feel forgotten, overlooked, insignificant, unheard. But he is able: to lift the weary, save the lost, heal the broken marriage, restore the broken relationship, save your children, build his church, bring beauty from ashes, and crush any addiction that has a stronghold on you. No one is out of reach; nothing is too hard for our God.

And he does it with the power already in you. There is nowhere to look and no box to check. If Christ is in you, his power is there too: the same resurrection power that raised Jesus from the dead is working in you right now. Take heart, because you can, because of Christ. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen. What we do here prepares us for an eternity where we will glorify Christ forever.

documents.excerpt: Have you ever prayed like Paul just prayed, gone on your knees before God and pleaded not just for him to step into your life but for those around you? Josh thinks this is what is wrong with the church: we don’t pray like this, and if we aren’t praying, we are dying.
excerpts: Have you ever prayed like Paul just prayed, gone on your knees before God and pleaded not just for him to step into your life but for those around you? Josh thinks this is what is wrong with the church: we don’t pray like this, and if we aren’t praying, we are dying.

Some have desperate prayers to make but are afraid to get out of their casual posture to make them. You need to pray for inner strength, and you need someone to pray on your behalf. Call on the Lord for a deeper love, a wider understanding, and a higher calling, and grab hold of the power in you with desperate prayers: “Lord, I need you.”

Many of you do not have because you do not ask God. But what would you ask for? Don’t ask God to take you out of it or stop it; pray that he would give you the strength to get through it. Ask him now. You aren’t alone: there are prayer benches up front to kneel before the Father, the one who is able, and pastors and elders will come pray with you. This is how we do battle together as a family of faith; we are warriors in Christ and have each other’s backs.

documents.excerpt: The communion tables are set out to force people to leave their rows. Josh thinks of the disciples at the first table: they weren’t in rows; they were looking each other in the eye as Jesus explained what was about to happen. excerpts: The communion tables are set out to force people to leave their rows. Josh thinks of the disciples at the first table: they weren’t in rows; they were looking each other in the eye as Jesus explained what was about to happen. He says, “Remember me,” and Josh thinks he means remember me together, in fellowship, love, peace, unity, joy, and hope.

Josh asks the church not to take communion until they have shared a prayer request or prayed over someone in the room, on their own timing: a spouse, children, or someone they don’t know. Grab them and pray, “Lord, strengthen them in their inner being.” He wants to see circles, not rows.

No one wants your mini-sermon during this prayer time; Josh loves the word of God too and gets excited, but fewer words are best. Love by being present and by speaking hope. Your prayers aren’t heard for your many words, and nobody is grading your prayer effort. Then come take the elements together.

If you are alone today, Josh sees you: come up and pray with his family, because if you are in Christ, you are his family. Engage in worship with your body, hands, and feet; dance before the divine, come to the front if you must. We have to stop being statues, because we aren’t statues. We are saints, so let’s act like it.

documents.excerpt: If we could peel back the ceiling and pull back the veil on the heavenly realms, we wouldn’t just see pews, lights, and a Sunday gathering; we would see a battlefield, a stage, and a throne room. The text in Ephesians today isn’t surface-level Christianity or tips for a better week.
excerpts: If we could peel back the ceiling and pull back the veil on the heavenly realms, we wouldn’t just see pews, lights, and a Sunday gathering; we would see a battlefield, a stage, and a throne room. The text in Ephesians today isn’t surface-level Christianity or tips for a better week.

Paul continues to pull back the curtain on the eternal plan of God, hidden for ages, now revealed through Christ and entrusted to the church. The gospel isn’t human invention; it is divine mystery unveiled in Christ and handed to us not to admire but to proclaim.
God didn’t save you so you could sit comfortably, but so you could speak boldly. He raised you from death so you could walk in life and victory, not shuffle around like some sort of redeemed zombie.

The church is the megaphone of God’s wisdom to the watching cosmos. Angels are leaning in, demons are watching, and the rulers and authorities are taking notes, and the sermon they hear is what you preach with your life: your holiness, unity, love, and boldness.

He asks the church to pray earnestly that God would protect it, from the elders and staff to the volunteers and congregation; that they would submit to Christ in reverence; and that they wouldn’t stumble into the church-growth models so much of the American church has fallen prey to, but trust the Lord to build his church in his time and way, by his Spirit. excerpts: In week five of a 12-week verse-by-verse series, about halfway through the letter, Elijah recalls where they have been. In chapter 1, Paul lifts us to the heavenly places, not to float but to see the sovereign God who predestined us before the foundation of the world, redeemed us by the blood of Christ, and sealed us by the Holy Spirit, so that we would praise his glorious grace with our very lives.

Chapter 2 drops us from the heavenlies into the graveyard: you were dead, not sick, struggling, or limping. Yet God, rich in mercy, raised us up with Christ and seated us with him. Salvation isn’t your achievement; it is a resurrection, grace from first breath to final heartbeat. And Christ shattered the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile; he didn’t call a truce, but made one new man, one household, one temple in which God now dwells.

So when Paul says in chapter 3, “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner,” he isn’t apologizing or explaining himself away. He is doubling down, because when you have been caught up in the mystery of Christ, chains and prison doors are a minor detail.

excerpts: Elijah reads verses 1–6 again. The mystery of Christ, hidden for generations and now unveiled by the Holy Spirit, is that Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in the Messiah through the gospel.

This isn’t God revising the script or changing his mind halfway through history; it is the curtain pulled back on a plan in motion from the foundations of the world: Gentiles grafted in, outsiders turned into heirs. That is great news for most in the room, who would qualify as Gentiles. God hasn’t loosened the borders of Israel; he has redrawn the map entirely.

The gospel doesn’t adjust; it reveals. What was hidden is now shouted from the rooftops. God isn’t subtle about his grace; he sends his apostles with fire in their bones and revelation in their mouths.

Modern minds despise this clarity. We live in a fog of spiritual relativism where truth claims are treated as closed-minded and bigoted, but Paul calls this the mystery made plain: not vague spirituality for private consumption, but revealed glory for public declaration.

God didn’t whisper this truth so you could mutter it politely; he revealed it so you could herald it boldly. The gospel isn’t confusing; it’s confronting. If the gospel has been background noise, it is time to turn the volume up. God wrote you into this story before time began, so don’t drift, downplay, or compromise; get in step with the plan.
excerpts: To those checking a box: Elijah loves them and would rather they be here than anywhere else, but their passivity is more harmful than helpful. If the gospel has been background noise, it is time to turn the volume up. God wrote you into this story before time began, so don’t drift, downplay, or compromise; get in step with the plan.

To those who think they have earned their way in: your self-righteousness does violence to your witness. The mystery of the gospel doesn’t flatter your résumé; it flattens it. Jew or Gentile, rich or poor, lifelong Christian or recent convert, the gospel makes one people, one inheritance, one glory, all to the praise of his glorious grace.

So are you living like a passive observer or a Spirit-empowered heir? What would change if you really believed God chose you to display the riches of his grace to the world? Elijah challenges the church to ask that this week.
