excerpts: Elijah reads verses 7–9. Paul was made a servant by the gift of God’s grace through the working of his power, and that grace was for preaching the boundless riches of Christ to the Gentiles.

This is grace with a job description. Grace didn’t give Paul a warm hug; it gave him a hammer. It didn’t put him in a spiritual hammock to coast and ponder the finest points of theology; it handed him a mission and said, “Go.” Paul isn’t floating on a cloud of forgiveness but marching with fire in his bones. This grace comes with power, and power never comes without purpose.

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · May 27, 2025 · Ephesians : From Death to Life
documents.excerpt: The modern American church has neutered grace: declawed, domesticated, soft, polite, sentimental, a slogan for T-shirts and coffee mugs, a spiritual bubble bath for people who don’t want to change. But grace made Paul a servant and turned a terrorist into a preacher.
excerpts: The modern American church has neutered grace: declawed, domesticated, soft, polite, sentimental, a slogan for T-shirts and coffee mugs, a spiritual bubble bath for people who don’t want to change. But grace made Paul a servant and turned a terrorist into a preacher.

The glorious grace of God puts steel in your spine and truth on your lips. Grace doesn’t coddle; it commissions. It wrecks you, confronts your sin, exposes your pride, and levels selfish ambition, and only then raises you up and sends you out. Paul didn’t receive grace and go on vacation; he got drafted. The man killing Christians was now building the church, and he knew what he had been forgiven of.

If your version of grace hasn’t radically reoriented your life, changed your desires, or made you dangerous to the gates of hell, what you are experiencing may not be grace but complacency. Elijah knows that didn’t land great, but he loves the church enough to tell the truth. If you say you’ve received grace, where’s the fruit, the fire, the fight? Grace isn’t a license to stay the same; it is power to war with your sin, serve when exhausted, speak when afraid, and love when it costs you.

documents.excerpt: If Paul could be beaten, tortured, imprisoned, and shipwrecked, call himself the least, and still preach to the nations, what is our excuse? You don’t need a title, a microphone, or permission. Thinking the work of the gospel belongs only to people with “pastor” in their title is a consumerist mentality that has produced passive, ineffective Christians and the emasculation of the American church.
excerpts: If Paul could be beaten, tortured, imprisoned, and shipwrecked, call himself the least, and still preach to the nations, what is our excuse? You don’t need a title, a microphone, or permission. Thinking the work of the gospel belongs only to people with “pastor” in their title is a consumerist mentality that has produced passive, ineffective Christians and the emasculation of the American church.

The Great Commission is for all believers. Our roles will look different, but we must not settle for a whisper when God has called us to shout. Stop waiting, get in the game, and proclaim the riches of Christ at home, at work, and in your circle. Grace sends.

In case the church has forgotten the mission, Elijah reminds them of Jesus’ words in Matthew 28: all authority has been given to him, so go and make disciples of all nations, and he is with us always. We have our marching orders; the only question is whether we will obey them.

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · May 27, 2025 · Ephesians : From Death to Life
documents.excerpt: God has promised the church victory, so why have so many churches traded the fight of faith for Sunday convenience? We have made Christianity about comfort, safety, and good vibes when the New Testament calls us to blood, sweat, tears, and triumph. Why are we playing church when commissioned as an army, tiptoeing through culture wars afraid to offend demons, asleep in the barracks while war rages in our homes, schools, pulpits, and souls?
excerpts: God has promised the church victory, so why have so many churches traded the fight of faith for Sunday convenience? We have made Christianity about comfort, safety, and good vibes when the New Testament calls us to blood, sweat, tears, and triumph. Why are we playing church when commissioned as an army, tiptoeing through culture wars afraid to offend demons, asleep in the barracks while war rages in our homes, schools, pulpits, and souls?

We weren’t saved to be safe or cozy, or filled with God’s power to post cute Bible quotes and stay quiet when the battle reaches the front door. The gospel isn’t therapy; it is transformation. Grace isn’t an anesthetic; it is ammunition. Paul writes in Romans 1:16 that he isn’t ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes; the righteous will live by faith.

Wake up: are you living by faith? You are the display of God’s wisdom, the voice that silences the accuser, ground zero of spiritual warfare. Don’t shrink back: stand up, speak up, bleed if you must, because the Lamb has already won. Will we walk in his victory or play well-behaved losers in a war already won?

documents.excerpt: Before responding in worship, Elijah rereads verses 12 and 13. Verse 12 is one of the most scandalous sentences Paul ever wrote. To the Jewish reader, access to God was restricted by temple curtains, sacrifices, and fear; to the Gentile reader, being welcomed into the presence of a holy and just God was absurd. But Paul says you can walk into the throne room, not head down, not through a priest, not after a guilt trip, but with freedom and confidence.
excerpts: Before responding in worship, Elijah rereads verses 12 and 13. Verse 12 is one of the most scandalous sentences Paul ever wrote. To the Jewish reader, access to God was restricted by temple curtains, sacrifices, and fear; to the Gentile reader, being welcomed into the presence of a holy and just God was absurd. But Paul says you can walk into the throne room, not head down, not through a priest, not after a guilt trip, but with freedom and confidence.

You aren’t a cosmic benchwarmer or a second-tier saint. In Christ you don’t need to grovel outside the temple; you have been handed the keys to the throne room, and the King calls you by name. This fuels everything Paul has said: we proclaim the mystery, suffer well, and love sacrificially, not to earn favor, but because we already have full access to the God of glory.

Romans 5 opens with it: justified through faith, we have peace with God and access by faith into this grace, and we boast in the hope of the glory of God. Are you boasting, believer? Access to God isn’t the reward of the spiritually elite but the birthright of the blood-bought. Don’t squander it by refusing to drag your sin into the light; God invites you into relationship and promises to go before you and set your feet on solid ground when you fall short.

documents.excerpt: Discouraged by your weakness? You have access. Overwhelmed by your calling? You have boldness. Afraid your pain or past sin disqualifies you? Paul says no, it is your glory. In Christ the mystery is revealed, the mission is clear, the cosmos is watching, and the throne is open. So approach boldly, suffer faithfully, live loudly.
excerpts: Discouraged by your weakness? You have access. Overwhelmed by your calling? You have boldness. Afraid your pain or past sin disqualifies you? Paul says no, it is your glory. In Christ the mystery is revealed, the mission is clear, the cosmos is watching, and the throne is open. So approach boldly, suffer faithfully, live loudly.

The world won’t applaud and hell will rage, but the sovereign God is for us and working in all things for our good. Elijah reads Romans 8: in all things God works for the good of those who love him, and those he predestined, called, and justified, he also glorified. Take heart in seasons of mourning and loss and of harvest and gain.

There is no better example than the cross: God used the darkest day in history to bring about the greatest good the world has ever known. How much more can we trust him to turn our mourning into dancing and our suffering and shame into glory?

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · May 27, 2025 · Ephesians : From Death to Life
documents.excerpt: Before the Lord’s Supper, Elijah implores the church not to make it empty tradition. At the table we proclaim the Lord’s death over our lives until he comes again. It is where the mystery of the cross becomes personal, where we stop striving and performing and start proclaiming, because the meal is about what he brought to us, not what we bring to God.
excerpts: Before the Lord’s Supper, Elijah implores the church not to make it empty tradition. At the table we proclaim the Lord’s death over our lives until he comes again. It is where the mystery of the cross becomes personal, where we stop striving and performing and start proclaiming, because the meal is about what he brought to us, not what we bring to God.

If you feel unworthy, good; that is the point. It isn’t about your résumé but his blood. If you have been discouraged, distracted, or disengaged, the throne is open and his grace is for you; if you have been coasting, this is the moment to repent, reset, and return to the call.

Come with freedom and confidence, not because everything is going well, but because Christ has won the war: as citizens of a kingdom, saints called to proclaim, sons and daughters with nothing to prove and everything to receive. The bread and cup are your access to the King, your commission to love and live boldly, and your glory to suffer if need be for the gospel.

Come with freedom and confidence, not because everything is going well, but because Christ has won the war: as citizens of a kingdom, saints called to proclaim, sons and daughters with nothing to prove and everything to receive. The bread and cup are your access to the King, your commission to love and live boldly, and your glory to suffer if need be for the gospel.

excerpts: In Paul’s day circumcision was a big issue, used like a racial slur today: “There’s one of those uncircumcised ones. What a dog.” After Peter preached at Pentecost, the first churches were mainly Jewish, but Paul’s missionary journeys reached Gentiles, and most converts in the Ephesian church were Gentiles.

For centuries the circumcised Jews had looked down on the uncircumcised Gentiles with an attitude God never intended. They called Gentiles dogs and unclean, wouldn’t do business with them, and viewed them as beasts unworthy to be mentioned with the seed of Israel.

The Gentiles returned the hatred, fueled by religious exclusivity, cultural separation, and economic tension. Jews refused to worship Roman gods or the emperor, the most severe edicts were passed against them, and Caligula publicly called them the most detestable of races. Tacitus tells us Gentiles accused Jews of child sacrifice; there is no evidence of it, but it didn’t need to be true, only effective. Jews were seen as antisocial because they held firm to their nationality and didn’t mingle, which always led to conflict.

There was also a wall in the temple separating the Court of the Gentiles from the rest. Think of a baseball game where Gentiles had to sit in the nosebleed section, and don’t you dare sneak down to an empty seat by the dugout in the third inning. Archaeologists found an inscription from Herod’s temple: no foreigner may enter the barricade around the sanctuary, and anyone caught will have himself to blame for his ensuing death.

Not even a Jew could bring a Gentile into the restricted part. Paul was accused of this in Acts 21 and would have been stoned to death if Roman soldiers hadn’t stepped in. For Jews and Gentiles to be reconciled, this wall had to be destroyed forever.

excerpts: We might not relate to a first-century street fight over circumcision, but we have our own fight here and now. We can’t let cultural divisions seep into our oneness; having differences is fine, but allowing division isn’t. “Jesus makes peace, but his church makes war. What has happened?”

Josh isn’t a pacifist and believes in just war, but he sees no room in Scripture ever for disunity and division in the church. Our culture is vicious and it is seeping in: men versus women, black versus white, young versus old, Democrat versus Republican, Calvinist versus Arminian, dispensationalist versus covenant.

You can’t hate someone because they are different. Christians are commanded to love God first and love others, and a violation of the second is a violation of the first. You aren’t given room to break off from people you disagree with or don’t like.

documents.excerpt: There is a beautiful connection between Genesis and Acts. Genesis 10, the table of nations, tracks the spread of the nations from the sons of Noah, and in Acts 10 God sends Peter to preach to the Gentiles. In Acts 8, 9, and 10, Noah’s families are united in Christ: a descendant of Ham, the Ethiopian treasurer, is saved; a descendant of Shem, Saul of Tarsus, becomes Paul the apostle; and descendants of Japheth, the Gentiles in the household of the Roman soldier Cornelius, are reconciled to Christ.

documents.excerpt: The second metaphor, probably Josh’s favorite, is a household. Through faith we enter God’s family under the headship of our heavenly Father, a family that lives in two places, believers on earth and those who have died in heaven, and one day those realities will collide.
excerpts: The second metaphor, probably Josh’s favorite, is a household. Through faith we enter God’s family under the headship of our heavenly Father, a family that lives in two places, believers on earth and those who have died in heaven, and one day those realities will collide.

Earthly experiences can distort eternal truths; for some, the word “family” starts the nightmares, and families can be messy. But Paul isn’t describing a nightmare family; he is describing a legendary one with a divine nature that thinks differently: God accepts this person, so how can I not? I will love them and serve them, because Jesus thought they were worth dying for.
It is the only place in the world where you can walk up to a complete stranger, bare your heart, and they will take it on and walk it out with you.

documents.excerpt: In his final metaphor, which Josh now says may be his favorite, Paul says we are united in God’s temple. Ephesus had two main temples: the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, where pagans worshiped their sleepy gods with feet that can’t walk, which Gentile readers would picture; and Herod’s temple, which Jewish readers would picture.
excerpts: In his final metaphor, which Josh now says may be his favorite, Paul says we are united in God’s temple. Ephesus had two main temples: the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, where pagans worshiped their sleepy gods with feet that can’t walk, which Gentile readers would picture; and Herod’s temple, which Jewish readers would picture.

Paul gives directions to neither. Both would be destroyed, but there is a new construction project underway, and the builder has gone on record that it will last forever. Matthew 16:18: on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.

In Genesis God walked with his people; in Exodus he dwelt in the tabernacle, then in the temple, until Israel sinned and his glory departed. Next his dwelling was the body of Christ: the Word became flesh and tabernacled among them, and man nailed him to a cross. Today, through his Spirit, God dwells in the church. We don’t go to a temple or need a holy magic place; God meets his people wherever they gather in his name and dwells in hearts that trust Jesus. So whose house are we doing church in next week?

documents.excerpt: Some still come to church feeling like foreigners and strangers. No matter how far you are from him, because of the cross, aliens become citizens, strangers become family, enemies become friends, idolaters become temples of the one true God, the hopeless inherit his promises, and those far off are brought near. Not even death can overcome what Christ has done.

Josh pleads: stop, turn to Christ by faith, and trust him. Romans 3 says righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe; there is no difference between Jew and Gentile, for all have sinned, and all are justified freely by his grace. Call on the name of Jesus and he will save you.

documents.excerpt: Josh opens on Mother’s Day by acknowledging that a day like this can stir up joy and pain: grief over a loss, longing for something unfulfilled, or a season of loneliness. God sees you; Psalm 34 reminds us the Lord is close to the brokenhearted.
excerpts: Josh opens on Mother’s Day by acknowledging that a day like this can stir up joy and pain: grief over a loss, longing for something unfulfilled, or a season of loneliness. God sees you; Psalm 34 reminds us the Lord is close to the brokenhearted.

The world wants to rob mothers of their God-given purpose of having and raising the next generation, telling young girls the greatest thing they can do is rise to a position normally reserved for a man, when in actuality it is motherhood. Moms and grandmoms are raising the next generation of pastors, preachers, mothers, CEOs, and Christians who will carry the gospel into the workforce.

Don’t find your worth in what others say about you as a mom; find it in the immeasurable and unconditional love of Jesus who calls you his own. In his hands nothing is wasted. “Be a daughter first and then let that spring into motherhood.”

Josh opens on Mother’s Day by acknowledging that a day like this can stir up joy and pain: grief over a loss, longing for something unfulfilled, or a season of loneliness. God sees you; Psalm 34 reminds us the Lord is close to the brokenhearted.
The world wants to rob mothers of their God-given purpose of having and raising the next generation, telling young girls the greatest thing they can do is rise to a position normally reserved for a man, when in actuality it is motherhood. Moms and grandmoms are raising the next generation of pastors, preachers, mothers, CEOs, and Christians who will carry the gospel into the workforce.
Don’t find your worth in what others say about you as a mom; find it in the immeasurable and unconditional love of Jesus who calls you his own. In his hands nothing is wasted. “Be a daughter first and then let that spring into motherhood.”

documents.excerpt: Most people don’t reject the truth because they don’t understand it; they reject it because it is inconvenient and they don’t like what it demands. The lie is usually easier on us, with less friction, so many take what Jesus called the wide road.
excerpts: Most people don’t reject the truth because they don’t understand it; they reject it because it is inconvenient and they don’t like what it demands. The lie is usually easier on us, with less friction, so many take what Jesus called the wide road.

Some reject the truth because they love the world they can see. Some reject it because it might cost them relationships, which Josh sees more within the church than anywhere else. God’s truth demands an admission of guilt, a guilty plea, so many do what Paul mentions in Romans 1: they exchange the truth about God for a lie, because it opposes behaviors they would rather not give up.

Do the math: the proper response to the truth is humility, but pride, fear, comfort, bitterness, pleasures, and stubbornness all stand in the way. There are many options for stepping into a lie and few for stepping into the truth. The truth isn’t complicated, but the lies are a mighty web, and Josh has prayed all week that the Lord would help open eyes to this great deception.

excerpts: Being alive in Christ isn’t what we deserve: we were by nature deserving of wrath. This phrase upsets most people. The NIV is pretty gentle; the ESV calls those apart from Christ sons of disobedience and children of wrath. And yes, the Greek says wrath.

Most churchgoers don’t know what they are saved from. You are saved from God. Romans 1 says the wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against those who suppress the truth by their wickedness. Too many believers sing love songs to Jesus with no idea what they actually deserve.

God is holy, righteous, and just, and he is holding back the conclusion of time because he desires all to be saved. Don’t mistake his patience for approval or think he has forgotten. We are uncomfortable with an angry God, but the God who holds the universe cannot look on sin without indignation. “Sinner, listen. God is angry at you.”
We are sinners by nature and by choice. God gave you breath and you used it to defy him; we have committed treason and tried to kick him off his throne and sit there ourselves.

documents.excerpt: Satan is the father of lies; the prince of the power of the air is a liar. Don’t underestimate him, but don’t overestimate him either: he can’t be everywhere like God, so he has an army of demons upholding his lies.
excerpts: Satan is the father of lies; the prince of the power of the air is a liar. Don’t underestimate him, but don’t overestimate him either: he can’t be everywhere like God, so he has an army of demons upholding his lies.

His campaign of lies has drifted into places we never thought we would have to defend. Our government went from printing “In God We Trust” to eliminating the Defense of Marriage Act in 2013, and Josh believes we will look back on 2013 as the year we truly lost this society. Christians were painted as hateful bigots for upholding marriage as the sacred bond between a man, a woman, and God for life.

We took the most God-centered human relationship and turned it into a drag show while we watched. Every able-bodied Christian should have been in Washington saying, “Not on our watch,” but we the people lacked backbone, and an entire generation walks around with gender dysphoria because we didn’t want to ruffle feathers.
Josh reminds himself our battle isn’t against flesh and blood. He doesn’t blame a politician or a party; Satan is a liar and a thief. Is he comfortable with God being angry at Satan? “You bet I am.”

God has intrinsic, unchanging attributes such as love and holiness, and relative attributes we see as he relates to creation. No. We do good because he loved us. The pressure is off; nothing depends on you. Salvation is a gift, not a reward; it removes chains rather than adding them.
When Jesus died, the veil of the temple was torn. Jesus our high priest entered the Holy of Holies on our behalf, and his blood spilled out on the altar. No more sacrifices are needed: one sacrifice, the Lamb of God, and God did it all by grace. The enemy thought he had you, but Jesus said, “You are mine.”

excerpts: The church continues its 12-week adventure through Paul’s letter to the Ephesians. Josh encourages everyone to stay locked in; perfect attendance should be the goal, but if you miss a week, catch up on YouTube.

Last week’s message, “Predestined for Praise,” saw Paul open his prison letter from Rome by drawing attention to God’s sovereignty over history and his plan of salvation through Jesus, using massive words like chosen, predestined, and adoption. God initiates salvation; he is its author, sustainer, and finisher, so there is no debate about who chose whom.

That is the best news ever: if you can’t earn it, you can’t lose it. Salvation isn’t like your car keys or your favorite flask left at church on Sunday. Even if you aren’t faithful, he is, and the moment you believe you are marked with the seal of the precious Holy Spirit. God’s salvation isn’t temporary; it is forever.

documents.excerpt: Keep reading, and in verse 15 is one of Paul’s many prison prayers; that is today’s text. The question that always comes up is: if God works out everything in conformity with his will, why pray? Christians tend to fall into fatalism, the belief that all events are predetermined and human actions can’t alter the future, so the outcome is the same no matter what.

The question that always comes up is: if God works out everything in conformity with his will, why pray? Christians tend to fall into fatalism, the belief that all events are predetermined and human actions can’t alter the future, so the outcome is the same no matter what.

This is where pausing for a week hurts our understanding. Josh hopes no one reads the Bible 15 verses at a time with a week in between: “Please stop.” Go read the entire book of Ephesians. Paul didn’t write chapters and verses; he wrote a letter, and it is all one thought. Paul has just said God’s plan never fails, the seal is a guarantee, and God chose his children in Christ before he created light, and then he launches into prayer.

Paul understands that God isn’t just in control of the ending. He works out everything: beginning, middle, and end, past, present, and future. The potter will take it all, shape it all, and conform it all to his good and perfect will.

documents.excerpt: Josh has run into more hyperactive Christians: the pastor who refuses to take a break, the staff member who won’t take a sabbatical, the person always asking, “Why don’t we do this? excerpts: Josh has run into more hyperactive Christians: the pastor who refuses to take a break, the staff member who won’t take a sabbatical, the person always asking, “Why don’t we do this? Have we tried that?” They fall in love with the grind, and you can see it on their face; they look like everything depends on them, and you are exhausted just being around them.

Beware the church that idolizes results and has no concept of rest: 19 weekend services and staff paid minimum wage. That isn’t a church; it is a corporation masquerading as a church. It usually comes with a preacher who won’t share the pulpit and talks about his teaching gift, when his job is to equip the body to use their gifts. “Put my message on TV in every city. I’ll preach 52 weeks a year. I’m irreplaceable.” These are the people we see fall all the time, and it isn’t a coincidence.
The hyperactive Christian misses something important: God can use you when you are energized, and he can use someone else when you need a break.

If you are a lazy Christian, and Josh has been lazy before, sign up to volunteer: get off the couch and into the game. If you are hyperactive, step aside and let someone else get experience. No judgment, just healthy Christian community; grab a pastor or elder and pursue your purpose.

excerpts: To walk this out in a healthy way, we need healthy prayer lives. Josh reads: for this reason, ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all his people, I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers.

Paul identifies them by two things: their trust in Jesus and their love for one another. Josh can’t think of a better definition of a Christian, and Jesus frames it the same way in the two greatest commandments: love God and love others. Love for all kinds of people without loving God isn’t Christianity, maybe just tolerance; loving God but not people isn’t behaving like a Christian.

Do people hear about your faith in Jesus? Do they see your love for his people? Are there rumors about your faith and your love? Nowhere in Scripture are the two separated. And they are just the beginning, which is why Paul keeps praying for them: amazing things happen when the church is filled with prayers for one another.

documents.excerpt: So how should we pray, and for what? Paul prays from prison several times, in the first chapter of letters like Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians; reading all his prison prayers would make a good study for a life group, spouse, or kids.
excerpts: So how should we pray, and for what? Paul prays from prison several times, in the first chapter of letters like Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians; reading all his prison prayers would make a good study for a life group, spouse, or kids.

Most compelling: Paul never asks to be released. He doesn’t request material things or health. He asks for spiritual sight, wisdom, and Christian character for others. He doesn’t ask God to give them something they don’t have; he prays God would open their hearts to see what they already have.
His prayer has four requests: God, help them know you; help them know your call; help them know your riches; help them know your power.

documents.excerpt: Verse 18: I pray that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened. Remember two facts about enlightenment: the sender and the receiver.
excerpts: Verse 18: I pray that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened. Remember two facts about enlightenment: the sender and the receiver.

The sender is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of wisdom and revelation. Isaiah describes him: the Spirit of the Lord will rest on him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. He reveals what man can’t understand on his own, illuminates truth from the word, gives wisdom to apply it and power to live it, and even the motivation to walk in it: the fear of the Lord.

The receiver is the believer. Seeing God with the eyes of your heart creates a deep affection for him, a love that drives out cravings for sin and shows up for the people around you. In Matthew 13 Jesus explains why he speaks in parables: though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand. You can’t intellectually grind your way to spiritual sight; the Spirit of God must open the eyes of the heart.

documents.excerpt: The English language has destroyed the word “hope”: I hope she says yes, I hope the kids move out soon, I hope my mother-in-law doesn’t stay an extra week. It feels like a roll of the dice. Biblical hope is certainty that what hasn’t happened will happen.
excerpts: The English language has destroyed the word “hope”: I hope she says yes, I hope the kids move out soon, I hope my mother-in-law doesn’t stay an extra week. It feels like a roll of the dice. Biblical hope is certainty that what hasn’t happened will happen.

Paul has been explaining in Ephesians 1 that God chose and loved you before creation and will keep you in his love until the story ends. That is our hope: beginning in his love and ending in his love. And if I begin and end in his love, I don’t need to go find another love while I wait for him. Our hope helps us overcome sin, temptation, suffering, and trials. If I see value in what God has for me in his kingdom, I don’t need to chase value down here; if the one true living God accepts me, I don’t need their acceptance.

excerpts: Before the third request, Josh pauses to honor different backgrounds and address confusion about who we pray to. In verse 17, Paul prays to the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father. We believe in one God in three persons, and we pray to the Father, through the Son, by the power of the Holy Spirit. Our Lord taught us to pray to God as Father, so we approach him with confidence, as a son approaches a loving father.

The only reason we can talk to God is the work of Jesus on the cross: our sins separated us, and Jesus died and rose to take them away and reconcile us to the Father. excerpts: We are so unworthy, yet God keeps placing worth on us. Josh tries not to talk about God’s love without also talking about what God hates; some ask why he says the Lord hates, but Scripture teaches it and the church teaches the whole counsel of God, not a fluffy version.

Proverbs 6:16: six things the Lord hates, seven that are detestable to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet quick to rush into evil, a false witness who pours out lies, and a person who stirs up dissension. Haughty eyes alone, a specific kind of pride, bring us all down; we have all looked down on someone.
So how can we behave in ways God hates and still be his treasure? Only one explanation: because of Christ, God now deals with us on the basis of our future, not our past.

documents.excerpt: No authority or power in the physical or spiritual world is greater than Jesus. He isn’t only Savior; he is sovereign. All we need is his name, which is above every other name. He is no longer in the grave; he has ascended, God exalted him, and no enemy can overcome him. Seated at the Father’s right hand, he is King of kings and Lord of lords: “You might as well tattoo it on a thigh.”
excerpts: No authority or power in the physical or spiritual world is greater than Jesus. He isn’t only Savior; he is sovereign. All we need is his name, which is above every other name. He is no longer in the grave; he has ascended, God exalted him, and no enemy can overcome him. Seated at the Father’s right hand, he is King of kings and Lord of lords: “You might as well tattoo it on a thigh.”

Paul prays believers would see the finality of God’s plan. Now we know what Jesus meant: “It is finished.” May we adopt Job’s mindset: “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted.” His power and authority are available to those who believe. Do you believe?

Jesus is the head of the church, the boss, and we are connected to him, the fullness of him who fills everything in every way. Josh loves that Jesus fills this church just as God’s presence filled the temple Solomon built, and through the resurrected, ascended, exalted Christ, the power of the Holy Spirit is available to all Christians by faith.

documents.excerpt: There will be times Christians are tempted to doubt, and Josh has carried heavy doubts. That is why we must pray for one another, so we never forget the power God displayed in faithfully accomplishing salvation through Jesus.
excerpts: There will be times Christians are tempted to doubt, and Josh has carried heavy doubts. That is why we must pray for one another, so we never forget the power God displayed in faithfully accomplishing salvation through Jesus.

How can we doubt when this divine mystery has unraveled before our eyes? How can we feel insecure when we are sealed with a guarantee, forsaken when we are so clearly forgiven, powerless when we have the same power that raised Jesus, or defeated when the power that seated Christ at God’s right hand has seated us there with him? It is time to live lives of power and prayer again. We may not always find resolutions or answers, but we can still love well and always pray with power.

excerpts: The church is launching a series on Paul’s letter to the church in Ephesus, verse by verse. Ephesians has six chapters, each with two sections, so it will be one section a week for 12 weeks: “buckle up.”

Paul isn’t writing in response to anything. The church hasn’t let in some heresy or started worshiping one of the many idols in Ephesus. Instead he writes to strengthen the church and encourage believers in their faith.

The key theme is simple: that every believer who sets eyes on this letter knows exactly what they have in Christ. We might be broke or dirt poor down here, with serious cash flow problems, but as believers we are rich in Christ, and when Christ is flowing, all your needs will be met.

Launching Ephesians, verse by verse
The church is launching a series on Paul’s letter to the church in Ephesus, verse by verse. Ephesians has six chapters, each with two sections, so it will be one section a week for 12 weeks: “buckle up.”
Paul isn’t writing in response to anything. The church hasn’t let in some heresy or started worshiping one of the many idols in Ephesus. Instead he writes to strengthen the church and encourage believers in their faith.
The key theme is simple: that every believer who sets eyes on this letter knows exactly what they have in Christ. We might be broke or dirt poor down here, with serious cash flow problems, but as believers we are rich in Christ, and when Christ is flowing, all your needs will be met.

documents.excerpt: Look at Ephesians like a football game. The first half focuses on our riches in Christ: what do I have now that I didn’t have before? The second half is about our responsibilities in Christ.
excerpts: Look at Ephesians like a football game. The first half focuses on our riches in Christ: what do I have now that I didn’t have before? The second half is about our responsibilities in Christ.

That shift in mindset brings Josh to Jesus’ parable in Luke 12 about faithful and wise servants, which he wants to be: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required. When God entrusts us with more blessings, knowledge, resources, leadership, and authority, he expects more from us in return.

Make a mental note, or write it down because it’s a long series: chapters 1 through 3 are riches; chapters 4 through 6 are responsibilities. You have something you didn’t have before, and now you are expected to do things you weren’t doing before. If you have Christ’s riches, you’ll have some Christ results.

Verse 1: Paul, an apostle
Paul is one of the most well-known names in Christian history. Originally Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin and likely named after Israel’s first king, he was, unlike that king, so obedient and faithful that he persecuted early Christians in Jerusalem in God’s name. Jesus blinded Saul, or gave him sight, depending on how you look at it.
Paul wrote 13 of the 27 New Testament books. A missionary at heart, he launched the church in Ephesus on his third missionary journey. For background, read about his ministry in Ephesus in Acts 20, which the series will reference throughout, and for the challenges he faced there, Acts 19 is a good place to start.
Nearly a decade later, as a prisoner in Rome, Paul writes to his close friends in Ephesus to share what the Lord had taught him about salvation, about Christ, and about his bride, the church.

excerpts: Depending on how you grew up, it may surprise you that Paul calls ordinary believers saints. We think of old dead people who achieved amazing things: St. Thomas Aquinas, St. Mary, St. Peter, or St. Nicholas, better known as Santa Claus.

The Roman Catholic Church formalized a process called canonization: investigating whether a life was above reproach, confirming at least two miracles through the person’s intercessory prayers, and sending it to the Pope for final approval. Josh isn’t against man-made processes that edify the body, but nowhere in the Bible is such a procedure authorized or even necessary; it seems like a process made by man to elevate man.
Nine times in Ephesians Paul refers to the saints, and he isn’t writing to Santa Claus. He is writing to any and all believers blessed enough to read it.

Think of an astronaut, a particularly handsome one in this case. Space doesn’t support life, so the astronaut needs specialized equipment. Believers are no more of this world than an astronaut is of space, and our special equipment is the Holy Spirit.
1 Corinthians 6:19: your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit; you are not your own; you were bought at a price; therefore honor God with your bodies. If you have the Holy Spirit, you are a saint. Every Christian has been set apart and made holy through the perfect righteousness of Jesus Christ credited to us. Josh is honored to be the first to welcome them to sainthood.

documents.excerpt: Note the timing. Verse 4 says he chose us in him before the creation of the world. That matters because salvation is by grace, not works: he chose us in Christ, not in us.
excerpts: Note the timing. Verse 4 says he chose us in him before the creation of the world. That matters because salvation is by grace, not works: he chose us in Christ, not in us.

Why did God choose me? Did he see I would be a good Christian who honors my parents and plays guitar, since the church is always hurting for musicians? “Doug seems like saint material, so let’s grab him.” That is not what the conversation in the Godhead sounded like.

In Deuteronomy God explains why he chose Israel: not because they were more numerous, for they were the fewest of all peoples, but because the Lord loved them and kept the oath he swore to their ancestors. God’s election comes from his love and his faithfulness, his oath-keeping and promise-keeping. That is why Josh keeps barking, “Keep reading,” when people stop reading to debate.

documents.excerpt: Another question: how is it fair that God chose us and not others? Ask questions; Josh feels the church has somewhat failed by making people feel they can’t. Skeptics are welcome as long as the relationship is healthy and fair. But approach God with reverence, or you may end up on the wrong end of a lecture from God like Job: where were you when he hung the stars, when the angels sang as he laid the foundations, when he filled storehouses with avalanches just in case? Who are we to give him a lesson on morality?
excerpts: Another question: how is it fair that God chose us and not others? Ask questions; Josh feels the church has somewhat failed by making people feel they can’t. Skeptics are welcome as long as the relationship is healthy and fair. But approach God with reverence, or you may end up on the wrong end of a lecture from God like Job: where were you when he hung the stars, when the angels sang as he laid the foundations, when he filled storehouses with avalanches just in case? Who are we to give him a lesson on morality?

If you want to talk about fair, fair would be God choosing none of us. The human race chose to reject God, and we rightly deserve judgment and death. “I wasn’t in the garden.” That is pride and inexperience talking; live longer and then let’s talk. If we put you in Eden, you would eat the forbidden fruit too. That God chose any of us is unmerited grace.

The election debate gets heated because people walk around deceived, thinking they don’t deserve God’s wrath and that God owes them salvation. We are so entitled. God isn’t the one with a debt to pay; we are. What we deserve is a global flood, but God kept his promise, and instead of flooding us with water again, he flooded us with grace. A flood of judgment is coming, and the only way through it is to be washed in the blood of Jesus Christ.

Homework: read all of John 6. In verse 37 Jesus says all whom the Father gives him will come to him, and whoever comes he will never drive away. excerpts: Jesus purchased slaves and set them free, and the price was his blood. We live in a sensitive culture and some may not like thinking of themselves as slaves, but that is exactly what you were before Christ redeemed you, and if you sit here unredeemed, you are a slave.

“I’m not a slave. I’m free.” Then don’t sin. How’s it going? You are probably already having sinful thoughts about Josh. If you are free, be perfect. You can’t, because you are a slave to sin, just as you can’t live forever because you are a slave to death.

Forgiven: the pardon that carries sin away
The blessings keep pouring out: he not only redeemed us, he forgives us too. They are similar but different. Redemption deals with our bondage to sin and is a payment that restores freedom; forgiveness deals with the guilt of sin and is a pardon that restores the relationship.
To forgive means to carry away, and Jesus has carried our sins far away: as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us. Not only will you not be held accountable for your sin, you don’t have to be a slave to it anymore.

excerpts: With all wisdom and understanding he made known to us the mystery of his will, to bring unity to all things in heaven and on earth under Christ. All of creation is witnessing this divine mystery now, waiting on the day of the Lord.

Listen to Joe Rogan go on for 15 minutes about a mysterious force behind all things, connecting everything, and you wonder whether he is describing Avatar or a Star Wars movie. When it is a mystery, all we can do is speculate; that is why we have religion and philosophy. God is revealing himself, but those who haven’t seen the mystery are guessing their way through, and it is painful to watch.

We know the mystery of God. He has revealed who he is, who we are, what sin is, and what had to happen to fix what was broken. Sin is tearing everything apart, but in Christ everything will be gathered up and made new. And we not only know about God’s will, we get to participate in it.

documents.excerpt: The Ephesians heard the word and believed, and that faith brought salvation. The same is true for us: when we heard and believed, we were marked with a seal.
excerpts: The Ephesians heard the word and believed, and that faith brought salvation. The same is true for us: when we heard and believed, we were marked with a seal.

First, the seal speaks of a finished transaction. Notice the Godhead: God started salvation before creation, Jesus accomplished it at just the right time, and the Spirit sealed it when we believed. What God starts, he will finish.
Second, it shows ownership. As the song Eli will lead says, he has given us his name; God has put his seal on us because he purchased us to be his own.

Third, it speaks of security and protection. God’s salvation is not temporary or conditional; it is eternal and guaranteed. Hebrews 10:14: by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy.

documents.excerpt: Josh wondered why the old-timers always sang about blessed assurance; now he knows. When he notices how filthy he still is, with thoughts he shouldn’t have and things he does that he doesn’t want to do, he looks at Jesus, then in the mirror, and wonders how he could possibly be saved. The closer you walk with Jesus, the more you notice how rotten you are, and a fear creeps in: am I the one who will hear, “Away from me, Josh, I never knew you”?
excerpts: Josh wondered why the old-timers always sang about blessed assurance; now he knows. When he notices how filthy he still is, with thoughts he shouldn’t have and things he does that he doesn’t want to do, he looks at Jesus, then in the mirror, and wonders how he could possibly be saved. The closer you walk with Jesus, the more you notice how rotten you are, and a fear creeps in: am I the one who will hear, “Away from me, Josh, I never knew you”?

That is when the seal comes in. His blessed assurance rescues Josh from the pit of despair every time he tries to throw himself in, and God whispers, “I started it. I’m going to finish it.” Jesus preaches to him: all whom the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes I will never drive away; this is the will of him who sent me, that I shall lose none of all those he has given me, but raise them up at the last day.

He will not lose you or Josh; we are going to be okay. He is a good shepherd, a great shepherd, and he will not lose a single one. God is the author, sustainer, and finisher of salvation. If it depended on you, you would certainly lose it, but because it depends on God, it is a guarantee. Trust him.

documents.excerpt: First, Jesus lived. Historians inside and outside the faith agree; no one who wants to keep their job would dispute it.
excerpts: First, Jesus lived. Historians inside and outside the faith agree; no one who wants to keep their job would dispute it.

Next, Jesus died, in the most brutal execution method ever conceived. He was beaten and nailed to a cross, and a professional executioner called the time of death at the scene. A spear went up through his rib cage into his heart, and water and blood poured out, indicating certain death.

Then he was buried. Joseph of Arimathea would have wrapped him head to toe in linen with a significant amount of spices. Throw away the picture of a single bed sheet laid over the body; it would have looked more like an ancient mummification, layers and layers of material and spices.

He claims to be God. In John 8 he says, “Before Abraham was born, I am,” using the name God used with Moses at the burning bush. In John 10 he doubles down: “I and the Father are one,” and the people picked up stones to kill him. He tells them to look at his works and let his actions speak.

In John 14 he says he is the only way to God: “I am the way and the truth and the life.” In John 6 he says God sent him on a mission: “I have come down from heaven not to do my will but to do the will of him who sent me,” a will the church reflected on in Gethsemane two days earlier. Jesus is God in the flesh, came to die to take away sin, and said he would rise and give newness of life.

excerpts: Jesus made sure to appear to people who knew him well before the crucifixion, who could identify him by his voice and by characteristics only they would notice. He invited Thomas to touch his nail marks and feel his side, gifting men with absolute proof.

These men grew up reading the scroll of Isaiah. For 40 days he developed witness reports, once appearing to over 500 people at one time. He ate, spoke, taught, moved through solid objects, and vanished instantly.
excerpts: Jesus put witnesses in place so we could share the joy of his victory 2,000 years later, and our grandkids until he comes. For 40 days he developed witness reports, once appearing to over 500 people at one time. He ate, spoke, taught, moved through solid objects, and vanished instantly.

The witnesses included his mother. How hard would it be to convince your mom you are God, when you can’t even take out the trash when she asks? Josh pauses to have everyone hug their mom or blow her a kiss.

They included James, the brother of Jesus. It would take a resurrection miracle for your brother to call you God, yet James became the pastor of the church in Jerusalem. They included Paul, who wrote today’s text, who persecuted Christians as worshipers of a false god until Jesus appeared to him and he started praying for them instead. Minds and hearts don’t change like that without divine intervention.

For centuries Christians have been baptized to identify with Jesus in his death, burial, and resurrection, believing that like him they will die, be buried, and rise.
excerpts: The trail of witnesses runs from one woman, Mary, to 11 men, to 500, to 3,000, to billions of believers across history. For centuries Christians have been baptized to identify with Jesus in his death, burial, and resurrection, believing that like him they will die, be buried, and rise.

In Romans 6 Paul says we were buried with him through baptism into death so that we too may live a new life, and Josh loves the last phrase: if we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.

So Christians were baptized worldwide, took communion to remember his body and blood, and started meeting on Sunday. Getting Jews who loved to meet on Saturday to change their calendar was a huge deal, but not after witnessing Christ raised. Do you see how little tradition matters when Jesus is at the center? Today Christianity is the world’s largest faith community and Jesus the most revered name in human history.

documents.excerpt: What does it mean that Christ is the first fruits? Josh travels back to Leviticus 23: when Israel entered the land and reaped its harvest, they were to bring the priest a sheaf of the first grain, and he would wave it before the Lord so it would be accepted on their behalf, on the day after the Sabbath.
excerpts: What does it mean that Christ is the first fruits? Josh travels back to Leviticus 23: when Israel entered the land and reaped its harvest, they were to bring the priest a sheaf of the first grain, and he would wave it before the Lord so it would be accepted on their behalf, on the day after the Sabbath.

In the Jewish calendar Passover came first, then a Sabbath, then the feast of first fruits. That is what Paul means in Romans 5 when he says Christ came at just the right time. Christ, the Lamb of God, died on Passover; his body lay in the tomb on the Sabbath; and early on the first day, as the sun came over the horizon, he rose on the morning of the feast of first fruits.

Christ is the sheaf waved before the Lord on your behalf. He is one sheaf out of an entire harvest, and when the first sheaf had been waved, the whole harvest was considered brought before the Lord: dedicated, consecrated, and accepted. When Jesus was raised, all God’s chosen were virtually risen in him.

Have you surrendered your life to him? Have you been crucified with Christ, or are you still living for yourself? If you see him on the cross and know it should have been you, then when you see the empty tomb, know that will be you one day.
excerpts: Josh has one question: are you part of the harvest? Do you believe in the resurrection of Jesus Christ for your sin, that eternal life is in him alone? Have you surrendered your life to him? Have you been crucified with Christ, or are you still living for yourself? If you see him on the cross and know it should have been you, then when you see the empty tomb, know that will be you one day.

Do you hate the things you once loved? Do you have more power against temptation? Do you want to be like Jesus, or do you just want his treasures? Josh can’t judge anyone, but he wants to empower them to judge themselves before God, uncover the truth in their hearts, and call on him to fix it.

He believes Jesus rose and that all who trust in him will be clothed in immortality and made new. On the day the last trumpet sounds, what Isaiah and Hosea wrote over 700 years before Christ will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?”

If you see him on the cross and know it should have been you, then when you see the empty tomb, know that will be you one day.
Do you hate the things you once loved? Do you have more power against temptation? Do you want to be like Jesus, or do you just want his treasures? Josh can’t judge anyone, but he wants to empower them to judge themselves before God, uncover the truth in their hearts, and call on him to fix it.
He believes Jesus rose and that all who trust in him will be clothed in immortality and made new. On the day the last trumpet sounds, what Isaiah and Hosea wrote over 700 years before Christ will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? documents.excerpt: Steve is the firstborn, and firstborns had a window with their parents’ full attention until something terrible happens: a sibling arrives, and the glorious throne must be shared, with fewer gifts, fewer photos, and more responsibility.
excerpts: Steve is the firstborn, and firstborns had a window with their parents’ full attention until something terrible happens: a sibling arrives, and the glorious throne must be shared, with fewer gifts, fewer photos, and more responsibility.

Researchers suggest explicit memories form around three or four, but one of Steve’s clearest came at two, when his baby sister arrived. It is also the first time he knew he had sinned. While his mom’s attention was on the new baby, he snuck into his parents’ bedroom, opened her Estée Lauder perfume, and jumped on the bare mattress with the bottle upside down. Maybe he wanted his mom to enjoy the scent forever; more likely it was vengeance for sharing the spotlight. She says the mattress was never the same.

When the last drop left the bottle, he knew he had done something very wrong, and his solution was the same as mankind’s since the Garden of Eden: he covered it and hid. He fetched a stack of paper plates and covered the whole bed. He did get his mom’s attention, just not the kind he or his backside wanted.

Steve thought of that first memory of sin while studying the last half of Ezra, where the people’s sin is exposed. Like Israel, through failure and forgetting what is important, we become exiles trying to get back to God, with much worse than spilled perfume and paper plates. Our capacity for sin can take us fast and far from God’s presence, but the good news is that redemption is more than possible through Jesus Christ, and God will reclaim and redeem his people throughout the end of Ezra.

documents.excerpt: Up to now Ezra, the man believed to have written the book, hasn’t appeared, but he takes the lead from here. His lineage shows he is a Levite, a priest, and verse 6 calls him a scribe or teacher well-versed in the law of Moses.
excerpts: Up to now Ezra, the man believed to have written the book, hasn’t appeared, but he takes the lead from here. His lineage shows he is a Levite, a priest, and verse 6 calls him a scribe or teacher well-versed in the law of Moses.

We may picture a scribe meticulously copying texts, and that was part of it. By Jesus’ time the scribes, closely associated with the Pharisees, had largely shifted from devout, reliable teachers to religious lawyers, and Jesus called them out, as in John 5:39–40: you search the Scriptures because you think in them you have eternal life, yet you refuse to come to me.

Ezra is unlike the scribes who followed centuries later. Verse 10 says he devoted himself to the study and observance of the law and to teaching it in Israel. He doesn’t let zeal for God’s law consume him into self-righteousness; that is where the line is. He uses his knowledge to teach, his heart is for God and his people, and in many ways he holds a pastoral role rarely seen in the Old Testament.

Verse 6 says Ezra came up from Babylon, the king granted him everything he asked, and the hand of the Lord his God was on him. Growing up among the exiles under Persian rule, unable to serve in temple worship because there was no temple, Ezra devoted himself to seeing God’s word kept and taught to those in exile. Out of that devotion God calls him to lead the next group back. The first group rebuilt the temple physically; Ezra must rebuild God’s people spiritually.

excerpts: A little extra study reveals something about the timeline. Verse 7 places this in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes I, better known as King Ahasuerus. That matters for two reasons. First, about 58 years pass between Ezra 6 and Ezra 7, easy for the casual reader to miss.

Second, and Steve loves this, the story of Esther happens inside that gap: on a timeline, Esther cuts Ezra in half. Mordecai stood against the evil Haman, who sought to wipe out the Jews across the Persian Empire, and when Esther hesitated to use her access to the king, he replied in Esther 4:14: if you remain silent, relief will arise from another place, “and who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this.”

Esther’s faith and boldness did more than save her people in one moment. The reclaiming God does through Ezra and Nehemiah is only possible because of her “such a time as this,” and both men benefited, still having access and favor with Persian royalty years later.

excerpts: Some estimate the Persian Empire was about 20% Jewish by then. That meant representation, but also a problem: syncretism, the blending of different religious beliefs and practices, a common phenomenon throughout history, had set in.

Far from oppressed captives, the Israelites were doing quite well in Persian-ruled Babylon. That is why only about 42,000 went with Zerubbabel and fewer than 2,000 go with Ezra. Life is good, with homes, families, and businesses; why go back? Nevertheless, Ezra gathers a willing band, whose names are given in chapter 8. Chapter 7, verses 8–9, says he left Babylon on the first day of the first month and arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth, “for the gracious hand of his God was on him.”
Steve loves how Ezra constantly credits God’s gracious hand: a humble follower of God, a keeper of God’s law, and a leader of God’s people.

documents.excerpt: The takeaway: God wants you to stay close to him no matter the season and be ready for his next in your life. Imagine the impact on a scribe of copying the Torah word by word; if young people today copied the whole Bible, it would take a long time but be very impactful. We have God’s full, living, active word at our fingertips 24/7. Do we treat it as such?
excerpts: The takeaway: God wants you to stay close to him no matter the season and be ready for his next in your life. Imagine the impact on a scribe of copying the Torah word by word; if young people today copied the whole Bible, it would take a long time but be very impactful. We have God’s full, living, active word at our fingertips 24/7. Do we treat it as such?

David declares in Psalm 119: how can a young person stay pure? By obeying your word; I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you. Ezra was devoted to God’s word, reading, studying, memorizing, and teaching it, and we have the privilege to do the same. We can, and we must.

Ezra held an important government job but never lost sight of his true role as God’s servant. God’s word kept him close to God in exile, amid Babylon’s distractions and a culture urging him to settle for less than God’s purposes. Though he wasn’t in a traditional priestly role, he held on tight to God and was prepared for what was next.

Ezra’s trepidation was justified: about 2,000 travelers carrying silver and gold worth several million dollars today. Perhaps he recited a psalm he knew well: the Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?

documents.excerpt: This was no small issue; Ezra knew it violated God’s covenant. The cause is apparent, even somewhat understandable: Zerubbabel’s large first wave was mostly young men, since it was a hostile place with heavy work, so men outnumbered women, and by Ezra’s arrival many had sought wives outside God’s covenant community.
excerpts: This was no small issue; Ezra knew it violated God’s covenant. The cause is apparent, even somewhat understandable: Zerubbabel’s large first wave was mostly young men, since it was a hostile place with heavy work, so men outnumbered women, and by Ezra’s arrival many had sought wives outside God’s covenant community.
It was still a clear breaking of God’s law. Steve reads Deuteronomy 7, which Ezra would have had memorized: make no treaty with them, show them no mercy, do not intermarry with them.

This is not racism at work; the issue is religious and cultural identity. The Jewish people were keepers of the line of promise going back to Abraham, and Ezra saw intermarriage as a threat to the lineage through which the promised Messiah would come and to Israel’s identity as God’s holy, set-apart nation. A foreign mother holding on to pagan practices would likely teach them to her children. As William Ross Wallace is famously quoted, “The hand that rocks the cradle rules the world.” The syncretism Ezra was trying to remove the people from in Persia had already gone ahead of him.

excerpts: This is a difficult section. Some read it and think it harsh toward the women and children sent away from husbands and fathers. But there is good news in the two-month process: Ezra could have ordered everyone to divorce their wives immediately, but instead he allowed each case to be investigated. Why?

Read the genealogy of Jesus: is every woman a pure Israelite? No: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba. So it might not be a big deal in every case, which is why they needed a process, and God’s mercy comes out here. Old Testament law permitted marriage to a non-Jew on one condition, and Moses had a foreign wife: she renounced her old religion and became a proselyte, fully devoted, with her ties to paganism and her family severed.

One man might prove his wife has converted, worships Yahweh alone beside him, and submits to God’s law while teaching their children: she can stay. The next might say she wants the children exposed to all kinds of thinking so they can decide for themselves, and her parents bring a few of their idols when they visit, no big deal: she must go.

Old Testament law also required a divorced wife to be cared for financially; they were well supplied, free to remarry, and not thrown to the wolves. Each man is listed by name in Scripture to show he had put away his wife, some with children, and been restored to proper standing before God.

A hard passage, and mercy in the process
This is a difficult section. Some read it and think it harsh toward the women and children sent away from husbands and fathers. But there is good news in the two-month process: Ezra could have ordered everyone to divorce their wives immediately, but instead he allowed each case to be investigated. Why?
Read the genealogy of Jesus: is every woman a pure Israelite? No: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba. So it might not be a big deal in every case, which is why they needed a process, and God’s mercy comes out here. In Ezra 9 and 10 the people confessed first, but they didn’t stop at “my bad, God” and carry on as normal, or “it’s too late now.” The next step was radical repentance: they turned from their sin by sending away pagan wives unwilling to submit to God’s law.

You can confess without repenting, admitting your sin and going right back to it, and that is a dangerous place to live. Repentance declares your intention to turn away in the power of the Holy Spirit and follow through: “God, I don’t want to do this anymore. excerpts: A major issue in today’s church is building a religion around our faithfulness when the world needs his true church built on his faithfulness. What is your foundation built on? In church everyone wants to shout “his,” but anyone can claim anything; what if we inspected the evidence flowing from your life, your marriage, your home?

Does it sound like, “As long as I do all the things right, everything will be fine; as long as I remain faithful”? That sounds exhausting. What sounds liberating is this: he finished all things. Everything is fine even when it’s not; if I fail today, he still lays me down to rest tonight; even when I’m not faithful, he is.

Depending on our own faithfulness has produced millions of heartless Christians so worried about their own standing with God that they have no time to worry about the stranger’s. The Christian journey is about the faithfulness of God, not the faithfulness of you.

Every generation needs constant reminding that God is faithful, and that’s why we gather. Many years later Paul told persecuted young Christians in Thessalonica, “The one who calls you is faithful. excerpts: All the way back to Moses, the message before Israel entered Canaan was: know therefore that the Lord your God is God, the faithful God keeping his covenant of love to a thousand generations, and repaying to their face those who hate him. Every generation needs constant reminding that God is faithful, and that’s why we gather. Many years later Paul told persecuted young Christians in Thessalonica, “The one who calls you is faithful. Hang in there. He will do it.”
God’s promises aren’t the empty promises of a politician; they are divine guarantees. As certain as you are that the sun will rise tomorrow, that’s how certain Josh is that his Son will return.

In The Knowledge of the Holy, A. W. Tozer wrote that God, being who he is, cannot cease to be what he is, cannot act out of character with himself, and is at once faithful and immutable. Josh couldn’t stop thinking about that line all week. The Christian journey is less about your pursuit of faithfulness and more about your view of the faithfulness of God.

Paul told Timothy that if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself: the Lord won’t back away from his promise to save those who trust him, just as he won’t back away from his promise to condemn those who don’t. Everyone’s theology would improve if they kept reading past John 3:16: God did not send his Son to condemn the world but to save it; whoever believes is not condemned, but whoever does not believe stands condemned already.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 7, 2025 · Reclaim: The Book of Ezra
documents.excerpt: Many Christians have become so focused on their faith that they have taken their eyes off the faithful one. Some trust the strength of their own faith rather than God himself; faith becomes what they celebrate and what carries them. That is pride decorated in religious wrapping paper; it leads to legalism and kills your witness.
excerpts: Many Christians have become so focused on their faith that they have taken their eyes off the faithful one. Some trust the strength of their own faith rather than God himself; faith becomes what they celebrate and what carries them. That is pride decorated in religious wrapping paper; it leads to legalism and kills your witness.

Others use faith to control God: if I just believe enough, God will bless me; if I come to church, maybe God will save my marriage or my children will call me back. That is a self-centered faith, not a God-centered one. Faith isn’t a tool to get what you want; it is a gift from God to illuminate one truth: you need Jesus Christ.

For some, being a Christian has become more about belonging to a group, denomination, or tradition than knowing Christ and sharing him. Many Christians idolize community and, to protect the idol, call it Christian community, as if the title made it an acceptable replacement for a personal relationship with the living God. Josh says these are hard things he has wrestled with all week, but he is commanded to remind God’s people: “If you don’t like it, take it up with him.”
True faith always keeps God at the center: not trusting our ability to believe, obey, or belong, but saying, “Lord, I need you every hour.”

Newton’s third law, that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, is true of the spiritual world too. A rocket launches by pushing gases downward; when God launches a work, Satan doesn’t like it. Eli showed last week that God turned on a light in Jerusalem, and in chapter 4 the bugs start circling the light. New Christians should remember that God’s work frustrates the enemy and expect pushback; it’s called spiritual warfare.
The year is 535 BC. The seventy-year Babylonian captivity has ended, Cyrus the Great is dead, and the temple foundations are laid.

excerpts: The Samaritans were part Jewish and part many other peoples, which is why in Jesus’ day Judeans saw them as half-breeds and not true worshipers of Yahweh; in John 4 the woman says, “You are a Jew and I’m a Samaritan woman. How can you ask me for a drink?”

Why is their help a big deal? If you start building a temple together, you might start building a life together. Josh imagines the invitation to ride donkeys after finishing the west wall; they start hanging out, then intermarry, which the law of Moses forbade. Israel was a nation set apart, called to be a conduit for God’s messianic worldwide blessing; if Israel is corrupted, the blessing is impacted. Israel’s battle with corruption isn’t unlike ours with the false gospel today.

The church has to stop involving itself in things that could compromise its testimony. Paul tells the Corinthians not to be yoked together with unbelievers: what fellowship can light have with darkness, and, Josh’s favorite, what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever? The church has given up much ground here, and Josh believes the Lord is trying to take some back today.

documents.excerpt: To anyone with influence over a young unmarried person, whether a three-year-old daughter, an eight-year-old son, or, in Josh’s case, an eighteen-year-old daughter: if you train your children in righteousness but fail to warn them of the devastation of not marrying a Christian, you have failed. excerpts: To anyone with influence over a young unmarried person, whether a three-year-old daughter, an eight-year-old son, or, in Josh’s case, an eighteen-year-old daughter: if you train your children in righteousness but fail to warn them of the devastation of not marrying a Christian, you have failed. To young adults in such a relationship: get out now. Run.

Like a doctor’s note that gets you out of work or a family reunion, Josh offers to write a custom pastor’s note excusing you from that relationship. If God hasn’t changed their heart, do you really think you can? A single believer can live a more fulfilled life than a believer married to an unbeliever.

Marriage and sex are amazing when used according to God’s blueprints and awful when not, but they are not the pinnacle of the human experience; knowing and following Jesus is. Believers live in Christ’s kingdom of righteousness, freedom, light, and eternal life; unbelievers in Satan’s kingdom of lawlessness, captivity, darkness, and death. With different standards, convictions, morals, hopes, and dreams, how will you build a home, or teach your children to obey the Lord when your spouse doesn’t? In short, you can’t.

Josh offers himself and Kristen to sit down with any couple. Don’t get married until you’ve gone through Christian-led, biblically based premarital counseling. Yes, it costs money, but not as much as a divorce. If the relationship is real and God’s best for you, it will work.

Marriage and sex are amazing when used according to God’s blueprints and awful when not, but they are not the pinnacle of the human experience; knowing and following Jesus is. Believers live in Christ’s kingdom of righteousness, freedom, light, and eternal life; unbelievers in Satan’s kingdom of lawlessness, captivity, darkness, and death. With different standards, convictions, morals, hopes, and dreams, how will you build a home, or teach your children to obey the Lord when your spouse doesn’t? In short, you can’t.
Josh offers himself and Kristen to sit down with any couple. Don’t get married until you’ve gone through Christian-led, biblically based premarital counseling. Yes, it costs money, but not as much as a divorce. If the relationship is real and God’s best for you, it will work.

documents.excerpt: We can’t isolate ourselves from unbelievers entirely, because we need to be a witness. But we can set boundaries, and we are never required to violate them to witness. Jesus sought out sinners to win them; he never sinned with them.
excerpts: We can’t isolate ourselves from unbelievers entirely, because we need to be a witness. But we can set boundaries, and we are never required to violate them to witness. Jesus sought out sinners to win them; he never sinned with them.

Josh reads Jesus’ prayer for his disciples: they are not of the world any more than I am; my prayer is not that you take them out of the world but that you protect them from the evil one; sanctify them by the truth; as you sent me into the world, I have sent them. Verse 18 is huge: why did God send Jesus into the world? Matthew 1: to save sinners.

So there is only one reason to have unbelievers in your life: to tell them about Jesus. It isn’t a popular take, but it isn’t to foster a friendship for years until you finally feel comfortable sharing the gospel. Are you the Holy Spirit? Can you read hearts? Tell them now and tell them often. They may reject you, but take heart, believer: they hated him first.

excerpts: Remember the law of motion: turn them away the first time and they won’t stop. Next, the peoples around them set out to discourage Judah and make them afraid to build.

Satan’s playbook isn’t very thick. Like football’s pass or run, it is deceive or devour. In verse 2 he took the role of a serpent and tried to deceive: let us help, we’re cut from the same cloth. Israel’s leaders said no.

If you get nothing else, get this: if you think victory comes after the first battle, you are in for a rude awakening. He’ll be back, and if he can’t deceive you like a serpent, he’ll devour you like a lion. If they can’t tear the project down from within, they’ll appeal to the king to stop it, and it worked: verse 5 says they bribed officials to frustrate their plans from Cyrus down to Darius.

excerpts: Here is where it gets interesting. Chapter 5 verse 1: Haggai and Zechariah prophesied to the Jews in the name of the God of Israel. Why didn’t the work restart when Darius took the throne? They are in the second year of his reign, so the remnant may have lost a year or more. The book of Haggai tells why: the people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the Lord’s house; is it a time for you to live in your paneled houses while this house remains a ruin?

What does this have to do with us? All Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness, and Josh believes there is a timeless truth here. The decree goes out and the work comes to a complete standstill, and much of the modern American church would applaud: look at those obedient, law-abiding Christians.

Then two minor prophets show up, and the gist of their sermon series is: what are you doing? You are perfecting your backyard barbecue and the guest house while leaving God’s house in ruins. Get up and build; do what God sent you here to do.

Josh imagines someone emailing Haggai and Zechariah: don’t you know that’s against the law, that it violates the king’s edict? He can see Haggai drafting a response, “because I’ve done this before”: yes, the law says don’t build; the law of God says build. So get up and build.

Obedience to earthly authorities is required, since they have been instituted by God, Romans 13; but we are to reject laws that contradict God’s commands. excerpts: If the law says stop and God’s law says don’t stop, we don’t stop. Obedience to earthly authorities is required, since they have been instituted by God, Romans 13; but we are to reject laws that contradict God’s commands. Christians are called to be the best citizens, but our ultimate loyalty is to God. If the law says don’t pray, but God’s word says pray always, will you stop?

Daniel kept praying when it was illegal, and God delivered him from the lions’ den. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar’s idol. When a powerful institution tried to shut down Peter and the apostles, they kept preaching Christ crucified and raised, saying, “We must obey God rather than human beings.”

If a Christian must be disobedient, we are called to be the most wonderful, peaceful, humble, kind disobedient citizens ever, like the disciples leaving the Sanhedrin rejoicing that they got to suffer for the name. Spoiled American Christians may never face this dilemma, but we should be ready in case the Lord considers us worthy to suffer for the name.

documents.excerpt: Another timeless truth in Ezra 5: God’s word spurs God’s people on to keep doing God’s work. Just as the gospel can rescue horrific men like Josh, God’s word can stir revival in the most horrific institutions. Give him a crooked church, the word of God, and a few good men, and it can be straightened out; give him the most messed-up man and the gospel of Christ, and that can be fixed too.
