excerpts: Jairus approached Jesus first, but the woman received help first. In the kingdom of God there isn’t upper class and lower class. Jairus was an important synagogue official; the woman was an anonymous nobody; Jesus welcomes them both.

Jairus was about to lose a daughter who brought him joy for 12 years; the woman was about to lose an affliction that brought her suffering for 12 years. Jairus was no doubt wealthy, but no money could save his daughter; the woman was bankrupt from doctors. He had every resource and people ready to do whatever he asked; she had simply run out of options. Both found everything they needed at the feet of Jesus.

excerpts: There isn’t much time, the crowds are chaotic, and then Jesus realizes power has gone out from him and asks, “Who touched my clothes?” The word for power is dynamis, where we get “dynamite”; he experiences an explosion of power and knows there has been a healing. The rescue mission grinds to a halt in the middle of the street.

Imagine Jairus’s heart hitting the floor, going from leading the charge to a miracle at home to standing still listening to this woman’s testimony. Everyone is confused: Jesus went to seminary, not medical school, but triage! She has had a chronic issue for 12 years and can wait 12 more minutes; the child is acute. In our day Jesus would probably get hit with a malpractice suit.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 9, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: Josh’s wife made him wait 45 minutes at the altar. Having grown up with two older sisters, he imagines every bridesmaid taking turns telling his fiancée it’s not too late to sneak out the back, with a chopper on standby, ending with his future mother-in-law’s final appeal, “Are you sure?”, and everyone redoing their makeup after each appeal. That, he speculates, is why weddings run late.
excerpts: Josh’s wife made him wait 45 minutes at the altar. Having grown up with two older sisters, he imagines every bridesmaid taking turns telling his fiancée it’s not too late to sneak out the back, with a chopper on standby, ending with his future mother-in-law’s final appeal, “Are you sure?”, and everyone redoing their makeup after each appeal. That, he speculates, is why weddings run late.

But 45 minutes late for his wife is actually right on time. When he saw her, she looked amazing, the wait was worth it, and she has only gotten more amazing; he’ll show up late anywhere with her. He is slowly learning that just because he says they are late doesn’t mean they are; timing is relative.

excerpts: Our culture would ask why Jesus didn’t protect her privacy and dignity when she wanted to keep it to herself. Josh gives a $5 answer and a $50 answer.

The $5 answer: God’s power in your life doesn’t belong in a closet. Show discernment, but by nature a witness must testify. Part of Josh’s testimony is that the Lord took a lust-filled man and made him a more loving husband, turning his lusts into love for his bride. He shares it only in appropriate spaces, and wouldn’t on a family Sunday, but he shares it because the power that changed his life, marriage, and home can change yours too. Call on the name of Jesus and meet him at his feet.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 9, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: No one really talks about mortality anymore; we are afraid of it. Josh thinks Christians need to be aggressive with this conversation, and nothing gets to the point quicker than asking, “What do you think happens when we die?”
excerpts: No one really talks about mortality anymore; we are afraid of it. Josh thinks Christians need to be aggressive with this conversation, and nothing gets to the point quicker than asking, “What do you think happens when we die?”

There are two leading views. The secularist or humanist, like Richard Dawkins and Bertrand Russell, believes death is the absolute end of existence. The theist, like Thomas Aquinas and C. S. Lewis, believes God made us eternal beings and that something is very wrong about death, which is why it terrifies us and why Josh believes Jesus weeps at the tomb of Lazarus. Which view do you hold?

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis argues that our yearning for eternity points to our being created for it. Fish don’t complain about being wet; they flop around when they are out of the water. If I find a desire nothing in this world can satisfy, the only logical explanation is that I was made for another world.

Josh puts it this way: conflict in the head, confidence in the heart, a gift from God. Ecclesiastes 3 says he set eternity in the human heart. The body is more than an accidental biological machine; it was designed for eternity, and it kicks and screams because we aren’t where we are supposed to be. Meanwhile Jesus sits next to your bed: “Hey sleeper, it’s time to wake up.”

excerpts: You know what it took and what it cost to make the extension of his hand possible. Jesus was forsaken so that every time we feel separation we can come back and reconnect. Paul tells the Corinthians he was crucified in weakness yet lives by God’s power; he became weak so we could be strong.

Jesus knew the only way to resurrection life was through death. In Gethsemane he asked if there was another way, and the answer was no. He didn’t push back, negotiate, or complain; he said, “Not my will, but yours be done.”

Josh calls the church to adopt this mindset: conform to his ways, journey with Jesus without worrying about his methods or timing, take his hand, and say, “Lord, do what you will. I know you love me. I will follow you to the grave because I know you made a way out on the other side.”

Jesus has already set himself apart from every other first-century street preacher; as last week showed, his take on the Sabbath drew a clear line in the sand. excerpts: The church picks up its journey through Mark in chapter 3. Jesus has already set himself apart from every other first-century street preacher; as last week showed, his take on the Sabbath drew a clear line in the sand. You either witnessed the great physician, loved him, and told the world about him, or you heard his teaching, hated him, and told Rome about him.

Every time he healed someone, that person told their friends, they came to see, and before long the multitudes came rushing in. Those who were healed bore witness to their unhealed friends. Sound familiar? The strategic plan for kingdom growth hasn’t changed: the healed invite the unhealed to Jesus.

If you’ve experienced the grace of God, the only logical next step is to tell others. As the kingdom grows we are robbing hell of men’s souls; this is the great robbery. You are not healed to stand still and keep your mouth shut. You are healed to serve the unhealed. This is why you have breath in your lungs.

documents.excerpt: The number twelve is significant because there are twelve tribes in Israel. It isn’t just to keep things neat; it is a strong statement from the Godhead. In Genesis God started with Jacob’s twelve sons, and Josh has the church try to name them together. excerpts: The number twelve is significant because there are twelve tribes in Israel. It isn’t just to keep things neat; it is a strong statement from the Godhead. In Genesis God started with Jacob’s twelve sons, and Josh has the church try to name them together. In Exodus God built them into a mighty nation chosen to bring the Messiah into the world so that through him all nations could be blessed.

That promise is in Genesis 12: “all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.” Israel walked into the promise but fell into a spiritual wilderness, ready to reject her own Messiah. Yet God was establishing a new, holy nation; Peter says we are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. As the twelve tribes founded Israel, the twelve apostles were the foundation of this new nation, and in Matthew 21 Jesus says the kingdom will be taken away and given to a people who will produce its fruit.

A disciple learns by doing, like an apprentice or, for Star Wars nerds, a Padawan. Jesus was training these men to keep establishing a kingdom that bears fruit until he returns. Many call this the church age or the age of grace; it started at Pentecost, is happening right now, and will continue until Jesus returns, and it all started with these twelve men.

That promise is in Genesis 12: “all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.” Israel walked into the promise but fell into a spiritual wilderness, ready to reject her own Messiah. Yet God was establishing a new, holy nation; Peter says we are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. As the twelve tribes founded Israel, the twelve apostles were the foundation of this new nation, and in Matthew 21 Jesus says the kingdom will be taken away and given to a people who will produce its fruit.
A disciple learns by doing, like an apprentice or, for Star Wars nerds, a Padawan. Jesus was training these men to keep establishing a kingdom that bears fruit until he returns. Many call this the church age or the age of grace; it started at Pentecost, is happening right now, and will continue until Jesus returns, and it all started with these twelve men.
documents.title: Twelve tribes, twelve apostles — Revealing the Kingdom

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 2, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: Naming is an act of authority, and whatever names you owns you. In pastoral counseling Josh tries to identify what has named a person. If your identity is wealth, you’re nothing without it; if it is being a mom, you’re nothing when they don’t need you; if it is being an athlete, you’re nothing when you can’t perform; if it is politics, every four years you face an existential crisis. When those things name you, you are always on the verge of crisis; when Jesus names you, you find solid ground.

If your identity is wealth, you’re nothing without it; if it is being a mom, you’re nothing when they don’t need you; if it is being an athlete, you’re nothing when you can’t perform; if it is politics, every four years you face an existential crisis. When those things name you, you are always on the verge of crisis; when Jesus names you, you find solid ground.

That changes everything. A Christian businessman praises the Lord when business is good and when it is slow, because his value is in what Jesus says about him, not the bottom line. A Christian mom raises her kids in service to the Lord, and when the kids start ghosting her, she is good, because her Savior always listens; mothers need to hear that they are his before they are theirs. A Christian athlete is still valuable when the strength is gone, because he is still his.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 2, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: Josh is clear: Jesus gives no permission here to disown or disrespect your birth family because you now have an adopted one. Most of us don’t come from an ideal family, and some really struggle with the families we have been given, but we must approach this with discernment in light of what all Scripture teaches about family.
excerpts: Josh is clear: Jesus gives no permission here to disown or disrespect your birth family because you now have an adopted one. Most of us don’t come from an ideal family, and some really struggle with the families we have been given, but we must approach this with discernment in light of what all Scripture teaches about family.

Remember the family’s accusation in verse 21: he is out of his mind. If Jesus went home with them, he would give his accusers more ammunition: “See, he knows something’s not right; gather round, he needs our prayers.” Instead he uses the moment to introduce a spiritual family of all who do the will of God. Since his half brothers didn’t yet believe, Jesus seems to have felt more at home with sinners, tax collectors, and even Zealots than with James or Jude.

Jesus isn’t telling believers to abandon their families to serve God; often your greatest service to the Lord will be within your family. God never commands that he be your only relationship, only your only God: God first and greatest, family next. A family emergency would be different, because it is God’s will that we care and provide for our families; in 1 Timothy the young pastor is told that anyone who does not provide for their own household has denied the faith. But caring for your family is different than letting it pull you off the front lines. We can’t let those dearest to us hijack us from the will of God.

documents.excerpt: Jesus asks whether you bring in a lamp to put it under a bowl or bed instead of on its stand; whatever is hidden is meant to be disclosed. “Consider carefully what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you,” and whoever has will be given more.
excerpts: Jesus asks whether you bring in a lamp to put it under a bowl or bed instead of on its stand; whatever is hidden is meant to be disclosed. “Consider carefully what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you,” and whoever has will be given more.

The lamp was a clay dish of oil with a wick, and it had to burn the oil, but if you use it up you will be supplied with more; if you choose not to use it, you lose it. The apostles were like that lamp, and they teach us to be too. To light the world with truth you must first be filled with the truth, so the more we hear the word, the better prepared we are to share it. The moment we think we know all there is to know, what we thought we had is gone. You can’t give what you don’t have; how much light you take in determines how much light you share.

This kingdom runs on his word, and his servants carry his word. Don’t waste your breath on cover-ups and pretenders: one day God will reveal all things, and there will be surprises. It isn’t your job to uncover them; the Lord will do it.

excerpts: As the band comes up, Josh closes with the parable of the seed: the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which grows into the largest of garden plants with branches where birds perch in its shade. Depending on where you stand, that is either a great encouragement or a grave warning.

Jesus predicts a kingdom of unimaginable size from tiny beginnings. He started with twelve, it grew to tens of thousands, then dwindled to only three. Just when all hope seemed lost, on that morning there was one, then three again, then ten, because Thomas was still doubting, then “My Lord and my God,” and there were eleven. The rock preached at Pentecost and there were 3,000; worship roared, baptism waters stirred, the Spirit was received, and the church of Jesus Christ was born. Then 5,000, 10,000, hundreds of thousands, nations turning to Christ.

The church is a mess and Satan seeks to destroy her, but the world keeps hearing about Jesus, the gospel keeps growing, and it still grows today. One day saints from every nation will gather before his throne and sing a new song: “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slain, and with your blood you purchased for God members of every tribe and language and people and nation.” Josh asks the church to stand and thank the Lord together.

documents.excerpt: Last week the church saw the announcement of God’s servant in two parts: his message, “Repent and believe the good news,” and his method, which has messed up people like Josh and the church.
excerpts: Last week the church saw the announcement of God’s servant in two parts: his message, “Repent and believe the good news,” and his method, which has messed up people like Josh and the church.

God is working on Josh, and part of him daily wrestles with the man he was: the heaviness of having hurt so many people with his words and actions, a trail of pain that can overwhelm him. He also wrestles with what is ahead. Everywhere he looks there is evil and temptation, and in one moment he could fail to say no and tarnish his Redeemer’s reputation. He looks at others falling and thinks he’ll never do that, then realizes they probably thought that too.

In a way he feels trapped between his past and his future, and in comes Jesus: repent and believe the good news. Each day there is a choice: look behind and drown in shame, look ahead and drown in anxiety, or look up and believe the good news.

documents.excerpt: Why does this matter for someone already saved? Paul told the Ephesians that when they heard the word of truth and believed, they were marked in him with a seal, the promised Holy Spirit, a deposit guaranteeing our inheritance. If you have faith in Jesus, the deposit is paid; it is just a waiting game. Eternity isn’t a coin flip; it is a guarantee. When a believer trips on Satan’s traps, he falls into the arms of Jesus.

documents.excerpt: If you have peace with God, would you stop going to war with yourself? Does your opinion of yourself matter more than God’s? Many believers struggle here, Josh included, and it is another form of pride.
excerpts: If you have peace with God, would you stop going to war with yourself? Does your opinion of yourself matter more than God’s? Many believers struggle here, Josh included, and it is another form of pride.

Because of the cross, God looks at you and sees Christ’s righteousness, not your sinfulness. Josh is concerned that many are redeemed in God’s eyes but look in the mirror with condemnation. He has been there. You are looking around when you need to look up: read the red letters, get to know the one who died to save your soul, read his promises, note his gifts, and hit your knees to tell God why you need a Savior. He already knows; you are the one who needs to hear it. Then believe Jesus was sent to save you from it.

documents.excerpt: Josh will show three gifts Jesus offers all who trust him: forgiveness, fulfillment, and freedom.
excerpts: Josh will show three gifts Jesus offers all who trust him: forgiveness, fulfillment, and freedom.

First, forgiveness, in Mark 2: when Jesus came home to Capernaum, the crowd was so large there was no room even outside the door. Four men carrying a paralyzed man couldn’t reach Jesus, so they dug through the roof and lowered his mat. Seeing their faith, Jesus said, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” Teachers of the law thought, “He’s blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Jesus, knowing their thoughts, asked which is easier to say, and to show the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, told the man to take his mat and go home. He did, and everyone praised God: “We have never seen anything like this!”

excerpts: Josh deals with this a lot in pastoral counseling. He is sensitive to church hurt and has some himself, but the question that usually needs asking is: did you contribute to your own hurt? Did you have unspoken expectations, bring traditions from a previous church, or expect your new pastor to have your old pastor’s gifts?

A few years ago a member called to say Josh wasn’t a true shepherd and didn’t care, which blew him away; he has been called many names, but uncaring, unavailable, and unapproachable usually aren’t among them, and his personal number is on his business card. Their close friend had been in the hospital without a visit from him. Josh apologized and said he didn’t know they’d asked, and the member said they hadn’t asked, but “a shepherd wouldn’t need an invitation.” Josh wholeheartedly disagrees. Unspoken expectations are unhealthy; if you have one, tell him.
We’re all different. Josh’s wife has strict instructions not to let visitors in if he is hospitalized; he’d love prayers, but those robes don’t close well in the back.

documents.excerpt: These men didn’t just say “Let’s pray about it,” maybe Josh’s least favorite Christian phrase; they made a plan to address the need. He commends anyone who stops and prays right then when asked. Pastor Ken screens the church’s prayer requests and sends them out, and Josh stops and prays every time he sees one; he would love the whole church on the prayer team, which people can join on the mobile app. Giving the churchy “I’ll pray for you” and never doing it is a lie; just say, “I’m here for you, man.”
excerpts: These men didn’t just say “Let’s pray about it,” maybe Josh’s least favorite Christian phrase; they made a plan to address the need. He commends anyone who stops and prays right then when asked. Pastor Ken screens the church’s prayer requests and sends them out, and Josh stops and prays every time he sees one; he would love the whole church on the prayer team, which people can join on the mobile app. Giving the churchy “I’ll pray for you” and never doing it is a lie; just say, “I’m here for you, man.”

We also fall short when we pray for someone’s physical need but do nothing about it when we could. Crossroads Cares isn’t just for people out there; it is for us. The lobby isn’t for talking about the playoff game; it is for asking a brother how to pray for him and how his marriage is going, offering to share it on the mobile app if he wants the church praying, and submitting any need to Crossroads Cares for him.

We are all called to be ministers so the spiritual and physical needs of the church family are met and no one goes unnoticed. If someone shares a need, close the loop, as these men did. Jesus noticed their faith and effort and rewarded it. Don’t just say you’ll carry someone’s mat; carry it, and when obstacles come, get creative and push through, because we are all shepherds.

Omniscience, God being all-knowing, is either the most terrifying or most comforting thing about him. Apart from grace it is terrifying that not a single thought in your head is your own. In grace it is a wonderful comfort: God knows every sin you have done, thought about doing, and will ever do, knows you better than anyone, and still loves you. That kind of love could change a person, and it has changed many, including Josh.

Verse 8 should open our eyes: immediately Jesus knew in his spirit what they were thinking. He proved himself God by forgiving sin and healing, then read the hearts of the front-row Pharisees, which only God can do. Josh’s preaching game would go up if he could read hearts.
Omniscience, God being all-knowing, is either the most terrifying or most comforting thing about him. Apart from grace it is terrifying that not a single thought in your head is your own. In grace it is a wonderful comfort: God knows every sin you have done, thought about doing, and will ever do, knows you better than anyone, and still loves you. That kind of love could change a person, and it has changed many, including Josh.

excerpts: Jesus goes head to head with several groups throughout Mark. The Pharisees were strict, influential tradition hardliners who taught obedience to the tiniest parts of Jewish law and rejected Jesus because he didn’t follow their traditions and spent time with sinners, essentially everything he is doing in Mark 2.

The Sadducees were a wealthy upper-class priestly group who rejected the authority of everything after Deuteronomy, profited from business in the temple (“hello, conflict of interest”), and denied the resurrection of the dead. The teachers of the law interpreted the law for a living, focused heavily on tradition, and rejected Jesus as Messiah because he didn’t obey their traditions. The Herodians, seen in chapter 3, were Herod’s supporters who tried to trap Jesus with questions, afraid he would cause political instability.
The theme: everyone against Jesus was for tradition, wealth, and power.

excerpts: In the rest of Mark 2, John the Baptist’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting, and people asked why Jesus’ disciples were not. Jesus answered that the guests of the bridegroom can’t fast while he is with them, but the day will come when he is taken, and then they will fast. No one sews unshrunk cloth on an old garment or pours new wine into old wineskins; new wine goes into new wineskins.

Fasting, like any discipline done the right way, can align us with God’s heart, humble us, and grow our faith; done the wrong way it is a meaningless ritual. The Pharisees fasted twice a week like clockwork and announced it so everyone would know how holy they were, but fasting is a tool applied when needed. John’s disciples fasted in repentance, anticipating Christ; now that he is here, why would they fast?

No, intermittent fasting isn’t biblical; trying to fit into a Speedo isn’t fasting, and neither is giving up Starbucks for a week or cutting carbs. Fasting is abstaining from food with an emphasis on prayer, meditation, reading the word, and focusing on God alone, quieting the noise to focus on his will. Through it God can help with grief, decisions, humility, and repentance, but if it isn’t motivated by love for God, it is just noise.

excerpts: This was a big deal: God gave Israel the Sabbath after the exodus as a unique gift, so violating Sabbath traditions was like declaring war on the religious establishment. In Exodus 20 Moses prohibited work on the Sabbath without specifics; reading on, it was wrong to kindle a cooking fire, gather wood, carry things in and out, or sell.

Jewish tradition kept adding: travel restrictions, and a ban on tying knots, except women could tie knots in their girdles, so you couldn’t tie a rope to a bucket at the well, but you could tie your wife’s girdle to it. It became a massive, crushing, legalistic burden.

Jesus wasn’t violating God’s command to keep the Sabbath holy or encouraging his disciples to; he was violating man’s additions to it, seemingly on purpose. His argument is simple: if a hungry king and his men could eat the holy bread from the tabernacle, the Lord of the Sabbath can let his men eat grain from his fields. God has always cared more about helping people than holding tradition. If Jesus cared about man’s tradition, why not wait a day?

Two chapters into Mark, they already want to kill him, because Jesus says time and again that human needs are more important than religious rituals. “I want the heart.” The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.

Believers who are tuned out for being firm in the faith shouldn’t be discouraged; their Lord knew exactly what that was like. One point from Jesus shuts down the legalists: since evil doesn’t take a Sabbath, why should good? Save this person or let them die? In the kingdom of God the answer is always save a life.

Jesus watched their hearts harden, and it made him angry. A house full of tax collectors and traitors, a dinner party with sinners and swindlers, doesn’t make Jesus angry; only the self-righteous can do that. They would rather protect their traditions than see a man healed.

Jesus watched their hearts harden, and it made him angry. A house full of tax collectors and traitors, a dinner party with sinners and swindlers, doesn’t make Jesus angry; only the self-righteous can do that. They would rather protect their traditions than see a man healed.

Most scholars agree Mark was the first gospel written; of its 678 verses, all but 31 are quoted in other gospels. excerpts: John’s message: after me comes one more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to untie; I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.

With many church backgrounds in the room, Josh addresses an issue. John was sent with authority to preach repentance and baptize in water, and Spirit baptism doesn’t make John’s baptism meaningless or mean water baptism would one day be replaced. John’s message and baptism were preparation so people would be ready to trust Jesus, as Andrew did. Water baptism demonstrated a willingness to turn from sin; when Jesus baptizes with the Spirit, the whole person is transformed, so Jesus offers both forgiveness and power to live godly lives.

Baptism on its own, apart from the Spirit, is just a bath. Its power isn’t in the ritual but in how it connects us to the redemptive work of Jesus, the work of the Spirit, and God’s promise in his word. Anyone the Lord is prompting about baptism can reach out to Josh for coffee.

Before Jesus calls his first disciples, Mark shows how unusual this servant is: Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan, heaven is torn open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice says, “You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.” Then the Spirit sends him into the wilderness for 40 days, tempted by Satan, with wild animals and angels attending him.

Mark calls Jesus the Son of God throughout his gospel. This was no ordinary Jewish servant but the Son of God who came down from heaven to die for the sins of the world. In the kingdom of God the greatest ruler is always the greatest servant; nobody saw it coming, but ready or not, the servant has arrived.

excerpts: “Good news” comes up twice in this first message. The Greek word euangelion is translated gospel or good news: angelos is a messenger, and the prefix means joyful, so it is news that brings joy.

excerpts: To understand that, go back to creation. Mark doesn’t give a traditional creation account, probably because it is assumed at Jesus’ baptism: only one can tear the sky, the one who made it.

In Genesis 1–2 we see a perfect world with perfect relationships with each other, God, and creation, because God and we were in our proper positions. In Genesis 3 Eve is deceived, and instead of leading her away from temptation Adam listens, and they break the only law in the garden. When God was King there was one law; when we chose to be kings there were 613. We didn’t do well with one; how did we do with 613?

No one could hold up the weight of the law. All we could think about was ourselves, and nothing kills relationships quicker than self-centeredness, so every relationship suffered. As humanity treads water and the law pulls us under, the only question worth asking is, who will rescue us? Paul asks it most authentically: “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?”

excerpts: Zebedee had hired servants, so his business was more of a fishing enterprise. In ancient cultures family was huge; today some people skip family Thanksgiving for “Friendsgiving,” which Josh thinks is stupid. For us, leaving family can feel like a crowning achievement of adulthood, but for these men it was a big deal.

Jesus wanting priority over mother and father may not bother many of us, but priority over your career has you sweating. “Come, follow me” is a call to prioritize Jesus over family and career. It doesn’t mean abandoning family: Zebedee had help, James and John talked with him again, and Peter will see his mother-in-law healed later this chapter. It isn’t dishonoring parents; it is a change of priorities: everything else comes second.

Your career is a way to serve him by building up the church and supporting his ministry. Your family is a way to serve him by making disciples, starting at home; men, your wife is the greatest earthly gift God has given you, and your opportunity to serve him by serving her.

A raise if you work Sundays: career or Christ? He is nobody’s backup plan, not even to family. If Dad wants more time only if you stop talking about Jesus, are you going to hush up? Jesus isn’t calling you to a cozy Christian life but to put him first and live with the results. Some relationships might suffer and some might thrive; your career might suffer, and God might lead you to a more fulfilling one. He doesn’t call you to a nominal, average Christian life.

But in Luke 14, Jesus turns to a large crowd and says, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters—yes, even their own life—such a person cannot be my disciple.” Nobody prints that on a T-shirt, and the crowd probably got thinner. “If anyone” means all of them, not just elders and life group leaders.
excerpts: Some think this radical call is for the pastor, not the pew people; these men were going into full-time ministry. But in Luke 14, Jesus turns to a large crowd and says, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters—yes, even their own life—such a person cannot be my disciple.” Nobody prints that on a T-shirt, and the crowd probably got thinner. “If anyone” means all of them, not just elders and life group leaders.

We are taught not to hate our enemies, so how can Jesus say hate father and mother? He wants you to follow him so passionately, consistently, wholeheartedly, and faithfully that your family devotion looks like hate by comparison. He won’t be your backup plan or play second fiddle; if you have stipulations, you don’t get him.

“I’ll obey if the cancer goes away, my career takes off, my children forgive me, my family reconciles.” If you say, “Jesus, I’ll drop my nets if blank,” your blank is what you really want and follow; that is your god. Jesus is not a means to an end and will not be used. If you want to follow Jesus, he is the ultimate goal, and you learn contentment with whatever he adds or takes away. You want relevance, fulfillment, purpose; Jesus is the only relevance and fulfillment you need, and he is your purpose.

excerpts: “Come, follow me, and I will send you out to fish for people,” perhaps more familiar as “I will make you fishers of men.” Josh’s stepbrother is a pro bass fisherman. Josh walks through what he has heard about fishing: look under the log, set the hook, take the selfie, fry it in peanut oil, go find its brothers and sisters, and dynamite works too.

Part of the point is that becoming a fisherman takes commitment and planning: skills, equipment, practice casting, trolling, and jigging, knowing where and when fish bite, rods, reels, hooks, bait, a nice bass boat (“you’re welcome, fellas”), knowing how to swim, and patience. It is a process, and Jesus is saying, “Come, I’m on a journey; I want to show you where I’m going.”

Jesus didn’t invent the term; it was a common phrase for teachers able to persuade minds, who baited their hooks with teachings and caught disciples. A fisherman’s life translates to ministry: teamwork, patience, courage when things get crazy, understanding how things work. Fishermen weren’t quitters or complainers, because you can’t quit on a boat, and nobody wants quitters and complainers in ministry either.

In biblical imagery the sea is a place of chaos and death, cold and dark, representing the kingdom of darkness where we tread water calling for rescue. “I will make you fishers of men” means: I will make you someone who knows how to grab people out of the kingdom of darkness and introduce them to the kingdom of light.

When he seeks a holy life because Christ loved him and gave himself for him, and because he is not his own but was bought at a price, that isn’t legalism; it is the leading of the Spirit. When he counts the cost and decides to die to self instead of living for self, that is the repentance Jesus is looking for.

We don’t want repentance without belief or belief without repentance; Jesus commands both, of new believers and gray-haired believers too. This sinner will spend the rest of his life repenting of a life of sin, and believing that Jesus did exactly what he was sent to do: he saved sinners like Josh.

Repentance that brings salvation
What Josh knows about repentance is that it makes him weep and hate his past life, because that is why Jesus had to endure the cross. Every time he takes communion and remembers that Christ’s blood washes away his sin, it drives him to repent, knowing he is part of the reason Christ had to die. When a person realizes they wounded Christ and their heart breaks because he was nailed to the cross for their sin, that is the repentance that brings salvation.
When he seeks a holy life because Christ loved him and gave himself for him, and because he is not his own but was bought at a price, that isn’t legalism; it is the leading of the Spirit. When he counts the cost and decides to die to self instead of living for self, that is the repentance Jesus is looking for.
We don’t want repentance without belief or belief without repentance; Jesus commands both, of new believers and gray-haired believers too. This sinner will spend the rest of his life repenting of a life of sin, and believing that Jesus did exactly what he was sent to do: he saved sinners like Josh.

documents.excerpt: Josh opens with a proverb for men in chapter 25, verse 28: a man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls. He reminds himself of it constantly: who wants to live in a city without walls, or a nation uninterested in protecting her citizens?
excerpts: Josh opens with a proverb for men in chapter 25, verse 28: a man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls. He reminds himself of it constantly: who wants to live in a city without walls, or a nation uninterested in protecting her citizens?

Throughout history walls have protected people from harm, and they have become more advanced; in 2023, 13–15% of the federal budget, $820 billion, went to defense. Where there is life there is a desire to survive, and this country is worth defending. Josh quotes his favorite president, Abraham Lincoln, at Gettysburg: “that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.”

The simple rule of life: when you have something precious, you defend it with all your strength. Josh loves that he can sing praises, share God’s word, and pray together without fearing for his life or family, and that the country doesn’t require Crossroads Church to pay taxes. We the people put a government in place that empowers the church to be the church; the First Amendment says Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. Do you realize how much that sentence has changed your life?

excerpts: Compare that with North Korea, where the Kim regime considers Christians a hostile class and possessing Scripture can mean arrest or even execution. The truth is American Christians are spoiled and soft; Josh honestly thinks most would deny their faith in less than ideal circumstances.

The church has a history of getting off track. In the first three chapters of Revelation, our Lord, who sees the enemy climbing the walls, writes to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Ephesus perseveres but forgot its first love and is called to remember and repent. Smyrna endures poverty and persecution, and the Lord doesn’t rebuke them; he tells them not to be afraid and remain faithful.

The Lord saves his harshest rebukes for those who have the most. The wealthiest church, Laodicea, said “we lack nothing,” and the Lord said, “Actually, you’re poor, blind and naked.” The more we have, the more likely we are to fall into complacency.

Every pastor in America wants to think his church is Philadelphia or Smyrna, all commendation and no rebuke, but most American churches are more like Thyatira and Pergamum: churches of tolerance that tolerate compromise, half-truths, and sin. Many are okay with the Lord outside the door as long as their biggest donors are inside. People leave when the church does hard things, but the Lord’s true church under his headship seeks only God’s approval.

Preserving the core teachings for thousands of years across continents and languages is, to Josh, clearly guided by God’s divine providence.

“Follow their own ungodly desires” has to be one of the biggest reasons so many deny God’s truth. Josh doesn’t think it is about the evidence; you could show a smart person all of it and it wouldn’t create faith. Many people don’t want God to tell them how to live. “I’ve got major objections to the Bible.” Translation: you don’t like the “shall not” part, or the die-to-self part.

That is low-hanging fruit for Satan: give them counterfeit truth, enough to feel good but not enough to save them. You can’t expect holiness or reverence from people who don’t have the Spirit. These mockers were scoffing at the second coming, “Where’s Jesus?”, causing division while living worldly lives. Paul told the Corinthians we can’t expect those without the Spirit to accept the things of the Spirit.

documents.excerpt: When the prodigal son was far from home, was he still his father’s son? Of course, though he was in rebellion and the relationship was wounded. But he wasn’t keeping himself where his father could actively show his love; he was disconnected, and his father didn’t know where he was. When he came home and the father ran out, put a ring on his finger, clothed him, and threw a party despite the grumpy older brother, the father could actively show his love.

When he came home and the father ran out, put a ring on his finger, clothed him, and threw a party despite the grumpy older brother, the father could actively show his love.

When we are in disobedience, God doesn’t stop loving us and we don’t lose our salvation; we are simply wayward, prodigal, moving away from the love we should move toward. In John 15 Jesus says, “I am the vine; you are the branches… apart from me you can do nothing.” Stay close. Be in the word and be doers of it. Love those around you, but love God first and most, with everything; he loved you first. So keep yourselves in his love.

documents.excerpt: When you aren’t praying for them, be merciful to those who doubt, snatch others from the fire, and show mercy mixed with fear. We don’t have to know someone’s heart to speak encouragement to it, or agree with people to build them up.
excerpts: When you aren’t praying for them, be merciful to those who doubt, snatch others from the fire, and show mercy mixed with fear. We don’t have to know someone’s heart to speak encouragement to it, or agree with people to build them up.

Those who doubt could be believers who are weak in the faith right now, as Josh has been. If you pray in the Spirit, you may realize God is tasking you with building them up. Our brothers and sisters came from lives of sin with influences that kept them from the Lord; instead of peering into their lives and looking down, invite them into yours and pull them up. If you are a mature Christian but actively build up no immature Christians, the only one calling you mature is you, and you aren’t supposed to nickname yourself.

Show them how wonderful their salvation is and encourage them back into the word; it’s never too late to turn around. Josh thinks the most vulnerable among us are those hurt in the church, maybe here. Reach out: “I don’t know what happened, I don’t need to know, but I care about you.” This is how we snatch people from the fire: we love them well even if they wronged us or we don’t agree with them.

documents.excerpt: “Show mercy mixed with fear” means that as we reach down to care for brothers and sisters caught in a trap, we must be careful not to fall in ourselves. Rescue swimmers are taught to subdue someone resisting rescue, or the victim controls the situation and down you go. Josh isn’t telling anyone to put people in choke holds and bring them back to church, but there is a balance: love God’s people and hate sin. We can do both.
excerpts: “Show mercy mixed with fear” means that as we reach down to care for brothers and sisters caught in a trap, we must be careful not to fall in ourselves. Rescue swimmers are taught to subdue someone resisting rescue, or the victim controls the situation and down you go. Josh isn’t telling anyone to put people in choke holds and bring them back to church, but there is a balance: love God’s people and hate sin. We can do both.

Not every believer is equipped for these situations. It takes strong knowledge of Scripture, a track record of faithfulness, and an often-forgotten awareness of Satan’s battle strategy. That is why Josh spends so much time dealing with sin in this church: it is easier to teach new believers to avoid bad doctrine than to snatch them out of the fire later.

He knows because he barely made it out of the fire himself. If not for loving believers showing him mercy mixed with fear, he wouldn’t be here, and God even used Christians unwilling to show him mercy to help him grow up.

excerpts: In one of Josh’s favorite Proverbs, Solomon says, “Buy the truth and don’t sell it.” One of the most precious resources in the life of a Christian is the truth. God is the God of truth, and he has given us the truth by his Son; in John 17 Jesus prays that the truth would set his people apart: “Father, sanctify them by the truth; your word is truth.”

The words of God spoke everything into existence, and the words of God shape us into his likeness. The church is adopted sons and daughters rallying under the banner of God’s truth, “a collection of misfits that are far from okay,” gathered to aim for perfection and celebrate that one day he will come and make everything good again.

Paul calls the church God’s household, the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. The God of truth created us, revealed his truth to prophets, and sent his Son full of grace and truth, who died the death we deserved; this is the message of his true church, as Romans 10 says: declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, and you will be saved.
That is what Solomon means in Proverbs 23: keep buying this over and over. Fill your homes, your hearts, your spouses, and your kids with this resource.

excerpts: Josh expects to take heat for this, but these odd new angles usually come from people who seem to love their titles. He isn’t knocking anyone’s education, but he wonders: are you the product of an education system or of God’s transformation system?

One speaker had an entire video listing credentials, something like “super duper doctor professor pastor and apostolic leader.” The sermon was polished and well delivered but felt more like a lecture. The next speaker wanted to be introduced only as a servant of Christ, didn’t care if you knew his name, and pointed to nasty stuff in Josh’s heart, reminding him the gospel didn’t just happen when he was 9 years old; it is happening every day.

Time after time the guy from an obscure town in Kansas explains the gospel more clearly than the doctor of theology. What is more powerful, the one taught how to teach the gospel or the one who desperately needed it? What is more impressive, your theology or your testimony? That is why Josh loves that Jude simply calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ.

Verse 5: though you already know this, the Lord delivered his people out of Egypt but later destroyed those who did not believe. Those who reject the truth will always be met with divine judgment.
excerpts: Jude, like Peter, gives Old Testament examples of how God deals with people who resist his authority, and he uses the nation of Israel. Verse 5: though you already know this, the Lord delivered his people out of Egypt but later destroyed those who did not believe. Those who reject the truth will always be met with divine judgment.

The exodus is a beautiful illustration of God’s love: he hears his people and in his timing gives a way out. In the Passover he says, trust me, obey my commands, I have heard your cries and I’ll send an advocate. Then the most amazing miracle in Scripture: God pulls apart the sea so his people pass on dry land and drops the water on Pharaoh’s army.

Brought to the border of the promised land, the people were afraid. Moses, Joshua, and Caleb urged them to walk in by faith, but they refused, and some leaders even floated going back to Egypt, where at least their plates were full. Going against the will and word of God never goes unpunished: everyone 20 and older would die within 40 years. Their unbelief was their undoing.
Do you act more like the first wave that refused to go in, or the next wave that believed God’s promises were bigger than their opponents?

excerpts: Jude 7: Sodom, Gomorrah, and the surrounding towns gave themselves up to sexual immorality and perversion and serve as an example of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire. In a culture with absolute pride in its perversion, Josh doesn’t like the NIV here. The ESV says “unnatural desire,” but the NASB, his favorite translation, says it best: “strange flesh.”

These towns didn’t just have a block party that got out of control one weekend; they gave themselves up to a lifestyle of unnatural desires. It is possible “strange flesh” refers not only to homosexuality but to bestiality, which God condemns in Leviticus 18, and Jesus upholds this warning in the New Testament. Genesis 18 and 19 serve as a constant reminder that God does hate sin.

Whether the object perverts creation or perverts grace, God will judge it all. Is there really a difference between people today who use grace as a license for sin and the people of Sodom and Gomorrah? How many Christians look down on these towns while having plenty of strange pursuits of their own? What might we see if we looked at yours? Take heed lest you fall.

excerpts: Nolan, 11, came to say good night after his shower and still kind of smelled. Josh had focused so much on teaching him to love Jesus, obey God, and love truth that he forgot to show him how to wash his hair. Nolan is a wonderful person on the inside; sometimes it is what’s on his head that makes him tough to be around.

The church’s problem is the opposite. Instead of cleaning up the inside first, we have built programs and ministry strategies for cleaning up the outside: a giving campaign for generosity, a parenting seminar for better parents, recovery programs for addictions. Josh understands the heart behind it, but were you taught to be generous, or shown the one who gave his life so you could live? You can listen to parenting podcasts until Jesus comes, or surrender your life to him, read his word every day, and learn how he guides you.

The gentle, approving-of-all, social justice Jesus of Super Bowl commercials says: blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and dish; woe to you hypocrites, like whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside but full of dead men’s bones. We have taught Christians to walk around with a perm while their hearts are still putrid. You need a new heart.

But even the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to condemn him for slander but said, “The Lord rebuke you,” while these people speak abusively against what they do not understand and are destroyed by what they understand by instinct like unreasoning animals.
excerpts: Jude describes the ungodly as blasphemous too: on the strength of their dreams they pollute their bodies, reject authority, and heap abuse on celestial beings. But even the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to condemn him for slander but said, “The Lord rebuke you,” while these people speak abusively against what they do not understand and are destroyed by what they understand by instinct like unreasoning animals.
“The Lord rebuke you”: what a powerful submission to God’s sovereign authority. The ungodly don’t look to God to exact revenge; like animals they want their pound of flesh. But not us.

What Jude says about Moses’ body is found nowhere else in Scripture. Everything we know of Moses’ death is in Deuteronomy 34: he died in Moab, the Lord buried him in the valley opposite Beth Peor, and to this day no one knows where his grave is. Josh sees God, aware of Israel’s tendency toward golden calves, sending Michael to hide the body. Satan would want it to lure Israel into worshiping shrines to Moses, sending another generation to die in the wilderness and keeping the line of Jesus from moving along.

documents.excerpt: Woe to them: they have taken the way of Cain, rushed for profit into Balaam’s error, and been destroyed in Korah’s rebellion. Jude takes after his big half brother with a woe series of his own, though Josh won’t spend long on verse 11.
excerpts: Woe to them: they have taken the way of Cain, rushed for profit into Balaam’s error, and been destroyed in Korah’s rebellion. Jude takes after his big half brother with a woe series of his own, though Josh won’t spend long on verse 11.

The Cain method is religion without faith; the way of Abel is faith-filled works. Hebrews 11 says by faith Abel brought God a better offering than Cain; the offering wasn’t better, the approach was. Everything Cain did he did for himself, and he ended up with everything except God.
Balaam’s error is similar: using the gifts God has given us to earn material gifts for ourselves.

Korah’s story is in Numbers 16, and that is homework. He rose up against Moses and opposed Aaron. Misunderstanding God’s authority is a tragic mistake, and we must not rise up recklessly against government or spiritual leaders. It may seem people are getting away with it now, but hang on: “The Lord rebuke you.” He’s coming soon.

Women in the room might picture the blemish at the love feast as a mother-in-law in a black dress at the wedding. Close. The word means a rock washed by the sea, a submerged or hidden rock. documents.excerpt: First, his authority. People don’t want to answer to anyone. Jesus says all power is given to him in heaven and on earth, and man says, “Cool, but I like pretending I have the power.”
excerpts: First, his authority. People don’t want to answer to anyone. Jesus says all power is given to him in heaven and on earth, and man says, “Cool, but I like pretending I have the power.”

Second, he hung out with sinners: Zacchaeus, Matthew, the woman caught in adultery, and more. That is a powerful statement of God’s love and forgiveness: no one is beyond redemption, and repentance, faith, and love matter far more than appearance or prestige.
Third, he stole their spotlight. They were threatened: what if people stop coming to the temple and go listen to him?

Fourth, he preached against sin. It isn’t the Jesus of the Super Bowl commercials, but yes, he ate with sinners and washed feet, and his message was the same: go and sin no more. In John 7 Jesus says the world hates him because he testifies that its works are evil. Repentance isn’t a nice “my bad, God”; it is turning away from the lifestyle: “I don’t want it. I want you.” People don’t like it when you point out their selfishness and wrongdoing.

Jehovah’s Witnesses call themselves Christians but aren’t, Josh says, because they don’t believe Jesus is God, teaching he was created and subordinate, and wrote their own Bible version to prove it. The true church builds on the apostles’ teaching that the Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation, which doesn’t mean he was created. Keep reading: in him all things were created, he is before all things, in him all things hold together, and God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him. Jesus is God.

Mormons believe Jesus is the Son of God and Savior, and you could talk to one in the park a long time before realizing something is off, but they don’t believe he is co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. The fastest-growing religion in the country can be deconstructed with one sentence from John 10: “I and the Father are one.”

documents.excerpt: “Josh, Jesus didn’t have children.” True, and it was a great shame for a Jew to die childless, but Jesus didn’t die childless. He gave birth to a spiritual family: we are adopted sons and daughters of God through Jesus Christ, and he is not ashamed to call us brothers and sisters. We are co-heirs with an inheritance that will never spoil or fade, bought at a price, standing confident in his righteousness, not our own. Paul said it best: God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · December 24, 2024 · Unto Us
documents.excerpt: A fun word from Bible school: propitiation. God is angry at sin because it offends his holiness and violates his law. In his holiness he must judge sinners; in his love he desires to forgive them. He can’t ignore sin or look the other way without contradicting his nature and his law. How does God solve this? Isaiah 53:12: he was numbered with the transgressors. The law’s demands have been satisfied, and God can graciously forgive all who call on the name of Jesus. It’s done.

documents.excerpt: Soon the room will fill with candlelight, one of Josh’s favorite moments of the year: a reminder of light breaking into darkness, of the faith of those around us, and that our hope is a living hope. As you sing, look around as the flame lights the faces of those near you and find joy that the love of our Savior lives in your neighbor’s heart. Reflect on God’s mercy and rejoice that your sins are no longer counted against you.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · December 24, 2024 · Unto Us
documents.excerpt: Some are struggling, and the weight of unconfessed sin is heavy. When did you last confess your sins to the Lord: a week, a month, years? David struggled, and so has Josh: “When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long… my strength was sapped.” If there is silence between you and God, break it this Christmas. Go to the Lord, then lift your candle; don’t be afraid.
excerpts: Some are struggling, and the weight of unconfessed sin is heavy. When did you last confess your sins to the Lord: a week, a month, years? David struggled, and so has Josh: “When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long… my strength was sapped.” If there is silence between you and God, break it this Christmas. Go to the Lord, then lift your candle; don’t be afraid.

Look how it turned out for David: “I acknowledged my sin to you and did not cover up my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the Lord,’ and you forgave the guilt of my sin.” When you lay your fears, burdens, sins, and anxieties at Jesus’ feet and rest in his grace, you are freed to love, sing, rejoice, serve, and teach. As the flames transform the room, God’s forgiveness will transform you. We are no longer defined by our failures, past, addictions, or family history, but by his love and mercy.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · December 24, 2024 · Unto Us
documents.excerpt: If the light of life has transformed you, show the world. Being a light isn’t just being nice and not yelling at people who cut you off on the freeway; it is sharing God’s grace with the whole world and pointing to a living, loving God who forgives and redeems through his Son. Let your candle remind you: you are deeply loved, and if you confess your sins, God will forgive you. Go tell the world what the Lord has done for you, and whether they accept or reject your message, when he returns your inheritance is forever with him in paradise. Rejoice in the Lord and be glad. Merry Christmas.

documents.excerpt: By show of hands, who loves their name? Parenting below average, but they nailed the name. Who is still trying to figure out what their parents were thinking? Josh offers grief counseling.
excerpts: By show of hands, who loves their name? Parenting below average, but they nailed the name. Who is still trying to figure out what their parents were thinking? Josh offers grief counseling.

Josh loves his name, a preacher’s name. His first name connects him with a man of God surrounded by a nation of wimps unwilling to walk into God’s promise, who went in anyway against insurmountable odds, a military leader who led his home well because they served the Lord. His middle name, David, is a shepherd who slew giants, a warrior king, poet, and songwriter filled with the Spirit who loved the Lord with all his heart, and also a royal screwup, “so that checks out.”

His last name makes people think of the legendary lawman known for Tombstone, Arizona and the shootout at the OK Corral, with a reputation for being gruff, tough, and fearless. His parents hit a bullseye; his sisters would tell you they didn’t get so lucky.

documents.excerpt: It could have gone another way. In 2020, some parents named their children Corona. Then there are names like Anita Bath, Amy Stake, and Terry Bow. One psychologist studied over 15,000 juvenile delinquents and found those with odd or embarrassing names were in trouble four times as often; of course they were, they had to fight to survive recess and defend their Snack Pack. Kids are cruel, so please research baby names and run them past a trusted friend.
excerpts: It could have gone another way. In 2020, some parents named their children Corona. Then there are names like Anita Bath, Amy Stake, and Terry Bow. One psychologist studied over 15,000 juvenile delinquents and found those with odd or embarrassing names were in trouble four times as often; of course they were, they had to fight to survive recess and defend their Snack Pack. Kids are cruel, so please research baby names and run them past a trusted friend.

We name children with no idea how they will turn out. Josh’s parents didn’t know he would be a strong leader who loves music and wants to punch mean people in the face (he doesn’t anymore; the Spirit tells him no). Joshua was a top-five boys’ name from 1983 to 2008, and plenty of Joshuas don’t know the Lord.
A name can be funny or embarrassing, but it usually isn’t informative. And his parents conveniently waited until they knew he was a boy; they just got lucky picking a name that describes him.

documents.excerpt: We know this prophecy refers to Christ because Matthew quotes it eight centuries later: leaving Nazareth, Jesus lived in Capernaum, in the area of Zebulun and Naphtali, to fulfill what Isaiah said: Galilee of the Gentiles, the people living in darkness have seen a great light.
excerpts: We know this prophecy refers to Christ because Matthew quotes it eight centuries later: leaving Nazareth, Jesus lived in Capernaum, in the area of Zebulun and Naphtali, to fulfill what Isaiah said: Galilee of the Gentiles, the people living in darkness have seen a great light.

Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee were devastated when the Assyrian army came; Galilee was lost, and a Galilean Messiah seemed crazy. John 7 shows the attitude in Jerusalem: some said he was the Messiah, while others asked, “How can the Messiah come from Galilee?” Matthew reminds his Jewish audience that Isaiah prophesied it long before.

If you are a skeptic, Josh hopes you wrestle with this all Christmas season: Jesus convincingly fulfilled Old Testament prophecy time and again, and if that isn’t enough evidence that the Bible is reliable, truthful, and authoritative, nothing ever will be. Just as Isaiah predicted eight centuries earlier, the despised, sin-stained, rebellious Galileans were the first to set eyes on the Messiah. Jesus launched his ministry in Samaria and Galilee rather than Jerusalem and Judea, a reminder that his gospel was for the whole world.

excerpts: He will be called Wonderful Counselor. Psalm 73: you guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will take me into glory. He is doing a work in Josh; is he working in you? As Josh leans on him and seeks his counsel, he knows him in a way he never has before, and it grows every day.

He is the Word; the Creator makes himself available to creation through the Counselor. When Josh leans on him, he is reminded that he is his rock and salvation; remaining in him he is sustained by the true vine; when he fails he has an advocate; when he calls out he has a mediator; when he confesses he has a Savior; when life gets shaky he has a cornerstone; when he needs help he has the Servant; and when he is not enough, one stands beside him saying, “I am.”

Josh loses sleep thinking you might not know him like this, and it saddens him to think you might celebrate Christmas with no idea whom you’re celebrating. All creation, history, humanity, and his church are shouting his name, and even those who don’t call on him are shouting his name. Are you prepared to receive his counsel? Step into the light.

God answered Eve’s disobedience with birth pains and then chose that way to send his Son, and people say God has no sense of humor.

The one who spoke something into nothing became an embryo. Josh remembers his first diaper change, black sticky tar and 58 wipes, and the fear of realizing he hadn’t thought this through: “Man up, you got a boy to raise.” He honestly wondered whether Jesus had a baby glow or a halo, and whether his first diaper was as rough on Joseph as Nolan’s was on Josh. He isn’t mocking; he struggled with the Creator of the universe depending on a young couple for life: God as a fetus, Jehovah in diapers.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · December 15, 2024 · Unto Us
documents.excerpt: People struggle with this title because these are names for Jesus: “Josh, I’m trying to keep my doctrine of the Trinity organized, and Isaiah comes in with Everlasting Father.” Break it down. “Everlasting” refers to his eternal nature; he existed before creation, and Hebrews 13 says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. It also speaks to his eternal kingdom: Daniel 7 says he was given authority, glory, and sovereign power, with an everlasting dominion that will not pass away. Christ reigns in believers’ hearts now, and “everlasting” also points to a future literal earthly kingdom where he will reign. He is our constant now and forever.

excerpts: First, peace with God. Romans 5:1: since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Second, peace with others. Hebrews 12: make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy. The Holy Spirit helps us be patient, forgiving, gentle, kind, and generous, especially with brothers and sisters in Christ.

Third, peace with ourselves. In John 16, speaking to men who would give their lives to preserve the message, Jesus says, “I have told you these things so that in me you may have peace. In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.” Jesus has settled our hearts: our sins are forgiven, our guilt is gone, our present is Christ, and our future is heaven. Is the Prince of Peace reigning in your life? If not, step into the light.

A dear brother in the church was concerned Josh had discouraged people from studying prophecy; they talked it through in unity, and Josh goes on record: neglecting prophecy neglects a massive portion of Scripture, robs our souls, and discredits the one who gave his word for our edification and comfort.
excerpts: Many Christians don’t give enough time to the prophetic word. A dear brother in the church was concerned Josh had discouraged people from studying prophecy; they talked it through in unity, and Josh goes on record: neglecting prophecy neglects a massive portion of Scripture, robs our souls, and discredits the one who gave his word for our edification and comfort.

Where Christians go wrong is tunnel vision on events. Prophecy is valuable because it occupies our minds with a person, the Lord Jesus Christ, who came once to suffer and is coming again to reign, and Isaiah foretells both advents. Prophecy isn’t fortune-telling; it’s a peek into the mind of God at a moment in time.

With the monarchy and priesthood failing, God ministered through the prophets, whose job had two bullet points: lay before the people the glories to come through the promised Messiah, and prepare them for his triumphant entry by leading them to repentance from idols to the one true living God. The God who split the sea has been working a master plan all along; pharaohs and kings can’t stop him.

Isaiah is like a miniature Bible: 66 books and 66 chapters; the Old Testament’s 39 books and Isaiah’s first 39 chapters on Israel’s past struggles and the promised Messiah; the New Testament’s 27 books and Isaiah’s last 27 chapters on future deliverance. Chapters and verses were added later, but Josh still thinks it’s cool. The theme of Isaiah is the theme of all Scripture: God’s salvation revealed in his blessed Son.

The most mind-blowing is Jesus in Luke 4: in the Nazareth synagogue he unrolled the scroll of Isaiah and read, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor,” then sat down and said, “Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”

Isaiah 61 was written around 680 BC, and some 713 years later Jesus, known in his hometown as a carpenter’s son, says, “I’m the fulfillment.” If that’s not Christmas card material, Josh doesn’t know what is. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy; it all points to Jesus. Isaiah 11 says the Spirit of the Lord will rest on him, the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and the fear of the Lord.

Large churches stuff the room with people who abandon the gathering for their careers, let you out on time for the football game, and push a baptism to next week so you keep your idols: “You don’t need to be sanctified, just justified, and then give your tithe.” Said out loud it sounds icky, but that’s the American church.

excerpts: Josh loves this part: the Lord told Ahaz, “Ask the Lord your God for a sign, whether in the deepest depths or in the highest heights.” Ahaz said, “I will not ask; I will not put the Lord to the test.” Now the law matters to him and he’s quoting Scripture. Isaiah answered, “Is it not enough to try the patience of humans? Will you try the patience of my God also?”

Josh has never understood people who challenge God’s mercy, patience, and kindness. Ask hard questions, fine, but notice God is presenting himself to an idolatrous child murderer who robbed the temple to pay pagan kings, giving this arrogant young king an opportunity to repent: “Ask for a sign, no matter what, and I will prove myself.”

What would you ask for? To see the sun go off for a second? Eight feet of snow and a white Christmas in Arizona? Your mother-in-law to disappear for a little bit? Calm down, people. God is not out to destroy you; he wants to rescue even the worst of us. If he is reaching out, don’t push him away; grab his hand, let him lift you out, and never look back.

excerpts: Josh loves talking about the source of our joy this Christmas: Immanuel. Today names follow trends like kitchen tile; Josh named his son Nolan after Nolan Ryan because it sounded good with the family’s last name, and later learned Nolan Ryan was a Christian, so now they pretend they knew all along.

Ancient names had deep meaning: Cain means “acquired” (“guess this is the one we got”), Seth “appointed,” Noah “rest” or “comfort,” Ishmael “God will hear,” Isaac “laughter,” and Jacob “may God protect” but also “overreach,” as if his parents weren’t sure how he’d turn out.

Mary didn’t need to Google it; God sent an angel so there would be no confusion. She called her son Immanuel, God with us. If his name doesn’t flood your life with peace, joy, and comfort this season, nothing will. What would you give to join the angels singing on high, “Go tell it on the mountain,” “Hark the herald angels sing, glory to the newborn King”?

In year 52, maybe prideful about his resume, he decided he could burn incense on the altar as well as the priests. When the high priest tried to stop him, he pushed the old man aside, was instantly struck with leprosy, and died a horrible death.

Isaiah was heartsick, because he and Uzziah were friends, maybe even family, and because Judah plunged into an even greater moral freefall. So in chapter 6 we find a discouraged man, but at least he is headed to the temple; God’s house is a pretty good place to go when you feel defeated.

documents.excerpt: Steve can’t say with certainty what Isaiah saw, but he knows what he didn’t see. The Bible says no one can see God’s face and live, and the apostle John made it clear that no one has ever seen God. Isaiah came close, though not as close as Moses, who saw God’s backside. Some scholars think he saw the trailing edge of God’s massive robe; what he clearly saw was where God sat, what he wore, who was with him, and the atmosphere of the room. Both are true: no one has ever seen God, yet to a degree unlike any other person, Isaiah saw the Lord.

documents.context: Steve Wyatt · December 1, 2024 · Unto Us
documents.excerpt: How did Isaiah respond? He didn’t check his phone and say, “Keep it moving, pastor, kickoff is in 20 minutes.” He said, “Woe to me, I am ruined, for I am a man of unclean lips, and I live among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Almighty.” In other words, “I’m not good enough to be here; somebody get me out of here.” Ushered into the most magnificent place imaginable, all he wanted was out.
excerpts: How did Isaiah respond? He didn’t check his phone and say, “Keep it moving, pastor, kickoff is in 20 minutes.” He said, “Woe to me, I am ruined, for I am a man of unclean lips, and I live among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Almighty.” In other words, “I’m not good enough to be here; somebody get me out of here.” Ushered into the most magnificent place imaginable, all he wanted was out.

That is what Bible heroes always did when they glimpsed God’s holiness. Job said, “I am unworthy… I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” Habakkuk said, “My heart pounded, my lips quivered.” Daniel said, “My face turned deathly pale and I was helpless.” Peter said, “Go away from me, I am a sinful man.” John fell at Jesus’ feet as though dead. Coming face to face with an utterly holy God is profoundly threatening, because God is holy and we are so very not holy.

“Woe to me, I am ruined”
How did Isaiah respond? He didn’t check his phone and say, “Keep it moving, pastor, kickoff is in 20 minutes.” He said, “Woe to me, I am ruined, for I am a man of unclean lips, and I live among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Almighty.” In other words, “I’m not good enough to be here; somebody get me out of here.” Ushered into the most magnificent place imaginable, all he wanted was out.
That is what Bible heroes always did when they glimpsed God’s holiness. Job said, “I am unworthy… I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” Habakkuk said, “My heart pounded, my lips quivered.” Daniel said, “My face turned deathly pale and I was helpless.” Peter said, “Go away from me, I am a sinful man.” John fell at Jesus’ feet as though dead. Coming face to face with an utterly holy God is profoundly threatening, because God is holy and we are so very not holy.
documents.title: “Woe to me, I am ruined” — Scabby Lips

excerpts: Something hit Steve hard as he studied: in every other Old Testament prophetic book where the prophet tells of his calling, he does it in chapter 1, but Isaiah waits until chapter 6. Why? Isaiah had correctly assumed God was selecting him as his prophet, but incorrectly assumed it was because of his amazing goodness: nobody else in Judah was as good as he was, so he had better get out there and get those heathens straightened out.

Flip through the first five chapters and you see him red in the face, teeth gritted, hostile at all those ornery, good-for-nothing sinners, storming in with his own specially prepared prophetic medication and no calling. Listen to some early condemnations: a sinful nation, a people loaded with guilt, brood of evildoers; your hands are full of blood; take your evil deeds out of my sight; go to the rocks, hide in the ground; woe to the wicked.

Judah was a hot mess that needed fixing, but until chapter 6 Isaiah was convinced he was the man for the job. In his mind Judah was a mess because they weren’t good enough; he had forgotten he wasn’t good enough either.

excerpts: Isaiah left a different man, a marked man, with a scab on his lip: a powerful, painful reminder that all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, including you, Isaiah.

Whenever someone in Scripture had a personal encounter with God, they came away less because of it. Time alone with God will take a toll on you. Isaiah left with scabby lips; Jacob wrestled with God and walked away with a hitch in his hip; Moses, after 40 days on Sinai, wore a veil over his face; Saul was blinded on the road to Damascus.

In regular communion with God you could get banged up, whether scabby lips, a gimpy hip, glow-in-the-dark flesh, or eyes blind as a bat. You will receive regular reminders that you’re not all that, that he alone is God and is holy and you are anything but, so that you watch your attitude when he calls you to deal with others’ weaknesses, inconsistencies, and failures.

excerpts: After chapter 6 there is a discernible change in Isaiah’s tone: the same message with a different demeanor. Judah still faced harsh judgment, but now Isaiah confronted them with a broken heart, not a prideful, judgmental attitude.

Listen to the new approach. Chapter 9: the people walking in darkness have seen a great light. “All my people, do not be afraid; very soon my anger against you will end.” Chapter 26: you will keep in perfect peace him whose mind is steadfast, because he trusts in you; the Lord is the Rock eternal. Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength and soar on wings like eagles.

There was still plenty of rebuke and woe that needed delivering, but with a kinder, gentler spirit, because Isaiah was different. Steve is convinced that every time he opened his mouth he licked his lips and realized, “I’m no different from these people, certainly no better. Man, I hope this lip never heals.” From then on his message had hope attached: the blessed hope of the world was on his way.

excerpts: Back in the throne room, Isaiah is still dabbing blood when the Lord asks, “Whom shall I send? Who will go for us?” Steve wondered for years why Isaiah made a big deal of it when he’d already been doing the prophet gig. Now he gets it: Isaiah had messed up and wanted another shot. “Here am I. Send me.”

John Newton said that when people are right with God they are apt to be hard on themselves and easy on others, but when they’re not, they are easy on themselves and hard on others. Could it be that your judgment is so swift, cutting, and divisive because your relationship with God isn’t what it ought to be? Maybe you need time in the throne room to lick your own lips or pull a log out of your eye, or an encounter that leaves you gimpy in the hip or briefly blind, so that if you still speak, you speak in a hushed and gentle tone.

Until then you can scream “Here am I, send me” till you’re blue in the face, and God won’t set you loose on the people he loves. He’ll say, “Go fish. If you think you’re good enough for this holy assignment, you’re way too good enough. What I need on my team are people with scabby lips and gimpy hips.” Anybody qualified on those terms? Steve is.
