That is why he chooses courage over fear: the Lord still listens to those who come to him. He is never alone or without hope; when the enemy says, “Josh, nobody’s for you,” he recalls the promises of old, lets Jesus’ words energize him, keeps praying, and doesn’t lose heart.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · July 7, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: God will fight for you wherever you are, but more importantly, he has already won for us. Jesus says, “In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.” So it’s time the church starts praying, singing, preaching, and acting like we’ve already won. What can you possibly be afraid of?
excerpts: God will fight for you wherever you are, but more importantly, he has already won for us. Jesus says, “In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.” So it’s time the church starts praying, singing, preaching, and acting like we’ve already won. What can you possibly be afraid of?

In John 14 Jesus says, “My peace I give you.” It is the same peace that kept him calm as he was mocked and crucified: they hurled insults, he suffered but made no threats, and gave himself over to the one who judges justly. That is why it was good for Jesus to leave and send the Advocate to bring us his peace until he returns. We have the peace of God because we have the Spirit of God in us, the glorious mystery Paul talked about: Christ in you, the hope of glory. This is why believers choose courage over fear.

Joshua 5–8: a roller coaster of success and failure
Today the church is in Joshua 8. Surveying the book from 30,000 feet, chapters 5–8 seem to be an intentional section: within the conquest of Canaan is a mini roller-coaster story of success and failure.
Jericho fell first, an incredible victory. Next to taste failure were the Israelites themselves, who had to deal with sin in their camp. In chapter 8 Joshua has dealt with that failure, the sin of Achan has been judged, and it is time to move forward to another victory by conquering Ai.

documents.excerpt: Before getting into chapter 8, Josh doesn’t want the church to miss a crucial lesson: the best Christian isn’t the one who makes the fewest mistakes. The Christian who stands out from the pack wins victories by reclaiming mistakes.
excerpts: Before getting into chapter 8, Josh doesn’t want the church to miss a crucial lesson: the best Christian isn’t the one who makes the fewest mistakes. The Christian who stands out from the pack wins victories by reclaiming mistakes.

Highly effective Christians have really bad memories. They move on from defeat quickly; they live, learn, walk in grace, and leverage those lessons into victories for God. They share an attitude with entrepreneurs: Henry Ford defined a mistake as an opportunity to begin again more intelligently.
Josh thinks Joshua had a similar mindset. His approach improves from chapter 7 to chapter 8, and he has learned a couple of lessons the church should take note of.

excerpts: After church last week Josh talked with a man about their brokenheartedness over yet another well-known pastor falling. Josh has struggled most with the situation surrounding Tony Evans, whose teaching ministry had been like a pastor to him and helped him grow in his faith.

The man said it was hard to tune in to their sermons now, which Josh understood, but added, “I’m just glad that I can still enjoy some of their old stuff.” Josh challenged him. Nobody can take away the change it had in him, but if a pastor is living in sin and also disciplined in the word, that man has to reject God’s efforts to reveal that sin almost weekly. Instead of confessing to the elders so they can pray over him for healing and restoration, he continues in sin.

documents.excerpt: That is one of the many reasons we need each other. James 5 says to confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. He isn’t talking about praying for a brother’s wrist he hurt playing pickleball; he means healing from sin, from temptation, from the tendency to lean into sin.
excerpts: That is one of the many reasons we need each other. James 5 says to confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. He isn’t talking about praying for a brother’s wrist he hurt playing pickleball; he means healing from sin, from temptation, from the tendency to lean into sin.

One of the great lies in the church today is that confession is entirely a private act between you and God. It begins there, but we are one body: how we live impacts the body, and where we suffer or rejoice, others do too. Paul says in Ephesians to put off falsehood and speak truthfully to your neighbor, for we are all members of one body. How can we speak truth in love if we aren’t even honest with one another about our sins? Paul says, do not lie to each other.

Not everything you confess to God needs to be spilled out in life group prayer time. But if the believers around you never know your struggles, how can you walk humbly with God, and how can they learn to love and show mercy? Secret sin kills the effectiveness of the body of Christ; his church suffers when we suffer alone. First John says that if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another and the blood of Jesus purifies us from all sin.

documents.excerpt: Not if you fail, but when you fail, don’t run from God; run to God. Again it seems like a no-brainer, but it isn’t. When we repent and receive forgiveness, the process of walking in the light and fighting sin should empower and grow us, not crush us.
excerpts: Not if you fail, but when you fail, don’t run from God; run to God. Again it seems like a no-brainer, but it isn’t. When we repent and receive forgiveness, the process of walking in the light and fighting sin should empower and grow us, not crush us.

There are no diminishing returns on God’s grace, no account of forgiveness that runs out at zero. Remember the song How He Loves: if his grace is an ocean, we’re all sinking. It is by grace you’ve been saved and by grace you continue; you run to God’s mercy and keep running to it. Maybe you figure things out the third time, the fourth time, or the tenth. Keep working out your faith and don’t give up.

The all-knowing, holy, passionate God, abounding in love and faithfulness, with mercy in his eyes, knows that a fallen creation that needed a second chance might need a third. If you’re a true believer, the only way you lose is if you give up. You have to surrender to lose.

documents.excerpt: Josh turns to verse 1 to watch God help Joshua turn things around: “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged.” “Thou shalt not” is not the most common command in Scripture. It’s hard to give an exact number across languages and authors, but alongside peace be with you, praise the Lord, rejoice, and give thanks, “fear not, do not be afraid” is given approximately 120 times.
excerpts: Josh turns to verse 1 to watch God help Joshua turn things around: “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged.” “Thou shalt not” is not the most common command in Scripture. It’s hard to give an exact number across languages and authors, but alongside peace be with you, praise the Lord, rejoice, and give thanks, “fear not, do not be afraid” is given approximately 120 times.

What does God want when he commands us not to fear? Josh thinks it’s simple: he wants us to recall and meditate on his promises. Joshua has just dealt with Achan and his disobedient family, comforted 36 families who lost loved ones in the first attack at Ai, and watched the conquest stall in complete failure. God says, remember my promise.

Which promise? Probably all of them. Josh jokes that he is Joshua, but not this Joshua. If he were, he would never forget the promise in chapter 1: “I will give you every place where you set your foot, just as I promised Moses.” You did it for Moses, and you’re going to use me.

excerpts: Surveying the wins and losses in Canaan, Josh keeps coming back to that promise. Joshua seems to have been present for the march around Jericho, and they won. In chapter 7 Joshua sent men to Ai, and while Josh can’t be certain, it doesn’t read like Joshua went with them, and they lost.

In chapter 8 the Lord tells Joshua to take the whole army and attack Ai, for he has delivered its king, people, city, and land into his hands; this time they may carry off the plunder and livestock. Yahweh is faithful to his promise to Moses and to Joshua: where his leader goes, God gives victory.

This drives home that obedience matters to God. 2 Chronicles says the eyes of the Lord range throughout the earth to strengthen those whose hearts are fully committed to him. Your strength isn’t something you muster up; God gives it on the basis of your commitment. That hasn’t changed: the night before he gave his life, Jesus told his disciples, “Whoever has my commands and keeps them is the one who loves me.” These are the ones who can have confidence in his promises.

documents.excerpt: For the first attack Joshua took instructions from the spies, who said they didn’t need many men, and it failed miserably. He learned his lesson: this time he awaited instructions from the Lord.
excerpts: For the first attack Joshua took instructions from the spies, who said they didn’t need many men, and it failed miserably. He learned his lesson: this time he awaited instructions from the Lord.

Learn from Joshua’s mistake. Don’t build your faith on human wisdom; build it on God’s power. You have the very words of God available to you: read of your Savior, become a scholar of his promises, seek him morning and night and in everything you do, and watch your faith grow.

If you lack wisdom, don’t ask your coworker or your father-in-law, don’t Google it, don’t YouTube Dr. Phil; ChatGPT and AI can’t help you here. James says if any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault.

documents.excerpt: This time God gave the soldiers the right to claim the spoils; they had to burn the city but could keep the loot. How ridiculous does Achan look now? If he had waited a few days he could have picked out a nice robe and displayed his silver on his nightstand instead of burying it, and now he is under some rocks somewhere in Canaan. Josh thinks of the seagulls in Finding Nemo: “Mine, mine.”
excerpts: This time God gave the soldiers the right to claim the spoils; they had to burn the city but could keep the loot. How ridiculous does Achan look now? If he had waited a few days he could have picked out a nice robe and displayed his silver on his nightstand instead of burying it, and now he is under some rocks somewhere in Canaan. Josh thinks of the seagulls in Finding Nemo: “Mine, mine.”

Wealth isn’t how much you have; it’s how content you are with what he has given you. Many struggle with what is called serpent theology, after the tempter in the garden who emphasized the one restriction God imposed rather than the riches he had lavished: one tree of “thou shalt not,” and no attention to all the other trees of “enjoy me.”

The key to a faithful Christian life is recognizing that God is generous. He isn’t trying to bankrupt you; he is trying to lavish you with generosity, love, and his provision, his way. Discontent people are never satisfied with more, so don’t be ruled by what you desire; be joyful in what he offers you.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 30, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: Next come Yahweh’s instructions for the ambush, God tapping into his inner Call of Duty strategy mode. Josh reads how Joshua sends 30,000 of his best fighting men out at night to lie in ambush behind the city while he and the rest draw the men of Ai out and flee, so the ambush can rise up and take the city. Josh loves that Joshua adds, “Do what the Lord has commanded”: last time they didn’t, and this time when the Lord says burn it, that means burn it.
excerpts: Next come Yahweh’s instructions for the ambush, God tapping into his inner Call of Duty strategy mode. Josh reads how Joshua sends 30,000 of his best fighting men out at night to lie in ambush behind the city while he and the rest draw the men of Ai out and flee, so the ambush can rise up and take the city. Josh loves that Joshua adds, “Do what the Lord has commanded”: last time they didn’t, and this time when the Lord says burn it, that means burn it.

Time and again, unless God’s promises are received in faith, nothing is accomplished. God made Abraham a massive promise, but nothing moved ahead unless Abraham went. Joseph knew God’s promises; Moses claimed them by faith, and so did his successor Joshua. The first attack failed because Joshua and Israel got happy feet and ran ahead of God, operating by human wisdom after hearing the spies.

Nothing has changed: even the gospel is of no value if it isn’t received by faith. Hebrews 4 says the good news was proclaimed to us just as to them, but the message was of no value to those who did not share the faith of those who obeyed. Hearing isn’t enough; we must run to God’s promises in faith, becoming doers and not just hearers.

In John 5 Jesus tells the Pharisees that they study the Scriptures diligently because they think in them they have eternal life, yet these Scriptures testify about him and they refuse to come to him to have life. It isn’t about what you know or what you do; it’s about who you trust. Joshua learned you can’t walk by faith out in front of God’s promises: you listen, you believe and take him at his word, and then the work begins.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 30, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: We should evaluate every opportunity on its own. It is easy to say God gave us Jericho, so let’s keep rolling with what’s working. But chapter 8 shows God seems to enjoy variety: from a daytime trumpet-blast approach to a midnight sneak attack with an ambush.
excerpts: We should evaluate every opportunity on its own. It is easy to say God gave us Jericho, so let’s keep rolling with what’s working. But chapter 8 shows God seems to enjoy variety: from a daytime trumpet-blast approach to a midnight sneak attack with an ambush.

It cracks Josh up, because he can’t think of a group that loves tradition more than Christians. Not all tradition is bad, and he isn’t anti-tradition, but to those who want to face off in the lobby over it he says: what if God wants to do something new, wants a little variety, or decides to adopt a new strategy? Who are you to say it is or isn’t from him?

So watch your tongue about different ministry strategies, like churches that pop up in nightclubs or bars, or the XXX church lifting people out of the porn industry and setting them on fire for Christ. Just because that isn’t how you do it doesn’t mean God can’t use it for his glory. Bruce Barton said, “When you’re through changing, you’re through.” Don’t get stuck in your ways; seek his ways, and don’t assume what worked back then will work again.

What he boasts in is that God took some of the most painful experiences of his life and uses them almost every week to help somebody avoid that pain. His humiliation has become God’s victory: he went from addict to someone God uses to help others out of addiction, and from a child of divorce to helping others fight for their marriages. The things he was most angry at God for allowing are the things he is most grateful for today.

God rewrites stories. We have been washed by the blood of Jesus so we can have a clean slate and he can write a new story: the old has passed away, the new has come. If you came in beaten down, tired, and in failure, don’t get hung up on the failures of chapter 7. Wait on the Lord, stay faithful, and in time he will show you what chapter 8 has for you.

Josh understands this is a difficult text, and their study through Joshua has no shortage of those, but please don’t mistake it for the killing of innocent people. documents.excerpt: Israel carries off the livestock and plunder as the Lord instructed, and Joshua burns Ai into a permanent heap of ruins. He impales the body of the king of Ai on a pole until sunset, then has it thrown down at the city gate under a large pile of rocks that remains to this day.
excerpts: Israel carries off the livestock and plunder as the Lord instructed, and Joshua burns Ai into a permanent heap of ruins. He impales the body of the king of Ai on a pole until sunset, then has it thrown down at the city gate under a large pile of rocks that remains to this day.

Did your parents ever cover your eyes during a gruesome part of a movie? Josh understands protecting young eyes from what they can’t process, but every believer needs to see the king of Ai on a pole. Don’t look away.

Deuteronomy 21 says the body of anyone put to death for a capital offense and exposed on a pole must be buried the same day, because anyone hung on a pole is under God’s curse. The body wasn’t under God’s curse because it was put on a pole; it was put on a pole because it was under God’s curse. It is a warning we should open our eyes to see; without visuals like this, would we really fear sin and its consequences?

In an effort to call you to faith, God gave another picture of judgment. A little over 1,400 years after the king of Ai hung on a tree in Canaan, the King of the Jews hung on a tree in Jerusalem. excerpts: Josh’s family called a too-quick change of subject “topical whiplash,” complete with “squirrel!” That is what the last verses of chapter 8 feel like: from war to worship real quick. To the reader it’s quick, but to the Israelites it was a 30-mile journey north to Shechem, where Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim are, about 40 miles north of Jerusalem.

The location matters because it was in this valley that Abram first received the promise of the land. Genesis 12 says Abram traveled as far as the great tree of Moreh at Shechem while the Canaanites were in the land, and the Lord appeared to him and said, “To your offspring I will give this land,” so he built an altar there.

Now in Joshua 8, Abram’s offspring return to the place of the promise as they experience its fulfillment: proof that God is faithful and his word never fails. Time may pass and generations come and go, but Yahweh has never failed, and he isn’t about to start now.

excerpts: Believers today aren’t living under the curse of the law, because Jesus bore that curse on a tree. In Christ, believers are blessed with every spiritual blessing; Josh could spend his entire life trying to understand the magnitude of that, all because of the grace of God.

Don’t take that to mean that because we’re under grace, the law of God no longer matters. It does. We aren’t saved by keeping the law; it reveals our sinfulness but cannot save us. Romans 8 says what the law was powerless to do, weakened by the sinful nature, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful humanity to be a sin offering, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fully met in us who live according to the Spirit.

excerpts: Josh prays for those in the room struggling to have hope in a difficult time, drowning in shame and beating themselves up over past mistakes they keep hanging on to, whether because of the pain it caused loved ones or because they feel they deserve not to be released. He wants to lead them to God’s throne, because God says that if we confess our sins he will forgive us and purify us from all unrighteousness.

When we fall into sin it feels like we’ve ruined everything and shame sets in quickly, but into that shame he speaks the name of Jesus, whose blood cleanses us. He prays for a cleansing in the room and that everyone would embrace their second chance, which may lead to more chances. We will not achieve a sinless state as Jesus did, but we can walk in the Spirit with confidence if we love him and commit our lives to him.

At Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus asked, “Who do you say I am?” God revealed to Peter, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” a confession every believer has echoed since.
excerpts: Peter went on special missions with Jesus, saw Jairus’ daughter raised, and witnessed the transfiguration with Moses and Elijah. At Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus asked, “Who do you say I am?” God revealed to Peter, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” a confession every believer has echoed since.

But in the upper room Josh argues Peter fell into overconfidence. Instead of seeking God’s will, he boasted in his own: “I will never betray you.” Loyalty is a great trait, but when God hands his Son over to take on the sins of the world, your will doesn’t matter, and when God raises a three-day-old corpse, you can’t cover that up.

Peter is so relatable. Have you ever walked so closely with Jesus that people think you’re weird, talking to Jesus in your car or singing about him while walking the dog to the mailbox, so content that nothing could shake you, and then out of nowhere you crash and burn and never saw it coming?

excerpts: When Josh was 14, his dad bought a motorcycle (picture his old man on a Harley with his NIV strapped to the back) and approved Josh’s first big purchase, a brand-new purple Honda Elite S. He picked up girls for dates and hit the McDonald’s dollar menu. As the baby of the family, his siblings said everything was handed to him; really he just watched them mess up and didn’t follow their example.

He rode it home, spit-shining it at every stop, and his two older sisters were waiting in the driveway, drowning in discontentment. Andrea, the oldest, asked to drive it and wanted none of his instructions: “I can drive a car. How hard can this be?” She headed down the hill, blew through the stop sign, hit the curb across the intersection, and was thrown into the neighbor’s yard; she couldn’t find the brake. She fell into overconfidence and crashed hard, and the moped never steered the same.
That is the lay of the land in the Christian life: sometimes we sit comfortably on top of the hill on a new purple moped, and sometimes we fly face-first into the blacktop, and it can happen fast.

documents.excerpt: Moses describes the promised land in Deuteronomy 11 as a land of mountains and valleys that drinks rain from heaven. He is describing geography, but kings, prophets, apostles, theologians, and pastors have used that language for the life of faith: as we claim our inheritance in Christ, we experience mountains of encouragement and valleys of discouragement.
excerpts: Moses describes the promised land in Deuteronomy 11 as a land of mountains and valleys that drinks rain from heaven. He is describing geography, but kings, prophets, apostles, theologians, and pastors have used that language for the life of faith: as we claim our inheritance in Christ, we experience mountains of encouragement and valleys of discouragement.

You aren’t on the mountain because of your great faith; God has you there and can move you down a peg anytime. You aren’t in the valley because you lack faith; you may be there because of sin, but you can be on a mountain with sin in your life too, which may be the worst place to be. Your faith is best described by how you respond to the mountains and valleys.

In Joshua 7 things are going to change: Joshua goes from the mountaintop at Jericho to the valley of defeat at Ai. Josh asks the church to watch him closely, learning where he comes up short and where he hits the mark, so they are prepared for discouragement or encouragement.

documents.excerpt: Church culture is drifting further from a godly view of sin. Every other week we hear about another so-called pastor living in sin for decades, then the parade of press drops: “I’m sorry for what I did.” No, you’re sorry you got caught. The church knows the difference between remorse and self-pity. An apology means nothing unless you show it by killing that sin; you had decades to repent and waited until you got caught. Get out of the pulpit. Insincerity reveals unbelief.

Josh isn’t suggesting we start stoning people, but how can you be lazy with sin and serious about pursuing holiness? You can’t. True belief is connected to true repentance.
excerpts: Look at how God handles sin in the camp after Jericho and compare it with how most churches, pastors, and elders deal with it. Josh isn’t suggesting we start stoning people, but how can you be lazy with sin and serious about pursuing holiness? You can’t. True belief is connected to true repentance.

Here is how repentance goes: by God’s grace the believer recognizes their sin, sees themselves as an accomplice in Christ’s crucifixion, no different from the Roman soldier holding the hammer and nails, and feels deep sorrow. Hearing the gospel, they confess, and everyone can witness them break free. It may not be immediate or permanent, and they may struggle on and off, but it is a break from the desire for that sin, and over time a deep hatred for all sin, because it robs us of our intended relationship with our Creator.

documents.excerpt: This is an issue of self-control. Achan says, “I coveted, I took, I hid.” At any of those three stages he could have confessed and turned away, and he could have spoken up as the tribes, clans, and families were called out. But he didn’t care to confess until he had to.
excerpts: This is an issue of self-control. Achan says, “I coveted, I took, I hid.” At any of those three stages he could have confessed and turned away, and he could have spoken up as the tribes, clans, and families were called out. But he didn’t care to confess until he had to.

If you see that you are coveting something you know you shouldn’t, don’t take it: turn your back, look away, walk away. If you took it and you are heading back to the tent, please don’t hide it; don’t pick up the shovel. Drop it where you are. You can still walk away.

People, even Christians, act like there’s no way out, but there is. In 2 Timothy Paul tells the young pastor that the Spirit God gave us doesn’t make us timid but gives us power, love, and self-discipline. If God’s Spirit lives in you, you have self-control. Use it. Don’t wait for God’s investigation or judgment; deal with it now.
This part is hard, but if people won’t recognize where they’ve missed the mark and won’t repent, as much as we love them, we must be willing to part ways. There comes a point when enough is enough.

excerpts: A man recently asked Josh for help with his porn addiction, which Josh is thrilled about; working together to eliminate sin is God-honoring. Josh asked if he owned a gun (“It’s Arizona, everybody owns a gun”) and told him to shoot his laptop. “Right now you’re pointing a gun at your marriage. You’re going to kill one. Which will it be?”

When the man said he would get fired without a laptop, Josh said, “So what? You’ll break your covenant with God if you lose your marriage.” Don’t you think God can provide a new job when you kill sin in obedience? It might even be better. Find a job in an office surrounded by people, because working from home behind that door isn’t working.

Those who actually love Jesus don’t see, take, and hide. Jesus says whoever wants to be his disciple must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him; whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for him will find it. Stop spending so much time in the tent with hidden sin and a shovel, and start living in the open with our loving Savior.

Joshua shows what a life devoted to the Lord looks like and the blessing of submitting to his will instead of selfish ambition. Service to the Lord isn’t without challenges, but when we realize the battle belongs to the Lord, we can be confident it is already won.

It illustrates Proverbs 3 in practice: let love and faithfulness never leave you; trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight. Why Joshua matters
On Father’s Day, Elijah says he jumped at the chance to teach when Pastor Josh said the teaching team would go through Joshua. The book is a historical testament to the earliest days of our faith and has practical application for every believer today.
Joshua shows what a life devoted to the Lord looks like and the blessing of submitting to his will instead of selfish ambition. Service to the Lord isn’t without challenges, but when we realize the battle belongs to the Lord, we can be confident it is already won.
It illustrates Proverbs 3 in practice: let love and faithfulness never leave you; trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight. Through faith and obedience Israel witnessed that with God all things are possible.
documents.title: Why Joshua matters — Justice in Jericho

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · June 16, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: In chapter 1 Joshua takes up Moses’ heavy mantle with a commission from God and the people’s acceptance. In chapter 2 God uses Rahab, a prostitute, not merely to protect the spies or show he can use anyone, but because her name in Jesus’ bloodline shows it was always the plan to preserve the Messiah’s line through her. “Hey, legalists.” Praise God he uses wicked, rebellious people like us.
excerpts: In chapter 1 Joshua takes up Moses’ heavy mantle with a commission from God and the people’s acceptance. In chapter 2 God uses Rahab, a prostitute, not merely to protect the spies or show he can use anyone, but because her name in Jesus’ bloodline shows it was always the plan to preserve the Messiah’s line through her. “Hey, legalists.” Praise God he uses wicked, rebellious people like us.

In chapter 3 God “pulls an Exodus 14” and stops the flooded Jordan so Israel crosses on dry ground, far from the last miracle in the book. All of it shows a sovereign God in full control who is also good and faithful, and as he made a way for Israel out of Egypt and into the land, he has made a way for us out of sin through Jesus’ atoning death and resurrection. Salvation and deliverance are written all over this book.

documents.excerpt: First, chapter 5. documents.context: Elijah Stanley · June 16, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: Because of that fear, Jericho added defenses to an already well-fortified city. Though small, it was the best-defended city in Canaan. Digs in the 1930s and ’40s and as recently as 1997 found an embankment and a double wall: a lower retaining wall 10 to 15 feet high topped by a mud-brick wall another 20 to 26 feet high and about 6 feet thick, then an embankment and a second wall of similar size sitting about 46 feet above ground, protecting the main living area of about six acres.
excerpts: Because of that fear, Jericho added defenses to an already well-fortified city. Though small, it was the best-defended city in Canaan. Digs in the 1930s and ’40s and as recently as 1997 found an embankment and a double wall: a lower retaining wall 10 to 15 feet high topped by a mud-brick wall another 20 to 26 feet high and about 6 feet thick, then an embankment and a second wall of similar size sitting about 46 feet above ground, protecting the main living area of about six acres.

Homes in the embankment between the walls likely housed the poorer citizens: if you’re poor, you only get one wall. The whole city sat on about ten acres, nothing for a town when Anthem is about 5,900 acres. At about 200 people per acre in small stacked one-room homes, owning three acres would mean 600 people in your backyard. Roughly 2,000 people were now tightly fortified, and verse 1 says no one went out and no one came in.

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · June 16, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: Commentators notice, and Elijah loves, Joshua’s initiative to immediately do what the Lord commanded, without hesitating. Have you struggled with delayed obedience? Elijah has, many times: God wanted him to give something up, get stronger in a weak area, or do something far outside his comfort zone, and in stubbornness and selfishness he kicked the can down the road until the burden became unbearable or blew up in his face. Looking back, acting right away would have spared so much stress and heartache.
excerpts: Commentators notice, and Elijah loves, Joshua’s initiative to immediately do what the Lord commanded, without hesitating. Have you struggled with delayed obedience? Elijah has, many times: God wanted him to give something up, get stronger in a weak area, or do something far outside his comfort zone, and in stubbornness and selfishness he kicked the can down the road until the burden became unbearable or blew up in his face. Looking back, acting right away would have spared so much stress and heartache.

Immediate obedience is a showcase of your faith. It shows you believe God’s will is best for you and that he will do what he says. That isn’t an endorsement to rush into big decisions without prayer, godly counsel, and discernment; “Eli did not tell you to do that.” But Scripture makes clear followers of Christ are set apart by love for one another, humble service, boldness to share the truth, and putting others first. None of these save you, but they speak to your consistency with what you profess and your witness to the world.

We all fall short of the glory of God, but if you are delaying obedience because you are comfortable, do some self-evaluation. Remember what Christ did for you while you were still a sinner and ask whether it is really his will for you to stay complacent. Paul calls us out of lukewarmness in Ephesians 4: put off your old self, be made new in the attitude of your minds, and put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.

Elijah prays the church would be excited to obey God’s commands, love his word, and stand boldly on its truth; not like so much of the American church with empty words of meaningless praise, but with genuine worship that bears witness to the amazing grace of our Lord.

documents.excerpt: First, the cities Israel destroys, Jericho, Ai, and Hazor, are military strongholds, not civilian population centers. Joshua Ryan Butler, a local pastor, writes that we should picture a military fort being taken, not a civilian massacre: God is pulling down the Great Wall of China, not demolishing Beijing; taking out the Pentagon, not New York City.
excerpts: First, the cities Israel destroys, Jericho, Ai, and Hazor, are military strongholds, not civilian population centers. Joshua Ryan Butler, a local pastor, writes that we should picture a military fort being taken, not a civilian massacre: God is pulling down the Great Wall of China, not demolishing Beijing; taking out the Pentagon, not New York City.

Second, God put explicit limits on the conquest, which is why those boring first five books matter. In Deuteronomy 2:9 God tells Moses not to harass the Moabites, because he saved that land for Lot’s descendants, keeping an earlier promise. Deuteronomy 7:22 puts a time boundary on it: God would drive the people out slowly, not lay waste to everything at once.

Third, Deuteronomy 20 lays out explicit rules for war, where Augustine got just war theory and the West derives its Geneva Conventions. “All is fair in love and war” isn’t biblical. We are not pacifists, but there is a moral way to decide when to go to war and how to conduct it. These rules included offers of peace, which were consistently rejected according to Joshua 11.

That is the setup for the study: as Israel prepared to enter the promised land for the second time, their leaders passed through camp saying, “We don’t know which way to go, because we’ve never been this way before.”

Was it true? For this crowd it was a different way, but not for the nation. Joshua was born in bondage
By Joshua 3, Israel has returned to the same place they started from. They had been in captivity in Egypt for over 400 years, never able to think their own thoughts, plan their schedules, or make their own decisions, for twenty agonizingly long generations.
During that time Joshua son of Nun was born and raised in bondage, as were his daddy, granddaddy, and great-great-great-granddaddy. Bondage was Joshua’s family business; he had no clue how not to be in bondage.

excerpts: The parting of the waters was only phase one of the rescue. Phase one was God calling them out of bondage; phase two was following God into a whole new dimension of living. Getting to the other side of whatever has had a hold on you doesn’t mean you have stopped thinking, much less behaving, as though you were still in bondage.

God wanted more for his people and told them so: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves; I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk with heads held high.” God doesn’t want you walking around with the title former slave, recovering addict, or unfaithful spouse.

So God didn’t take them straight from the outhouse to the penthouse. He removed them from their bondage and let them languish a while in the wilderness. From slavery to the desert doesn’t sound like an upgrade, and it wasn’t intended to be. But Steve has learned from his own desert time that when God is your guide, great blessings come from the toughest of times, and when you break through, you will have become relentless.

excerpts: Then the ten made it back. However wonderful an opportunity is, there will always be the ten, full of negativity: the walls are fortified, the people are like giants, we seem like grasshoppers, and one of those big grapes could crush us.

It was ten versus two, and Steve has experienced ten against thousands. Negativity carries enormous power; its voices can drown out the most positive opportunity and spread fear, doubt, and anxiety to everyone within earshot. If ten are willing to say “we can’t,” thousands will be willing to say “we won’t.”

Sure enough, the former slaves voted no, even though it meant forty more years in the wilderness, taking laps around Sinai: no longer in Egypt but still in bondage, until that entire generation of “stinking thinkers” died off and a new generation came back to try again.

That is why following Jesus sometimes feels really hard. You look, pause, and strain, never sure you are seeing. “Do you see me, Steve?” “Oh yes, Lord,” while under his breath he says, “I can’t see him, and I have no clue where he’s going.” But actually it isn’t hard: face forward and press on, because Jesus is always just ahead. When in doubt, keep looking ahead, don’t be distracted, and press on.

excerpts: After you do the holy thing, you also have to do holy things. Do the holy thing at the altar, in the baptistry, or at communion, but don’t neglect doing holy things afterward.

God put it this way in Leviticus: consecrate yourselves and be holy, for I am holy; I am the Lord who brought you up out of Egypt, therefore be holy. James says don’t merely listen to the word and deceive yourselves; do what it says, or why bother listening? In Ephesians Paul urges believers, already in Christ and already consecrated, to put on the new self, created to be like God in true holiness.

So Paul goes on: put off falsehood and speak truthfully. Everybody blows a cork now and again, but don’t let the sun go down while you are still angry. If you have a history of stealing, cut it out. If you have used your mouth destructively, use it only for what builds others up. That is what Joshua means by consecrate: do what needs doing to be made holy, then by your actions be holy.

Joshua told the priests to take up the ark and pass on ahead of the people. There is that word again: ahead, always straight ahead. Then the priests were told that when they reached the edge of the water, they should go and stand in the river. “Seriously, God, have you seen this river?”
As soon as the priests set their feet in the Jordan, the waters flowing downstream were cut off and stood up in a heap.

documents.context: Steve Wyatt · June 9, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: Steve pauses to marvel at God’s creativity. Forty years before, God told Moses to raise his staff and stretch out his hand, and all night the Lord drove the sea back with a strong east wind, and Israel walked through on dry ground between walls of water. Forty years later it is not a sea but an angry, flooded river tangled with brush, and priests not known for their machismo must step into a raging torrent before the water stops and piles up in a heap. What happened on the other side of that heap is on Steve’s list of things to ask.

documents.context: Steve Wyatt · June 9, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: Having been around church stuff all his life, Steve imagines a Former Blind Man Christian Conference. The man from John 9 gives the keynote about the mud; the man from Matthew objects that you have to say “Lord, Son of David, have mercy”; the man from Mark 8 insists you can’t be healed unless Jesus spits in your eye. Like most church groups, they would leave with four new denominations: the mudball Christians, the spit-in-the-eye Christians, the word of faith Christians, and the Orthodox “Lord, Son of David” Christians.

excerpts: Biblical archaeologists strongly believe that when the priests’ feet touched the water, what seemed like nothing was actually an earthquake about 20 miles upstream at the town mentioned here, Adam. Steve’s God doesn’t need the earthquake, but that doesn’t mean he won’t use one.

Earthquakes evidently happen at that spot every 300 to 400 years. In 1927 the cliffs overlooking the Jordan there fell into the river and blocked its flow for about 21 hours, plenty of time for two and a half million people. If God used an earthquake, what a reminder that he really does work upstream, a thousand yards or twenty miles ahead, so he can meet you in the mud and turn your chaotic life into a masterpiece.

excerpts: In verse 17 the priests stand in the middle of the Jordan as two million people cross by, and turning the page to chapter 4, verse 10, they are still standing in the same place; the story hasn’t advanced. Why? The Lord told Joshua to choose twelve men, one per tribe, to take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, where the priests stood, and carry them to where they would stay that night.

They built an altar to remind everyone who has ever been stuck in the mud: don’t miss the amazing. Don’t be in such a hurry to get to the other side that you miss what God was doing for you in the muddy middle, because that is where God loves to do amazing things.

There is a second reason: one day your kids will look at those stones and ask, “Mama, what are those stones for?” and you can tell them what God did when you were stuck: “I got stuck, baby, but God set me free.”

Stones from the middle
In verse 17 the priests stand in the middle of the Jordan as two million people cross by, and turning the page to chapter 4, verse 10, they are still standing in the same place; the story hasn’t advanced. Why? The Lord told Joshua to choose twelve men, one per tribe, to take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, where the priests stood, and carry them to where they would stay that night.
They built an altar to remind everyone who has ever been stuck in the mud: don’t miss the amazing. Don’t be in such a hurry to get to the other side that you miss what God was doing for you in the muddy middle, because that is where God loves to do amazing things.
There is a second reason: one day your kids will look at those stones and ask, “Mama, what are those stones for?” and you can tell them what God did when you were stuck: “I got stuck, baby, but God set me free.”

excerpts: Joshua had a second set of stones. The first set was for all the people to see and remember; the second would remain unseen. While the priests stood in the middle, Joshua built his own private altar as the people hurried across, not knowing how long the water would hold. Steve would hurry too and do his remembering once he got to shore.

Please don’t be in such a hurry that you neglect remembering time, because what God is doing in your muddy middle you don’t want to miss. If the mud is where you are, God wants to meet you right there.

Joshua paused in his muddy middle and carefully set up the stones, knowing the water would soon cover them and no one would ever know but Joshua and his God. Still he took the time in the raging waters to select them and build the altar at the very spot where the priests had stood, and they are there to this day.

excerpts: Do you have visual reminders of how faithful God has been? Steve learned long ago the power of a tangible reminder, and he brought a few. His dad gave him a small figurine in 1979 when he started preaching, and writing this message he realized it was time to pass it on to his son.

He scavenged a rod from the Sea of Galilee during a hard season and saw the Lion of Judah in it, remembering that the Jesus who walked on those waters could carry him across his. A portrait of the laughing Jesus, his favorite, reminds him of a time stress nearly stole his joy. His kidney pillow, used after his transplant, reminds him God gave him more time. A picture cube Josh made him not long after his voice changed has an audio message Steve listens to more often than Josh knows, thanking God for his part in the man Josh is today.
These aren’t valuable to anyone else, but they are so valuable to him. Do you have them?

Identify some of your own stones, a picture or a voicemail, something that takes you back to the moment he pulled you out or provided when you were about to go under. Then build an altar to the God who specializes in pulling the people he loves out of the muddy middle. Do it even if you feel too stuck to imagine how, because he will meet you there. You may not see him yet, but he is up ahead, and though he is ahead of where you are, he always knows where you are.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 2, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: When Josh thinks of women in the Bible, he thinks of godly women who have their stuff together, like Mary, who hears from the angel that she will have a baby and essentially says, “Here to serve God, let’s do this,” or Sarah, first lady of the Hebrew race, who gets an honorable mention for her faith in Hebrews 11.
excerpts: When Josh thinks of women in the Bible, he thinks of godly women who have their stuff together, like Mary, who hears from the angel that she will have a baby and essentially says, “Here to serve God, let’s do this,” or Sarah, first lady of the Hebrew race, who gets an honorable mention for her faith in Hebrews 11.

Only two women are named in Hebrews 11, and the other is Rahab. Verse 1 tells us Joshua secretly sent two spies to look over the land, especially Jericho, and they stayed in the house of a prostitute named Rahab. Whatever you call her, harlot or hooker, we know what she did: she made a career selling herself to men.

How can Hebrews 11 mention these two women in the same breath? James 2 mentions Rahab alongside Abraham, and Levi the tax collector puts her in the genealogy of Jesus with Jacob, David, Solomon, and Josiah. How does this prostitute keep making headlines in God’s redemptive plan? That is what Josh wants to show.

excerpts: After church, a skeptic thanked Josh for his courage in discussing his journey with addiction and shared his own transformation. The difference was that Josh gave credit to God and the man took the credit himself. He asked, “People outside the faith have transformations too. How do you know yours is from God?”

Josh told him the NIH cited in 2019 that 74% of addiction treatment is rooted in some sort of spirituality within the church, so conquering addiction without faith isn’t common. And if someone did, he would ask what they replaced it with. When the man finally told him, Josh looked him in the eye: “I didn’t replace my addiction with anything. It was just gone. That’s how I know God did it for me.” It isn’t everyone’s story, but it was his.

excerpts: Rahab grew up worshiping pagan gods under leaders who made laws to benefit themselves, not under leaders who kept the law on their lips. Expecting a non-believer to convert and immediately act like a mature believer is ridiculous.

Josh has baptized people and gone out to eat with them while their hair is still wet, and they are dropping bombs in the lobby. The church prays, shows patience, and trusts God to work on their hearts, as he did with Josh over more than a decade. Someone following Jesus five minutes won’t look like someone following him fifteen years; expecting it is higher expectations than Jesus had. Spend more time in the red letters: Jesus says be merciful as your Father is merciful, and that was about our enemies, so how much more for a brother or sister in Christ?

Rahab acted like any pagan in the city would, and you probably would too if cornered; and if you would have told the truth, to God be the glory, not you. It drives Josh mad when Christians reach the other end of holiness and act like they got there on their own. That is pure pride and causes others to stumble. Be humble is a command, not a suggestion; it is evidence you are in the kingdom. Spend less time on the speck in theirs and more on the plank in yours.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 2, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: If we looked at your life with a fine-toothed comb, what would your decisions tell us? Not your decision to be here today, but Monday afternoon when you are fed up with your boss, Tuesday night when you are exhausted heading home, or when your adult children act like adult children. Are you following the God of heaven or the lowercase gods of this world?
excerpts: If we looked at your life with a fine-toothed comb, what would your decisions tell us? Not your decision to be here today, but Monday afternoon when you are fed up with your boss, Tuesday night when you are exhausted heading home, or when your adult children act like adult children. Are you following the God of heaven or the lowercase gods of this world?

Saving faith isn’t a weekend-warrior lifestyle. Genuine faith doesn’t just believe God is real; it believes God is our refuge. Faith isn’t holding a set of right beliefs; celebrating someone’s strong theology is basically saying they are smart. Faith is clinging to hope in our most desperate hour: “Lord, I’ve got nothing else; you’ve got my life.” The question isn’t whether your theology is strong but whether, when you suffered, you blamed God or rejoiced that you are his child and a co-heir with Christ, clung to fear or drew near.

excerpts: Rahab includes herself among those melting in fear, but in verse 12 she realizes the source of her fear can be the source of mercy. She asks the spies to swear by the Lord to show kindness to her family, spare her father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all who belong to them, and save them from death.

In effect she says, “I understand your God is the one true God, and he has guaranteed you victory. I want in. When you march on Jericho, please spare my family.” She isn’t taking out an insurance policy in case something happens; she believes it is happening and aims to cut a deal with God. She believes God is good, fair, wonderful, and worthy of her sacrifice and worship.
Isn’t it incredible how much we learn about faith from a prostitute? Some might be offended to come to church and get taken to school by a prostitute.

James 2 asks what good it is to claim faith without deeds; can such faith save? James, Rahab, Paul, John, and Peter all say the same thing: what you do reveals who you are. Saving faith is best seen by works, not words; share your faith by showing it. A dead faith turns the spies over to the Jericho FBI and tries to protect its own family by getting in good with the king. The question is which king you are getting in good with.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 2, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: God didn’t reach down and grab Josh’s addiction one morning. At first he didn’t think he needed to be saved from it or that it would get in the way. It took years of the Spirit convicting him. He didn’t make a fancy plan with medications on the nightstand; he said, “God, you need to take this now. Carry me through the sleepless nights. Don’t let me become a crabby husband or an awful father. These withdrawals are killing me, but I don’t want this anymore because I know you don’t want it for me. Take it.” And he did.
excerpts: God didn’t reach down and grab Josh’s addiction one morning. At first he didn’t think he needed to be saved from it or that it would get in the way. It took years of the Spirit convicting him. He didn’t make a fancy plan with medications on the nightstand; he said, “God, you need to take this now. Carry me through the sleepless nights. Don’t let me become a crabby husband or an awful father. These withdrawals are killing me, but I don’t want this anymore because I know you don’t want it for me. Take it.” And he did.

Many are waiting for God to reach in and grab things from their lives, but that isn’t how it works. Bring it to him with open hands, not clamped ones, lay it at his feet, and he will either take it or he won’t. If he does, praise God, and don’t closet that testimony: God doesn’t sanctify you for your silence; he saves us for our song.

If he doesn’t take it, praise God; he has something for you. He isn’t confirming that what you’re doing is okay, but you can still do kingdom work with some mud on your boots. Keep working it out with him, ask him for help, keep talking to him, waiting on him, and being around people who love him. Keep the faith.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 2, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: We know Rahab had faith because we saw it at work. She believed God could change her circumstances and her family’s circumstances.
excerpts: We know Rahab had faith because we saw it at work. She believed God could change her circumstances and her family’s circumstances.

The Israelites camped east of the Jordan were eyewitnesses to the Red Sea; they saw Moses. Rahab, a long way off on foot, only heard about it, and even heard it as the sea drying up. She isn’t an eyewitness, yet she believes so much that she commits treason against her earthly king, hoping her heavenly king will protect her family. Rahab never made it about Rahab. That is faith that works.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 2, 2024 · Courage Over Fear
documents.excerpt: In biblical covenants God often assigns a visual reminder: circumcision for Abraham, the book and the people sprinkled with blood at Sinai, the rainbow for Noah, and the bread and the cup Jesus gave his disciples, which the church took earlier in the service. Paul says whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
excerpts: In biblical covenants God often assigns a visual reminder: circumcision for Abraham, the book and the people sprinkled with blood at Sinai, the rainbow for Noah, and the bread and the cup Jesus gave his disciples, which the church took earlier in the service. Paul says whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

The scarlet rope would mark Rahab’s house as under the protection of Israel’s army when they took the city. It may have seemed insignificant to the neighbors, but not when the invasion began. Its color reminds us of blood. It was a sign of her faith, which led to the salvation of her family, much like the blood of the Passover lamb: every home marked with blood was spared that night.

There isn’t just a scarlet thread in Rahab’s window; there is a scarlet thread running through Scripture from beginning to end, a stream of blood pointing to Christ’s sacrifice on the cross. Hebrews 9 says the law requires nearly everything be cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Two thousand years ago on a hill in Israel, Jesus shed his blood for every sin that ever was and ever would be, and if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and purify us from all unrighteousness.

Josh carried this all week: he can’t think of anything worse for a believer to endure than an unbelieving family member. If they don’t hang the scarlet rope now, keep praying and never lose hope. The Prince of Egypt and the fathers in the homes
The Prince of Egypt came out on December 16, 1998, when Josh was 13, and he watched it over and over. He wept at the midnight Passover scene. He wasn’t angry at God; he knew why it was necessary. He was frustrated with the fathers in the homes: why didn’t you do it, why did you ignore the warnings and the signs, why didn’t you listen to Moses or follow your neighbor’s lead?
Those emotions still hit him when he reads Exodus 12: there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead. It became a theme for his ministry.

excerpts: In the past we shared common values, goals, and interests and could move together. Now everyone perches in their own social nest and minds their own business, and Josh thinks it has been a massive progress killer in the country and in the local church.

The flow from generation to generation isn’t as smooth as it once was. Smartphones are one reason; he traces the most massive cultural change of all time back to Steve Jobs announcing the iPhone. excerpts: Josh reads verse 1: after the death of Moses, the Lord tells Joshua to get ready, with all the people, to cross the Jordan into the land he is about to give them. He pauses on “Moses my servant is dead. Now then.”

If we’re honest, many of us would be offended. Someone as valuable as Moses, and God doesn’t command a beautiful arrangement or a well-orchestrated procession? There has never been anyone like Moses; surely they should stop and celebrate him.

Most people would respond that way, but great leaders don’t. They take a successful transition as the ultimate compliment, because everything they do is for the master, so they are uncomfortable when it is about them even for a moment. Leadership transitions are nearly impossible when the focus has been on the servant and not the master, and there is no wisdom in transitioning leadership overnight.

documents.excerpt: How you endure trials determines how others experience your faith; your faithfulness is a display of your faith. Joshua was not an overnight decision or the next hot up-and-coming leader. He had been faithful all along: he watched Moses face Pharaoh, drive his staff into the Red Sea, and crush idols.
excerpts: How you endure trials determines how others experience your faith; your faithfulness is a display of your faith. Joshua was not an overnight decision or the next hot up-and-coming leader. He had been faithful all along: he watched Moses face Pharaoh, drive his staff into the Red Sea, and crush idols.

Josh imagines Moses telling him about doubting his abilities at the burning bush, sitting him down in the tent where he spoke face to face with God and saying, “It’s not about you or what you can do. It’s about what you will allow God to do through you. Obey him, trust him, submit to him. I will die someday, but God’s promise lives on.”

Moses did die, but Yahweh didn’t go anywhere. They still had God’s promise, presence, word, and people, and that was enough to press on to the prize. The church still has all of these: the promise of eternal life, the presence of his Spirit, his word, and his people. Stop weeping and whining about what you don’t have; God is faithful and enough. “I press on toward the goal to win the prize.”

documents.excerpt: God chose Joshua, and everyone knew he was the new leader. Saying goodbye to faithful kingdom workers doesn’t mean kingdom work stops. This generational promise traces back to Abraham, and the connections between Genesis 12 and Joshua 1 can’t be ignored. Josh loves how Joseph put it at the end of his life in Genesis 50: God will surely come to your aid and take you to the land he promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
excerpts: God chose Joshua, and everyone knew he was the new leader. Saying goodbye to faithful kingdom workers doesn’t mean kingdom work stops. This generational promise traces back to Abraham, and the connections between Genesis 12 and Joshua 1 can’t be ignored. Josh loves how Joseph put it at the end of his life in Genesis 50: God will surely come to your aid and take you to the land he promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

This is who we are: lovers of God cling to his promises. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Moses didn’t know how God would do it. God’s people don’t wait for explanations; they move forward on his promises.

Big leaders are dying, big rivers are raging, and armies are developing, but we trust God will do it because he said he would. “Not this church.” The secret things belong to God, the revealed things belong to us and our children; his will be done on earth as it is in heaven, and we will keep our eyes fixed on heavenly things.

documents.excerpt: Joshua is given three tasks that the series will uncover: cross the river, defeat the enemy, divide the land. God encourages his new leader with a promise for each. The first is that everywhere his feet go is his.
excerpts: Joshua is given three tasks that the series will uncover: cross the river, defeat the enemy, divide the land. God encourages his new leader with a promise for each. The first is that everywhere his feet go is his.

The second: the territory will stretch from the desert to Lebanon and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean, and no one will be able to stand against him all the days of his life. Joshua had been at Kadesh Barnea and saw what happened when the people hesitated at the first sign of resistance. He knew God had already given them the land; it was their responsibility to go and grab it.

It must have been tempting to look across the Jordan and think, “This is the land of the Canaanites and the Hittites and all the other ‘ites.’” But God says he has been setting it up for them the whole time: the fields are prepped, the wells are dug, and their enemies are working the ground for them. If they stay in Egypt or hesitate in the desert, they will never see what he has for them. So cross.

Don’t give God all the reasons it can’t work; meditate on his words, his promises, and what he has said is true. There will be challenges, but “I’m Yahweh, I’m simply too much for them.” You might not have the numbers, the talent, or the strength, and it may look like you are about to fail, but lead not according to what you see but according to what God has told you is true.

He fast-forwards to Joshua’s final address before he dies at 110: be very strong, be careful to obey all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, without turning to the right or the left. excerpts: Josh stops to define prosperity and success in the Christian life. He fast-forwards to Joshua’s final address before he dies at 110: be very strong, be careful to obey all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, without turning to the right or the left. It should sound familiar; it is what God told Joshua before the conquest began.

That is success in God’s kingdom: from the start of the conquest to 110, keep the faith and keep his words on your lips. Joshua not only kept the faith but built the faith of those around him; you couldn’t be around him without feeling part of something big.

Build your 401k if you want; saving and caring for your family matters. But if that is your treasure, it is worldly success, not kingdom success. A lot of unhappy people are rich, living in massive homes with toys and worried about losing it. You would be surprised how little you can have and still build up the faith of those around you. Are you chasing kingdom success?

As a church we might not always agree, and with 5,000 words a week Josh is bound to say something you don’t like. But we must never be careless with or discourage one another. Learn to recognize the gifting God has placed in someone and build them up: “You have a beautiful gift. How can I pray for you?” A culture of encouragement is modeled in Joshua 1.

Whatever side of the river they were on, Joshua encouraged them, and they answered, “Whatever you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.” They could have said, “Nah, we’re good; good luck, Joshua,” but they heard the call and got on board.

Outside the essentials there is a lot of room for unity, and we spend too much time picking fights. Josh’s exercise for the week: look for someone you can build up. They might not need it, but you probably need to grow your gift of building others up.

excerpts: If there is one verse to memorize, it is Romans 5:8: God demonstrates his own love for us in this, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Those who love God immediately ask how they can demonstrate that love, and having been comforted, saved, and redeemed by it, the redeemed soul starts singing praise in how it lives.

We show God’s love by being open-handed: showing kindness, strengthening the weak, sticking by brothers and sisters through adversity, sharing food with the poor, seeking justice, defending the oppressed, fathering the fatherless, and coming alongside the widow. Micah: act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God.

Jesus didn’t abolish these but said whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me. If you have two shirts and a guy is shirtless, give him one. Store up treasures in heaven; whoever sows sparingly reaps sparingly; carry one another’s burdens; value others above yourselves; don’t grow weary of doing good. Our call to love others is radical.

There is one place to give, with multiple layers of accountability and controls and sufficient oversight to make sure gifts actually advance his kingdom. No elder or staff member will ever ask for money by email or in any unofficial capacity, or ask for gift cards or personal financial help; if anyone does, come to Josh immediately. Requests are made officially when the church gathers, through the app, website, or envelopes.

The one time Josh asked someone for money, the man had told him to let him know if things got tight. In a stewardship meeting where they were simply trusting God, the text came in: “Do you need anything?” Josh replied that he needed about $50,000 and was praying God would show up, and the man answered, “Done.” Josh praises God for his faith and generosity.

These controls don’t come from a desire for control, authority, or power, but from understanding that Satan has a strategy to infiltrate the church. The church is on the offensive but also takes defensive measures, and the only way to expose his deception is by knowing the truth.

As a youth pastor he told students after camp that Satan knew they had taken big steps with Jesus and would try to make them slip, so watch out. What he wishes he had told them, and now tells the former students listening: celebrate the progress, but never forget that one step back was a bit of theft by the evil one. Mourn the regression, but don’t be overcome by it.

excerpts: There are countless examples, and Josh dips a toe in. The most polarizing issue in the culture is homosexuality. Instead of recognizing their offense against God, many stand tall in pride, claiming God has offended them. Some walk away from the lifestyle and seek God, and the church praises God for those stories; others have made it their mission, even going to seminary, to prove it isn’t sin.

To defend continuing in it they use a one-liner that has deceived many: “Jesus never addresses homosexuality.” But he does, in Matthew 5 and Matthew 19. Asked about divorce, he refers back to creation and uses porneia, illicit sexual activity, usually translated sexual immorality, a word used 25 times in the New Testament. To learn which acts are immoral, refer back to the porneia code in Leviticus 18.

Few will fight Leviticus 18: don’t have relations with your mother’s sister (“seems like a good idea”); don’t take your wife’s sister as a rival wife (“some of you can’t handle one wife”); don’t have relations with an animal. Everyone agrees these are good for health, joy, homes, and society, until verse 22, and then there is a debate.

Jesus simply says porneia because he knows we can go back to the written law; it is like Josh saying he is pro Second Amendment without explaining it. Paul and John do the same. Those who love God protect and defend his word instead of doing gymnastics and back tucks over what they don’t like, even when it means killing sin in their own lives.

A church full of people who love the truth rejoices when it hears it. Josh’s hands don’t go up in worship because Eli picks the strings so nicely; they fly up when he hears timeless truth sung by God’s most precious creation and sees God working around him.
He gets hyped when lives are surrendered to the truth: God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, not to condemn the world but to save it, and whoever believes is not condemned. God took on flesh to save your soul. If you are ready, the waters are ready; be baptized, because through faith in Christ you can approach God with freedom and confidence.

Hold Fast: truth and love
Today begins a two-week series through 2 John called Hold Fast. The letter addresses how believers live together, and John sets the standard for Christian living with two concepts: truth and love.
A community with truth but no love is missing the mark, and so is a community with all love and no truth; some have been in churches like both. To avoid falling out of balance, we must hold fast to both.
documents.title: Hold Fast: truth and love — Love in the Truth

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · May 12, 2024 · Hold Fast
documents.excerpt: We like to talk about truth and love more than we practice them, and each of us leans one way. Some gravitate toward speaking and acting in love; others toward speaking truth and “tough love.” You know who you are, and it shapes how you minister and share the gospel.
excerpts: We like to talk about truth and love more than we practice them, and each of us leans one way. Some gravitate toward speaking and acting in love; others toward speaking truth and “tough love.” You know who you are, and it shapes how you minister and share the gospel.

The love crowd memorizes all the verses about grace and none on holiness; the truth crowd memorizes the holiness verses and none on grace. To the truth crowd: speaking the truth is love, but how you do it matters, and you don’t have a license to be a jerk. To the love crowd who want to love first and share truth later: you can do both at once; “I believe in you.”

Jesus didn’t make the distinctions we make. He is truth and love in flesh, and his followers will be committed to both equally. John witnessed that perfect blend and was changed forever; he contends you cannot separate truth and love, neither dominant nor informing the other, but wrapped together in perfect balance. That is called godliness.

excerpts: If Josh could summarize John’s message in one sentence, it would be: love divine truth. Remember Mary and Martha: Martha busied herself keeping the house in order while Mary sat at Jesus’ feet hanging on every word, and Jesus rebuked Martha. There is no better use of your time than listening to his words.

God is the author of truth, and he pours it out like a rainstorm. Deuteronomy 32: “Let my teaching fall like rain and my words descend like dew.” His words give life. There is only one truth, and it belongs to God, but he pours it out like rain.

His word even took on flesh: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us… full of grace and truth.” The faithful church declares that the God-man is declaring divine truth. Have you heard him? “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

Remember Mary and Martha: Martha busied herself keeping the house in order while Mary sat at Jesus’ feet hanging on every word, and Jesus rebuked Martha. There is no better use of your time than listening to his words.
God is the author of truth, and he pours it out like a rainstorm. Deuteronomy 32: “Let my teaching fall like rain and my words descend like dew.” His words give life. There is only one truth, and it belongs to God, but he pours it out like rain.
His word even took on flesh: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us… full of grace and truth.” The faithful church declares that the God-man is declaring divine truth. Have you heard him? “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

The leadership model comes from Jesus in Matthew 20: the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, “not so with you”; whoever wants to be great must be your servant, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom for many.

excerpts: Attendance isn’t the goal; service to the mission is. A healthy church isn’t measured by a filled auditorium but by how many believers come to be filled with the word so they can pour themselves out in service. That is the metric that matters, and it is also the hardest to track, so many churches track other things.

The mission, to change the way people see the church, admits that something is wrong. Complacency comes first to mind: the church growth movement of the past 50 years filled auditoriums with people passively observing rather than actively serving. Works of service should be non-negotiable; as James says, don’t merely listen to the word and so deceive yourselves, do what it says.
Josh feels he has the best job in the world and loves using his gifts to serve the church, and he wants every believer to know that joy. If we only sit and observe, we waste the gifts God gave us.

excerpts: Josh grew up close to the inner workings of the church, maybe too close: two churches before this one, one around 2,000 and one approaching 5,000, with immediate and extended family on staff. He knows some have had great experiences with megachurches and rejoices with them, but not him.

When things get sexualized where young people are supposed to learn to live like Christ, his blood boils, and yours should too.

excerpts: Josh believes the growth model went wrong. When a church thinks about growth in numbers more than growing mature disciples, priorities shift and the foundation becomes brittle. You can’t judge a church’s health by how many are there; rooms are packed in unhealthy churches.

Focused solely on growth, you chase benchmarks instead of chasing and shepherding souls, which is how unqualified youth pastors end up at camps like the ones he saw. If you leave bodies behind in pursuit of the mission, something is horribly wrong with you or with the mission. “Josh, we want to reach more people.” Of course, but at what cost? Lives and souls are at stake.

documents.excerpt: Crossroads Cares began in a difficult time. During COVID, churches closed their doors, and it began to weigh on them that the church should be out helping the sick, the last ones worried about getting sick, with more faith than the rest. They carried that burden, and it became a way for people to share needs in real time and for the church to step in.
excerpts: Crossroads Cares began in a difficult time. During COVID, churches closed their doors, and it began to weigh on them that the church should be out helping the sick, the last ones worried about getting sick, with more faith than the rest. They carried that burden, and it became a way for people to share needs in real time and for the church to step in.

Chris used to tell Josh that it used to be “if you build it, they will come,” but now if you build it, people just don’t care. The church has to get outside its four walls and take God’s love to people so they will care to hear the message of Jesus Christ, staying mobile and flexible while large churches close their doors.

Last year 400 needs were met, with more than 1,800 actions, people physically doing something. Year one met 124 needs, year two 294, year three 400. Public schools have made more than 200 requests for shoes for kids with holes in theirs; one put new shoes on and said, “I can run without it hurting.” Schools that are trying to get God out are coming to the church to help meet needs.

Once, as a youth pastor, one of them was only allowed to have lunch with students in a private room, so seeing counselors, teachers, and nurses feel the church’s support is an amazing feat. Kicks for Kids is going international, adopting schools and likely a first orphanage. Many needs are met within 24 hours, and when people ask who did it, the answer is the church, Jesus Christ’s church, which opens the door to share Christ. It has become a reputation: “You’ve got a need? Ask Crossroads Cares.”

documents.excerpt: You can’t meet needs without money. Crossroads Cares is well funded; as it is spent, it is replenished, sometimes shockingly fast, because God owns the cattle on a thousand hills.
excerpts: You can’t meet needs without money. Crossroads Cares is well funded; as it is spent, it is replenished, sometimes shockingly fast, because God owns the cattle on a thousand hills.

The church stretched its budget 18 percent this past year, the biggest leap it has ever taken, and the church met it and exceeded it. There were moments of asking God whether it was the right thing, and he provided. Crossroads Cares remains funded for another year.

A new future improvements plan will address the nearly two-decade-old chairs from the days of unpacking them from a U-Haul at the Anthem school every week; a white stain is probably Christmas Eve candle wax, and a purple one is from the individual communion cups during COVID.

There were 104 new givers, 25 with recurring gifts. That matters not as “more people, more money,” but because it shows faithfulness and discipleship; the wallet usually lags behind when someone follows Christ, as with the rich young ruler and our tendency to hold on with a tight grip.

When your eyes are set on things above, your money, talents, and desires flow freely toward his church and the mission; when your own concerns are in mind, nothing flows. The heart behind it: the church has lost its way and gotten distracted, and there is a call to lead it back to the mission, back to its first love, to seek and save what is lost. All that is left to ask is, are you with us?
