documents.context: Crossroads Teaching Team · April 28, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: Every Christian has to remember that faith informs politics, not the other way around, and we have lost the plot a little. Many political philosophies put man and the state in the place of God, and we must reject them. Francis Schaeffer said that if there is no God above the state, then the state is God, a terrifying thought.
excerpts: Every Christian has to remember that faith informs politics, not the other way around, and we have lost the plot a little. Many political philosophies put man and the state in the place of God, and we must reject them. Francis Schaeffer said that if there is no God above the state, then the state is God, a terrifying thought.

Take every thought captive and hold it up against God’s revelation. Colossians 1 says Christ is before all things and in him all things hold together, so whatever the result of an election or vote, it is part of God’s sovereign plan to show grace and mercy, and also justice and holiness. Accepting his sovereignty brings peace: even the bad things have their purpose and aren’t meaningless evil.

excerpts: The scattering of peoples began with sin, when man tried to build a tower to the heavens and God scattered them by language and location, yet we are still rooted in the same mother and father.

At first everyone was Jewish: Jesus, the disciples, the 120 in the upper room, and the 3,000 at Pentecost, so for a short time people assumed you had to become Jewish to follow Jesus. Then, in Acts 10, came Cornelius, a Gentile, which is who most of us are; until this was clarified, we would be out.

Peter didn’t want to go to him. On the roof, hungry, he saw a blanket of food unclean under the law and heard, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat,” and refused more than once until he understood the kingdom was bigger than he had known. He told Cornelius it was against their law for a Jew to associate with a Gentile, but God had shown him not to call any man impure or unclean. That opened the door and broke down the dividing wall of hostility.

To close out the identity series, he tells who every man on the panel was and is. Measured against the Lord’s law, Josh fails miserably; he is a transgressor and a sinner, and he would gladly share his list over coffee. He grew up in a Christian home and walked away in rebellious years. It was never about belief but obedience: he always believed but didn’t like it, because he knew what it required. The same grace is available to anyone who puts their faith and trust in him today. The church will baptize anyone ready to follow Jesus, the most amazing decision they will ever make. documents.excerpt: A lawyer asks Jesus which is the greatest commandment, and Jesus answers: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself; all the law and the prophets hang on these two.
excerpts: A lawyer asks Jesus which is the greatest commandment, and Jesus answers: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself; all the law and the prophets hang on these two.

Jesus quotes the Shema, the best-known passage in Judaism, which every faithful Jew recited twice a day. But reciting something might check the box of “with all your mind,” and that’s about it: a head thing, not a heart thing. Many believers today do the same; they sound like Jesus, but the heart isn’t involved.

Your pursuit of God is extremely shallow if you don’t first understand your true identity in Christ. Christ stirs our affection for God and transforms how we see God, ourselves, and others. Without that, you might perform it or pretend it, but it will get exhausting; unless your identity changes, you’ll never find joy in it.

Your pursuit of God is extremely shallow if you don’t first understand your true identity in Christ. Christ stirs our affection for God and transforms how we see God, ourselves, and others. Without that, you might perform it or pretend it, but it will get exhausting; unless your identity changes, you’ll never find joy in it.

While his wife was away on business in Colorado, he texted her: how does she think he is doing at leading their home to love, obey, and fear God, and teaching her and the kids the commands of God? Then he stared at the three bubbles. “Three bubble anxiety”: it’s a real thing.

He called himself out: does he wait for God to speak like he waits for his wife to text? He has a bad tendency to make requests of God and go about business as usual. When was the last time you waited on God?

To rearrange your life, you may need to start by repenting to your family. One of the most liberating things you can show your family is that Daddy and Mommy need grace too.

Many Christians prefer to think they were choking on their sins: that they could still signal for help or force it out, self-medicate, or “Home Depot it” by doing a bunch of good things to cancel out the bad. documents.excerpt: Skeptics ask why an all-powerful God can’t just forgive. Our culture screams for justice but has no idea what justice looks like. For God to turn his back on our sin and not make it right would be unjust.
excerpts: Skeptics ask why an all-powerful God can’t just forgive. Our culture screams for justice but has no idea what justice looks like. For God to turn his back on our sin and not make it right would be unjust.

If someone stole your gold bars, you would press charges; if someone cut you off on your way to prayer meeting, you would honk, because you love justice. When we do it we call it justice; when God does it we call it unjust. We accept justice legally, defending the righteous and condemning the guilty, but not spiritually.

God’s wrath is his perfectly just response to sin; Josh put it this week as “his holy impulse towards evil.” No one wants to talk about it, yet Proverbs says the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, and we aren’t likely to fear God by his kindness. If you don’t understand who God is fully, you will understand nothing else.
We need to hear how severely he will punish sin: the wages of sin is death, two deaths; death came through sin and spread to all men because all sin.

God’s wrath isn’t just an Old Testament tactic like the flood or Sodom and Gomorrah. The Lord does not change, and in the book of Acts, Ananias and Sapphira lied to Peter about the tithe and both died.

documents.excerpt: Verse 4 holds the two most amazing words in the universe: “But God.” Because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions; it is by grace you have been saved. Hallelujah.
excerpts: Verse 4 holds the two most amazing words in the universe: “But God.” Because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions; it is by grace you have been saved. Hallelujah.

Isn’t it strange how much we struggle to admit our rebellion and our title, children of wrath, yet how quickly we come around to God’s love? This is why so many Christians have sleepy worship and prayer lives: either we don’t care to admit how helpless we were, or we believe culture’s lie that we are so lovable that God’s great love doesn’t seem so great.

You can’t understand how great his love is until you understand how far he went to save you, from Genesis 3 to Calvary to this room. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Our disobedience took place around a tree, and God completed our salvation on a tree. He took on flesh, a high priest tempted in every way yet without sin, the blemish-free lamb and final sacrifice.

God made him who had no sin to be sin for us. Jesus didn’t die for his sin; he died for ours. In Colossians 2, God made you alive with Christ, canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, nailed it to the cross, and disarmed the powers and authorities. There is now no condemnation; Christ paid your debt in full, past, present, and future.

documents.excerpt: It is by grace you have been saved through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast. Faith is trusting God completely, more than believing in God: taking God at his every word and placing your life in his hands.
excerpts: It is by grace you have been saved through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast. Faith is trusting God completely, more than believing in God: taking God at his every word and placing your life in his hands.

We are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works prepared in advance. Salvation is by faith, but it always produces good works. That is more loving kindness from God: how tragic for someone to think they have saving faith when they don’t.

When you’re saved, God remodels your heart and gives you new desires; if your desires don’t change, you’re not saved. It isn’t overnight, but if you today looks the same as you a decade ago, that looks more like your handiwork than his. Just like Josh, you need Jesus.

Believe, give him your heart, open his word, read it, memorize it, and trust him with your life, and the good works will show up. Apart from faith your work is meaningless; walking by faith, your works impact eternity. Good works respond to God’s good gifts by offering your time, talents, money, and entire life with open hands: “God, it’s all yours.” That’s who we are.

documents.excerpt: Your relationship, or lack of one, with your father may shape it. An abusive, cold, uncaring, or absent father can make it hard to call God Father or understand what a loving Father means. Matthew 7 says if you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good gifts to those who ask him. If you never received a good gift from your father or parents, that verse seems foreign and distant.
excerpts: Your relationship, or lack of one, with your father may shape it. An abusive, cold, uncaring, or absent father can make it hard to call God Father or understand what a loving Father means. Matthew 7 says if you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good gifts to those who ask him. If you never received a good gift from your father or parents, that verse seems foreign and distant.

If your father was absent, overly critical, demanded perfection, or berated you, your view of God may carry those traits: “If I mess up, God’s going to punish me. He can’t possibly love me because I’m worthless.” When you sin, do you avoid God because you’re afraid he is disappointed in you? If so, stick around; good news is coming.

documents.excerpt: Others have had a false teaching about God burned into their minds by someone they or their parents trusted. Chris has dealt with several, and the most harmful for him was the idea that God couldn’t look upon sin or sinners. If he sinned, even as a follower of Christ, he had to ask forgiveness before God could interact with him; every prayer started with forgiveness. At times he hid from God in shame, believing God must be ashamed of him too. He has talked with others in this body who had the same teaching drilled into them, and he wants to help them walk out of it.

documents.context: Chris DeWald · April 14, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: That is one example of the dangerous, damaging untruths some have been taught about how God sees us, and there are many more. Few have lived this long without being scarred by broken relationships: rejection, abandonment, abuse, neglect, being unwanted. These seep into our self-perception and alter our identity. Some close off from relationships to spare themselves more hurt; others exhaust themselves chasing approval through perfectionism and codependency.
excerpts: That is one example of the dangerous, damaging untruths some have been taught about how God sees us, and there are many more. Some close off from relationships to spare themselves more hurt; others exhaust themselves chasing approval through perfectionism and codependency.

This carries into our relationship with God. How you see God directly relates to how you believe he sees you, so if your understanding of God comes from anywhere but his word, you risk being led astray. He has already told us everything he wanted us to know about himself and about us; all we have to do is read it and believe it.

excerpts: When you heard the gospel and believed, you were marked in him with a seal, the promised Holy Spirit, a deposit guaranteeing our inheritance. When you received Christ and the Holy Spirit, he sealed you.

In the ancient world a stamp pressed into clay or wax sealed something important. It served as a trademark, proved goods weren’t tampered with, and proved ownership: a seal indicated ownership, protection, and authenticity. The Holy Spirit is the mark that you belong to God, that he is your protection, that you are truly his, and that one day he will fully complete his work in you.

excerpts: Verse 5 from last week: he predestined us for adoption to sonship through Jesus Christ. God has given us the family rights and privileges as if we were born into the family.

William Barclay wrote that under Roman law, when adoption was complete, the adopted person had all the rights of a legitimate son in his new family and completely lost all rights in his old one. In the eyes of the law he was a new person, so new that all debts and obligations connected with his previous family were abolished as if they never existed.

Paul writes in Galatians 4 that when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship, and sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying “Abba, Father.” You are no longer a slave but God’s child, and since you are his child, God has made you also an heir. From slave to child is a far jump.

But we are heirs of the promise made to Abraham: if you belong to Christ, you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. That is a pretty good promise: we are God’s chosen people.

But we are heirs of the promise made to Abraham: if you belong to Christ, you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. That is a pretty good promise: we are God’s chosen people.

We are also heirs of the kingdom. James 2: has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him? Studying this week how God loves him and what he gives him because he made him his son has blown Chris away. Those in Christ, sealed and adopted, don’t have to worry about what happens after they die; they inherit the kingdom he promised.
Are you starting to see how God sees you, and where your identity needs to come from?

But we are heirs of the promise made to Abraham: if you belong to Christ, you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. That is a pretty good promise: we are God’s chosen people.
We are also heirs of the kingdom. James 2: has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him? Studying this week how God loves him and what he gives him because he made him his son has blown Chris away. Those in Christ, sealed and adopted, don’t have to worry about what happens after they die; they inherit the kingdom he promised.
Are you starting to see how God sees you, and where your identity needs to come from?

documents.excerpt: Jesus knew what he would face. In the garden in Luke 22 he prays, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done.” An angel strengthens him, and in anguish his sweat is like drops of blood. He knew the cost of our sin and the horrific pain ahead, and so did the Father, yet his will was for his Son to drink that cup and bear our filthy sin. Jesus took the beatings, endured the humiliation, and ended up on the cross.

He knew the cost of our sin and the horrific pain ahead, and so did the Father, yet his will was for his Son to drink that cup and bear our filthy sin. Jesus took the beatings, endured the humiliation, and ended up on the cross.

Matthew 27:46 hits Chris in the gut: about three in the afternoon Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli,” which means “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Taking the punishment for all our sin, he cries out Psalm 22:1 to his Father.

God’s love for his children is unconditional and beyond imagining. He loved us so much that he had his Son leave heaven, come to a place that didn’t want him, and die a horrific death while we were still sinners deserving nothing. Our Father wanted to adopt us and spend eternity with us so badly that he sent his own Son to the cross in our place. That is God’s mic drop.

documents.excerpt: We are sealed: God has given us the Holy Spirit to seal us and ensure our inheritance and eternity with him. God isn’t losing you. When you declared with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believed in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you were saved, and the Spirit sealed you as God’s, under his protection and authority. This comforts Chris more than he can express: he knows who he belongs to.
excerpts: We are sealed: God has given us the Holy Spirit to seal us and ensure our inheritance and eternity with him. God isn’t losing you. When you declared with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believed in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you were saved, and the Spirit sealed you as God’s, under his protection and authority. This comforts Chris more than he can express: he knows who he belongs to.

We are adopted, sons and daughters. “Adoption to sonship” is a legal term for the full legal standing of an adopted child. Chris’s research found that under Roman law you could disown your natural-born children but never an adopted child. It doesn’t get more secure: God adopted you because he wants you.

We are heirs, inheriting God’s promise and his kingdom, and co-heirs with Christ. And God sent his one and only Son to take on a flesh suit, live a perfect life, and pay the debt we should have paid. Chris has a son, and he can’t imagine sending him through that torture: “God, I don’t know how you love us that much.”

documents.context: Chris DeWald · April 14, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: Where does your identity come from? Someone who beat you down, a parent who didn’t know how to love you or wasn’t there, a teacher or someone you trusted who told you unbiblical things, as happened to Chris? If you have let an abuser, a well-meaning but off-base Christian, a Sunday school teacher, a pastor, a friend, even Chris, or anyone but God’s word tell you who you are, your identity isn’t right. Chris couldn’t tell the church about their identity without being in Scripture; God is the one who tells you who you are.

Brothers and sisters, if your Father has adopted you, has an inheritance for you, has sealed you, and sent his Son to take your blame and punishment because he wants you in his family, doesn’t that tell you he sees you with infinite worth and value? Hold on to that, don’t let anyone take it from you, and go back to his word if you need to. How he sees you matters, not how anyone else sees you, not even how you see yourself.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 7, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: Some say identity fades as you start adulting, but Josh thinks it just changes. We define ourselves by race, career, which side of the aisle we’re on, net worth, neighborhood, appearance, children, grandchildren, and connections. Social media is addicting and dangerous because it lets you be seen exactly how you want to be seen, which usually isn’t how those closest to you see you.

Social media is addicting and dangerous because it lets you be seen exactly how you want to be seen, which usually isn’t how those closest to you see you.

Questions like where you grew up, whether you’re married, and what you do help us understand someone. The problem comes when we take one part of our identity and define everything else by it. Josh grew up in Indiana with a Hoosier heart; what happens when he moves across the country? If your life centers on your marriage, children, or career, what happens when the marriage ends, the kids grow up, or you get laid off? Asking “what if” usually isn’t healthy, but with identity it is productive.

Ephesus sat on the west coast of Asia Minor, founded by the Greeks in 1000 BC and under Roman control from 133 BC. documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 7, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: Paul starts by addressing the most important question of all: who is God? Your family, job, friendships, and life won’t reflect the fullness God intended unless you know who he is. If everything that makes you you isn’t connected to the living God who made you in his image, there will always be an emptiness you can never fill.
excerpts: Paul starts by addressing the most important question of all: who is God? Your family, job, friendships, and life won’t reflect the fullness God intended unless you know who he is. If everything that makes you you isn’t connected to the living God who made you in his image, there will always be an emptiness you can never fill.

Two questions form our identity: what does God say about himself, and what does God say about you? Not who you say or think God is; the only reliable source on God is God himself, and he has revealed himself in his word. Some things about him are mysterious, but much has been revealed.
Only after answering who God is and who he says we are can we discuss church, family, parenting, marriage, sexuality, career, spiritual warfare, and suffering. We have to do the legwork first.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 7, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: Answering who God is runs into big things theologians have discussed for thousands of years, like being chosen from all eternity to be his child. That should bring incredible joy and fuel love for the one who loves you, but we have reduced it to foolish debate. Questions like why God chose me, why not this person, or how predestination fits with free will are great questions, but we have to trust God with the unanswered ones.

That should bring incredible joy and fuel love for the one who loves you, but we have reduced it to foolish debate. Questions like why God chose me, why not this person, or how predestination fits with free will are great questions, but we have to trust God with the unanswered ones.

Bible memory alert, one Josh’s family just added: Deuteronomy 29:29. The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever. Show obedience to the things we know and faith in the things we don’t.

Josh is saved because God chose him and drew him, yet he also knows God wants no one to perish and is being patient. He isn’t sure how those fit together, but he doesn’t need it to make sense; he believes both are true and that God is good. Intellectual Christians, be careful: making the secret things revealed isn’t in your job description.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 7, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: For 3,000 years Jews believed in one God; then Jesus says in John 10, “I and the Father are one,” and everyone freaks out: blasphemy, angry leaders, confused disciples. The Spirit descends, the Gospels, Acts, and Epistles are written, the early church fathers study what happened, and the doctrine of the Trinity is born: each member of the Godhead has a unique role in perfect unity.
excerpts: For 3,000 years Jews believed in one God; then Jesus says in John 10, “I and the Father are one,” and everyone freaks out: blasphemy, angry leaders, confused disciples. The Spirit descends, the Gospels, Acts, and Epistles are written, the early church fathers study what happened, and the doctrine of the Trinity is born: each member of the Godhead has a unique role in perfect unity.

At Jesus’ baptism the Father says he is proud of his Son, and the Spirit descends like a dove. In the Great Commission in Matthew 28, Jesus says all authority has been given to him: go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and surely I am with you always.

Does Josh fully understand the Trinity? No. But he sees intimacy, diversity, and unity: three persons, each with a distinct and crucial role. He praises the Father who made a way to peace through Jesus, the Son who is the suffering servant and Savior of his soul, and the Spirit who lives in him and convicts him. That is why Paul asks, “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?”

excerpts: Whenever you hear “redemption through his blood,” think back to the garden: do not eat or you will die. Obey me, or there will be consequences. Parents know: “Don’t touch your sister.” “You can have one Oreo,” and yes, there are groundings over Oreos in Josh’s house. If the child goes for four and you look the other way, that doesn’t make you a good or loving parent. You must follow through.

God promises punishment for disobedience because he is holy, perfect justice, and unblemished integrity; he can’t turn a blind eye. But because he is also merciful and kind, he develops a plan, and while we sit in the curse eating our Oreos, he works to restore every spiritual blessing in Christ.

God’s justice and mercy meet at Golgotha, and his wrath is satisfied on the cross: God made him who had no sin to be sin for us. Jesus was tempted in every way yet without sin; every spiritual blessing belonged to him, but he willingly became the curse. We lived lives worthy of the curse, but through Christ we receive every spiritual blessing. He reversed the curse; we can be forgiven.
Then Jesus was raised to claim victory over sin and death and prove he is the one true God come to save sinners, the promised Messiah, the lover of souls who reconciles us to God forever.

documents.excerpt: Josh doesn’t get why the church seems so worried. Christians are freaked out about every little thing, maybe from too much Fox News or CNBC. For several elections he has heard that this is the most important election ever, every time. He isn’t saying don’t vote or speak up: if you’re a Christian here and not registered to vote, you are failing as a citizen; go register. We should take strong stances on important issues.
excerpts: Josh doesn’t get why the church seems so worried. Christians are freaked out about every little thing, maybe from too much Fox News or CNBC. For several elections he has heard that this is the most important election ever, every time. He isn’t saying don’t vote or speak up: if you’re a Christian here and not registered to vote, you are failing as a citizen; go register. We should take strong stances on important issues.

But Psalm 2: “Let us break their chains,” say the nations, and the One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord scoffs at them and says, “I have installed my king on Zion, my holy mountain.” Josh wonders what God’s laugh is like, maybe contagious, but he loves that God doesn’t just laugh; he is a doer who has installed his king.

Imagine if every believer truly believed this King will not lose. Many act like it is a jump ball: “Come on, God, try harder; let me help.” No, stop; it is already done. Josh prays for unshakable confidence in the divine execution of God’s plan, like Jesus before Pilate: “You would have no power over me if it were not given to you from above.”

Pilate had a choice, but either way Jesus would have found his way to bear our sins on the cross. God’s sovereignty is breathtaking: he guides man’s plans and lets us choose freely, and Josh doesn’t know how. When the world turns its back, he calls Noah; when a nation is enslaved, Moses; when land must be conquered, Joshua; to announce the Messiah, Isaiah; to call for repentance, John the Baptist; and to take the gospel to the nations, fishermen, cowards, and murderers. The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · April 7, 2024 · Identity
documents.excerpt: Election and predestination overwhelm many people, so avoid labels. People try to label Josh, and sometimes he veers a little just to throw them off. The goal isn’t to label people but to hear what the text says and how to respond.
excerpts: Election and predestination overwhelm many people, so avoid labels. People try to label Josh, and sometimes he veers a little just to throw them off. The goal isn’t to label people but to hear what the text says and how to respond.

God, the lover of our souls, worked out a plan over thousands of years to save us, and we get hung up on how he did it. Sit in the arrogance of that. Verses 4 and 5 say he chose us before the creation of the world and in love predestined us for adoption. That should be the most comforting statement we ever hear, yet many sit appalled: “My life, my choice; my free will has been violated,” treating it like a date gone horribly wrong and drafting the restraining order. Our response should be, “Praise be to God; he made a way for us.”

Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws them, and later that he is the bread of life. You only eat bread when you’re hungry, and guess who gave you a hunger for Jesus? God changes your heart so you want him. The next chapter of Ephesians says we were dead in our sins; when did you last see a dead person perform CPR on themselves? (There is a defibrillator by the back doors; help yourself.) The heart change that lets you see your offense and call on God is the work of his word and his Spirit.

documents.excerpt: Parents know what it is to overrule a child’s will to protect them, holding them while they kick and scream, “Let me go,” because they don’t know any better. Our job is to override their twisted desires with our love.
excerpts: Parents know what it is to overrule a child’s will to protect them, holding them while they kick and scream, “Let me go,” because they don’t know any better. Our job is to override their twisted desires with our love.

Our rebellion against God is no different. He steps in and says, “That’s my son, that’s my daughter,” even while we scream that we want to be free: “That’s not freedom; it leads to death, and you can’t see it yet, but trust me.” The only reason you chose God is that God made the choice possible. He predestined us for adoption to sonship.

documents.excerpt: Josh thinks of his 18-year-old daughter Madison, who doesn’t share his DNA. He and Kristen met when she was two and married when she was four. When they planned another child, Josh told Madison he was praying for a boy because he already had a girl. They have different last names, but he tells her all the time that he considers her more family than most of the people who share his name. She looks a lot like him, loves Jesus, serves Jesus, and has experienced his grace.
excerpts: Josh thinks of his 18-year-old daughter Madison, who doesn’t share his DNA. He and Kristen met when she was two and married when she was four. When they planned another child, Josh told Madison he was praying for a boy because he already had a girl. They have different last names, but he tells her all the time that he considers her more family than most of the people who share his name. She looks a lot like him, loves Jesus, serves Jesus, and has experienced his grace.
Madison and Nolan have complete equality in his home: equal access to Dad, Mom, resources, and inheritance, though as a pastor he can promise more of a trust piggy bank than a trust fund.

The one thing you can never give an adopted child is your nature. Madison will never have Josh’s nose (she is probably excited; she got her mom’s) or his blue eyes. What amazes Josh is that those God adopts begin to take on the family resemblance. He makes them sons like his divine Son, people who reflect his values and character and bring him glory.

documents.excerpt: How do you really know you’ve been forgiven, redeemed, adopted, and chosen? You will be marked by something that appears four times in that one long sentence: praise, in verses 3, 6, 12, and 14.
excerpts: How do you really know you’ve been forgiven, redeemed, adopted, and chosen? You will be marked by something that appears four times in that one long sentence: praise, in verses 3, 6, 12, and 14.

You don’t just know in your head that you’re saved by grace through faith and not by works so that no one can boast; that’s memorizing, not believing. The word Jesus uses for believe means to have faith, entrust, commit, give yourself. It isn’t just in your head; it blows you away every time, stirs your affections, and makes you want to sing, serve, kill your sin, and praise God. That is what the blessings do: they stir praise.

So ask yourself what captivates you, what rules and reigns in your heart. If you know Jesus, what used to grab your attention won’t anymore. Under his authority and reign as Lord, your entire identity will change.

According to the National Institute of Mental Health, about 12.5% of US adults will deal with a specific phobia, an anxiety disorder involving excessive and persistent fear of a situation or object. There are social phobias and agoraphobia, the fear of being somewhere escape is hard, which some may feel after being moved into the middle of a row.

Few struggle with extremes like that, but everyone is afraid of something. Some fears are rational, born of a terrible experience; others are irrational, just something inside that demands we run the other way.

documents.excerpt: Our culture fears death but doesn’t fear the one who conquered death. We have lost a healthy fear of God, so much that the president can try to say this day is something different than it has always been, using the name of the Lord in the day of the Lord on his press release.
excerpts: Our culture fears death but doesn’t fear the one who conquered death. We have lost a healthy fear of God, so much that the president can try to say this day is something different than it has always been, using the name of the Lord in the day of the Lord on his press release.

That is what happens when a culture elevates the individual: we have built a fantasy land where everyone is perfect as they are and nobody needs to change, disregarding our history. The culture calls evil good, and if evil is good there is no evil, and you don’t need God. Satan is having a field day in America, even taking ground in churches, and Josh is convinced it is because we fear all the wrong things; Satan uses little fears to distort our view of reality.

Jesus teaches about fear in Matthew 10: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. If you pictured a little red dude in tights, you’re wrong. Don’t give Satan more power than he has; only God has that power. Satan isn’t even in charge in hell. He’s a ticked-off inmate, not the warden.

The fear Jesus teaches isn’t terror; it is reverence, awe, and honor. The believer’s destination is heaven and the unbeliever’s is hell. God’s unlimited, permanent power is far superior to Satan’s limited, temporary power, and only God determines the eternal destiny of souls. That is what Easter is about.

Paul makes it clear in Romans 14 that we will all stand before God’s judgment seat: every knee will bow, every tongue will confess to God, and each of us will give an account. To those who believe in God: do you give that day enough thought? Does it inform your decisions, priorities, and what you do with the gospel and the gifts God has given you?

Josh echoes Joshua: if serving the Lord seems undesirable, choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, but as for me and my household, we will serve the Lord. Who do you serve? You might as well figure it out today.

excerpts: Josh’s only explanation for this corporation of love called the church is the resurrection. We must keep preaching and not grow weary of doing good. This building exists because first-century Christians chose gospel preservation over self-preservation.

This isn’t just a story; it is history. For thousands of years Christians have said that Jesus Christ, crucified and buried, has been raised, is seated at the right hand of the throne of the universe, and will reign until all things are under his feet. They preached it when it meant losing their jobs, with the church promising to feed them; when it meant they might starve; and when it meant they might die.

excerpts: In his research on world religions, Josh finds that most have tremendous respect for Jesus. Muslims say he was a prophet, a wise teacher sent from God; Hindus call him a holy man and wise teacher; Buddhists say he was enlightened and a wise teacher. Yet they seem uninterested in accepting his teaching.

So look at his words the night before his death: do not let your hearts be troubled; trust in God, trust also in me. In my Father’s house there is plenty of room; I am going to prepare a place for you, and I will come back. When Thomas says they don’t know the way, Jesus says, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

People don’t like Christians for saying there is only one way to heaven, but all we are doing is quoting Jesus, the one everyone agrees is holy, enlightened, good, wise, and a credible source sent from God.

excerpts: A couple of days pass, and Jesus says he is going to wake Lazarus up. The disciples think he is napping; there were no iPhones, so someone had to shake him awake. Jesus tells them plainly that Lazarus is dead, “and for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. Let us go.”

Hebrews calls Jesus the author and perfecter of our faith, and here he grows the disciples’ faith. This is why we shouldn’t complain about the Lord’s timing: what if he seems late in order to grow someone else? We always ask what’s in it for me. Believer, are you open to being used for his purposes even at your expense? Jesus was, and that is why we are here today.

documents.excerpt: The resurrection was heavily debated in that day. The Pharisees believed there would be a resurrection; the Sadducees didn’t, “and that’s why they’re sad, you see.” Jesus would sometimes start talking about the resurrection between them, let them fight, and slip out the back. You can do the same in the church lobby: say “predestination” between a Calvinist and an Arminian and walk away.
excerpts: The resurrection was heavily debated in that day. The Pharisees believed there would be a resurrection; the Sadducees didn’t, “and that’s why they’re sad, you see.” Jesus would sometimes start talking about the resurrection between them, let them fight, and slip out the back. You can do the same in the church lobby: say “predestination” between a Calvinist and an Arminian and walk away.

Those who believed in a resurrection expected one big resurrection of all Israel at once; a singular resurrection didn’t fit anyone’s beliefs. Isaiah doesn’t use the word, but he speaks of the servant alive after suffering: after he has suffered, he will see the light of life and be satisfied. That is a promised resurrection for God’s servant.

There is also a promised resurrection for God’s people. Daniel says multitudes who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt. Everyone will rise; who you spend your time with after that depends on what you do with the good news. Jesus confirms Daniel’s vision in John 5: a time is coming when all who are in their graves will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to live and those who have done evil to be condemned.

documents.excerpt: There are two realities in what Jesus tells Martha: he is the resurrection, and he is your resurrection. Josh imagines people came today because they believe Jesus was raised, but do you believe he was raised for you?
excerpts: There are two realities in what Jesus tells Martha: he is the resurrection, and he is your resurrection. Josh imagines people came today because they believe Jesus was raised, but do you believe he was raised for you?

It isn’t enough just to believe Jesus was raised. He was delivered over to death for our sins and raised to life for our justification. Death was the penalty for our sins and Jesus paid it, but how can a dead Savior mediate between God and man? He had to be raised to present his righteousness before God for our justification. We have peace with God through Jesus Christ. Happy Easter.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · March 31, 2024 · This Way to Life
documents.excerpt: Praise God, through Christ death is not just an enemy; it is a defeated enemy. Paul says, “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?… Thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Paul is talking trash to death at the Super Bowl for your soul, chest painted: “You couldn’t hold him down, so you can’t hold me down, and I’m with him.”
excerpts: Praise God, through Christ death is not just an enemy; it is a defeated enemy. Paul says, “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?… Thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Paul is talking trash to death at the Super Bowl for your soul, chest painted: “You couldn’t hold him down, so you can’t hold me down, and I’m with him.”

For the Star Wars nerds, Josh pictures Obi-Wan before Vader strikes him down: “I will become more powerful than you can imagine.” That is the Christian mindset: death, do your worst. The worst thing that can happen to a Christian is actually amazing, which is why disciples left the Sanhedrin rejoicing that they got to suffer for Christ. Death is just a doorway into resurrection life.

The harder you hit me, the stronger he makes me. That is why we suffer with joy, and why Paul boasts in Romans 8 that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us. This is how a Christian lives: singing at the top of his lungs, smiling ear to ear, serving others and forgetting selfishness, praying for enemies even as they persecute.

excerpts: Josh prays in awe of God’s goodness and his story of redemption in humanity and in Josh personally: that God knows every hair on his head, even though he shaves it; that he didn’t just say he loved Josh’s soul but did what it took to save it, even sending his Son to be humiliated.

That isn’t where the story ends: God raised his Son, exalted him, and gave him the name above every name, that every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Josh joins them: “You are Lord. I give you my life. Take it. Use me.” He asks God to use the church, to move it from chattering tongues to feet and hands anxious to wash feet and serve others, and thanks him for the empty tomb.

excerpts: Josh usually gives homework; this week he gives a project. He spent his time off building a popsicle-stick bridge with his son (blame the school district) and kept thinking he needs to hand out more projects to the church.

Most churches think an amazing Holy Week takes pageantry and performance, early mornings and multiple services. Nothing is wrong with those, but a church that doesn’t plead with you to read the word of God is a church that doesn’t love the word of God.

The project: read from the triumphal entry to Good Friday, John 12 to John 19, eight chapters in six days, and do it together as a household, whether one or eleven. Read a chapter or two and pray over it; bring in family by Zoom or FaceTime, even Grandma in Michigan. Josh thinks it could be one of the best Holy Weeks they’ve ever had.

The Road to Redemption
A project for Holy Week
Josh usually gives homework; this week he gives a project. He spent his time off building a popsicle-stick bridge with his son (blame the school district) and kept thinking he needs to hand out more projects to the church.
Most churches think an amazing Holy Week takes pageantry and performance, early mornings and multiple services. Nothing is wrong with those, but a church that doesn’t plead with you to read the word of God is a church that doesn’t love the word of God.
The project: read from the triumphal entry to Good Friday, John 12 to John 19, eight chapters in six days, and do it together as a household, whether one or eleven. Read a chapter or two and pray over it; bring in family by Zoom or FaceTime, even Grandma in Michigan. Josh thinks it could be one of the best Holy Weeks they’ve ever had.

excerpts: Picking up in chapter 21, Jesus has appeared to the disciples twice, and you can’t help but wonder where Peter is. He has returned to what was familiar: he failed Jesus, so he went back to the thing he always found success doing, fishing.

Josh can relate. You are all in for Jesus, then you get pressured and cornered and do what you know you shouldn’t. Instead of running to Jesus, falling face down in prayer, and repenting, many of us let the failure lead us to the fishing hole. Shame drives you to silence, and the whispers of discouragement come: “I’m a failure. I’m too far gone. There’s no way he can use me now. I might as well go back to the way things were.”

But God works out victory differently than you might think. It isn’t always a first-quarter blowout; often it is a nail-biter coming into the fourth quarter with bumps and bruises. God isn’t interested in the fresh, confident, hyped pregame you; he is waiting to use the tired, weak, humiliated, fourth-quarter, blood-and-grass-stained you. If you have felt like there’s no way God can use a bum like you, chapter 21 is for you.

documents.excerpt: Jesus appears a third time. Peter is with them, and they’re fishing, or really sailing, because they’re catching nothing but wind. Jesus calls from the shore, “Friends, haven’t you any fish?” and tells them to throw the net on the right side. excerpts: Jesus appears a third time. Peter is with them, and they’re fishing, or really sailing, because they’re catching nothing but wind. Jesus calls from the shore, “Friends, haven’t you any fish?” and tells them to throw the net on the right side. They can’t haul it in for the number of fish; the disciple Jesus loved says, “It is the Lord,” and Peter wraps his garment around him and jumps into the water.

Some say Peter is still trying to prove something, to be the greatest disciple: John recognized him, but Peter swam. Maybe. Or maybe he is carrying the weight of his denial so heavily that nothing else matters but the Lord’s forgiveness. It isn’t as if Jesus needed the fish; he has been appearing at people’s dinner tables for days.

The key to following Jesus with longevity is hustling to him after failure. Peter gives a pure, unrehearsed display of what a personal relationship with Jesus looks like. Sadly, many of us hide from him instead, which reveals a lack of faith: if you believed he would forgive you, you’d be in the water too.

Adam and Eve hid from God in the garden, but Jesus made a way for sinners to stop hiding and start running to him. That doesn’t mean we don’t fear or revere God; it changes how we interact with him about our sin and failures.

documents.excerpt: The religious elite try to discredit Jesus for the company he keeps, prostitutes, tax collectors, and sinners: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” The word isn’t a casual “hi, come on in”; it is prosdechomai, an eager welcome, the host waiting at the door for you to arrive. excerpts: The religious elite try to discredit Jesus for the company he keeps, prostitutes, tax collectors, and sinners: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” The word isn’t a casual “hi, come on in”; it is prosdechomai, an eager welcome, the host waiting at the door for you to arrive. There is something personal and intimate about it. Praise God, Jesus welcomes sinners.

As you battle that nagging sin, don’t forget that word. Jesus isn’t sitting with arms crossed saying, “Really, Josh, this again?” He is pleased that you call on him for help and smiling when you trust his forgiveness. He wants to wage war with you, not shame you for getting your face punched in.

Josh knows at least a dozen people who decided in the last 30 days to dethrone an idol. Satan will toss haymakers at this church because he sees affections stirred for Christ and people making distance swims to Jesus. So when the whispers come, “You’re a failure, you’re too far gone,” remember: forgiveness is eager to welcome you; forgiveness is on the shore. You can stay in the boat and drift, or you can dine with Jesus.

excerpts: “Do you love Jesus?” means: are you a Christian, a disciple, saved? It isn’t “Am I in your top five?” but “Do you love me more than these?” Josh recalls the words he thinks best separate the committed Christian from the consumer Christian: anyone who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than me is not worthy of me.

This isn’t the shallow, half-devoted love we promote today; it is love willing to walk away from anything that would harm your relationship with him. Celebrate Jesus as Savior, but also revere him as Lord. You don’t become a Christian by raising a hand, filling out a card, saying a prayer, or walking an aisle. Salvation is by faith alone apart from works, and genuine saving faith develops an unshakable commitment: to live is Christ, to die is gain.

We are called to love family, but our commitment to Christ must never yield to anyone else. You don’t have to sell your possessions or abandon your family to follow Jesus, but would you? Don’t trick yourself; search your heart: do you love Jesus more than these?

documents.excerpt: Many have been deceived: they felt something when the lights changed or the haze hit right during a favorite Chris Tomlin song, or a preacher’s passion moved them, and mistook it for the work of the Spirit. What happens when the emotions fade, on Monday morning?
excerpts: Many have been deceived: they felt something when the lights changed or the haze hit right during a favorite Chris Tomlin song, or a preacher’s passion moved them, and mistook it for the work of the Spirit. What happens when the emotions fade, on Monday morning?

In ten years of youth ministry, Josh saw the fourth night of CIY play out the same way every time: everyone crying, repenting, calling home, going up front, for the same reason everyone wore a mask when COVID broke out. First we deceive ourselves, and then Satan grabs the lie: “But you said a prayer; you went up front.” Belonging to a church on earth doesn’t mean you belong to him; having your name in the church’s system doesn’t mean it is written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.

Self-examination is vital, and Satan hates that hearts are being searched. But your own search is faulty at best, so delegate it to God. Make Psalm 139 your prayer: search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts; see if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.

Jesus loves you, and he knows whether you love him; you aren’t fooling anybody. But he is waiting patiently. He wants no one to perish and everyone to come to repentance, to turn from sin to faith in God. documents.excerpt: Steve begins by doing something usually saved for the end: he asks the church to bow in quiet reverence and take an unhurried, thoughtful look at the one who endured the cross and scorned its shame. excerpts: Steve begins by doing something usually saved for the end: he asks the church to bow in quiet reverence and take an unhurried, thoughtful look at the one who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Picture him in agony, listen as the nails are driven into his hands, look into his face as the spit from the angry crowd mingles with his blood from that awful crown.

Then, eyes still closed, ask him why he so willingly endured such undeserved abuse. As Steve sees it there are two reasons: respectful obedience to his Father, and unbridled compassion for you. The death of Christ was directed by the Father but driven by his love. He died that we might live; he was wounded that we could be healed.

The truth is inescapable: the cross had your name on it, the crown of thorns was fitted for you, and the pain you deserved he took, all of it.

But Steve says the phrase should read “by his wound,” singular. The treatment of Jesus was so awful that not even The Passion of the Christ could capture it; his body was so mangled that he didn’t have wounds so much as one long unbroken wound. Isaiah said his appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and according to Peter it is that one wound that has allowed you to be healed.

documents.context: Steve Wyatt · March 17, 2024 · The Road to Redemption
documents.excerpt: Before you judge Peter, Steve says, you know that look. You fall prey to your own weakness, something you swore you would never do again, and then a reminder flashes, a picture, a line from a song, a knowing look, and you are in the same courtyard seeing the same mutilated, bloodied face of Jesus, now lined with the disappointment and heartache your betrayal caused. The look lasts a moment, but like a laser it burns a hole in your soul.

documents.excerpt: Before time began, God knew he would have to respond to our sin. He knew we would persistently do what belittles his name and robs him of his glory, and that we would betray him by surrounding ourselves with God’s stuff rather than God himself. Because God is utterly holy, he can’t ignore these hits to his glory.
excerpts: Before time began, God knew he would have to respond to our sin. Because God is utterly holy, he can’t ignore these hits to his glory.

God’s first response is hell, and it is still very much part of God’s plan: a real, literal, eternal place. From Jesus himself, those not in the kingdom will be thrown into the darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, where the worm never dies because your flesh is never consumed and your torment will never end. It is the blackest darkness, filled with the stench of burning sulfur and the smoke of an unquenchable fire.

documents.excerpt: Before the beginning, God promised that at history’s perfect moment a lamb would come, the Lamb of God, to do for us what we could not do for ourselves. As bad as it got on the hill, the cross was not an accident or an afterthought; it was Jesus’ ultimate assignment.
excerpts: Before the beginning, God promised that at history’s perfect moment a lamb would come, the Lamb of God, to do for us what we could not do for ourselves. As bad as it got on the hill, the cross was not an accident or an afterthought; it was Jesus’ ultimate assignment.

In the very first gospel sermon, Peter said Jesus was handed over by God’s set purpose and foreknowledge. Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired against Jesus, but they only did what God’s power and will had decided beforehand should happen. The death of God’s one and only was his idea all along, not added after Adam was found in the bushes or scrawled in the margins after the fruit crossed Eve’s lips.

So unwavering was God’s plan that Jesus planted the tree from which the beams of his cross would be carved and placed in Earth’s belly the ore for the nails. Jesus knew his destiny from infancy: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. He even knew how: just as Moses lifted up the snake in the desert, the Son of Man must be lifted up. He knew it meant mocking, flogging, beating, and betrayal, and he came anyway.

documents.excerpt: Many view the cross as an ancient version of Harold and the Purple Crayon, a children’s book Steve used in consulting work: a kid draws himself out of every complication, a shortcut, a pie, a boat. Steve would hand leadership teams a crayon to inspire creative solutions.
excerpts: Many view the cross as an ancient version of Harold and the Purple Crayon, a children’s book Steve used in consulting work: a kid draws himself out of every complication, a shortcut, a pie, a boat. Steve would hand leadership teams a crayon to inspire creative solutions.

But God the Father isn’t Harold, and Jesus didn’t sketch our redemption by the seat of his pants, as if only after the world got screwed up God nervously grabbed a crayon and drew a cross. The cross was always the plan. Seven hundred years before Jesus arrived, the prophet said it was the Lord’s will to crush him, and crush means blood, a lot of blood. Later Peter described the gore and made sure we knew Jesus did it in our stead.

documents.context: Steve Wyatt · March 17, 2024 · The Road to Redemption
documents.excerpt: In Leviticus, Israel’s constitution, God said the life of a creature is in its blood, given to make atonement on the altar. Blood is the reconciling agent, the cleansing, covering connection that delivers the forgiveness we must have because we have belittled his name and robbed him of his glory. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sin.
excerpts: In Leviticus, Israel’s constitution, God said the life of a creature is in its blood, given to make atonement on the altar. Blood is the reconciling agent, the cleansing, covering connection that delivers the forgiveness we must have because we have belittled his name and robbed him of his glory. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sin.

That is why God in the Old Testament can come across as grumpy: you can’t stroll into his presence having robbed him of his glory without incurring his wrath. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sin.

The sons of Aaron approached the Lord without the benefit of blood and were struck dead; the well-meaning Uzzah tried to steady the falling Ark and was struck dead. You cannot come near to God still covered in sin.

excerpts: Whenever we, Peter included, choose earthly comforts over the comfort of God himself, blood must flow, but for the plan to work it has to be someone else’s blood.

Substitute blood finds its genesis in Genesis. After Adam and Eve ate the fruit, their eyes were opened and they knew they were naked, so they covered themselves with fig leaves, a wardrobe malfunction waiting to happen. God made them garments of skin, and to get skin you have to kill an animal. Steve imagines Adam’s horror watching a defenseless creature struck down: “Why did I eat that stupid apple?”

On Mount Moriah, God told Abraham to take his only son Isaac to the altar. Isaac asked, “Dad, we’ve got wood, we brought fire, but where’s the lamb?” Abraham, choking back tears, said God would provide the lamb. As he raised the knife, a voice called out, and he found a ram caught by its horns and sacrificed it instead of his son. That story was a foreshadowing of an even greater substitute: another only son, who would not be spared, offered as the full payment for all of humanity’s sins.

So in the Old Testament people at church knew what you had been up to by the animal tucked under your arm. Today the bigger the Bible, the more holy the carrier; back then, the bigger the animal, the bigger the screw-up. You stroll in with a scrawny pigeon while Brother Daniel hauls in a 900-pound bull: “Hey, Brother Daniel, have a bad week?”

At the altar the sinner laid his hand on the animal and leaned his weight on it, saying in effect, “I transfer my guilt, my sin, to this lamb.” That is rule four: having selected the substitute, I must lean on it and personally apply its blood over my sin. Then an amazing transfer takes place: my sin becomes the lamb’s sin, and I walk away forgiven.

excerpts: If the people were frustrated, God was more so: “Your sacrifices, what are they to me? I have more than enough of burnt offerings; I have no pleasure in the blood of bulls and lambs.” In other words, it was never about the sacrifice. God was showing how disgusting, horrible, and costly sin is, and the people turned it into another religious routine to impress him.

So when Isaiah said he was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, it was a breath of fresh air. People had been piercing and crushing animals for years, but now, instead of an “it,” there was coming a “he”: we all like sheep have gone astray, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

Instead of trading my sins to an animal, God would send another kind of lamb and transfer the sins of all mankind, past, present, and future, to his shoulders. Instead of temporarily covering sin, this lamb would remove it forever.

excerpts: Blood is required to cover sin, and the him who would come did come and provide the blood, so rule one is already accomplished in Jesus.

It took 700 years, but when the time was right a stranger appeared in the wilderness, a total freakazoid in camel hair, eating locusts and drinking honey, “venti, extra whip, definitely not decaf.” John the Baptizer said the one coming after him was so great he wasn’t worthy to lace up his Nikes. When he saw him, he remembered Isaiah’s prophecy and shouted, “Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.”

Out of obedience to the Father and love for us, Jesus willingly emptied himself and became our lamb. Yet hardly anyone recognized him. The religious crowd tried to trip him up and then tear him down; his own family scorned him; the crowd that waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna” screamed “Crucify him” five days later.

Jesus carried his own instrument of death to a bloody hillside, nails were driven into his hands and feet, and his cross dropped with a thud between two thieves. For six hours the promised Lamb dangled between heaven and earth while the crowd taunted, “Come down from that cross, then we’ll believe you.” There was no rescue, only a shout of agony, “My God, why have you forsaken me?” He knew why, and he stayed there until he died, the lamb who would give up his blood for the Peters of this world, and the Steves, and you.

Steve prays that words escape him to thank God for what he has done. He doesn’t understand how the plan came to be, but God is God and he is not, and he freely receives the gift of Jesus’ blood. He gave his heart to Jesus at nine years old, almost 60 years ago, and is grateful for the grace showered on him time and again.
He thanks God for the meal that celebrates his body broken and blood shed for our sins, asks the Lord to meet them at the table, and prays for the peace of knowing there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ.

documents.excerpt: Today begins a three-week series called The Road to Redemption. As the church prepares to celebrate the Lord’s resurrection, it is a reminder that Christ’s death and resurrection have undeniable power. Gazing into Peter’s life during the Lord’s final hours will transform how you read Romans 5:8: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. There is tremendous encouragement in seeing the fisherman become an apostle, and in Peter’s denial and restoration.
excerpts: Today begins a three-week series called The Road to Redemption. As the church prepares to celebrate the Lord’s resurrection, it is a reminder that Christ’s death and resurrection have undeniable power. Gazing into Peter’s life during the Lord’s final hours will transform how you read Romans 5:8: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. There is tremendous encouragement in seeing the fisherman become an apostle, and in Peter’s denial and restoration.

Peter’s fall is recorded in all four gospels, “which I’m sure Peter’s thrilled” about. Hardly a day goes by that Josh doesn’t consider what Jesus endured, beaten, mocked, crowned with thorns, spit upon, crucified, yet he can’t imagine any of it hurting as much as hearing Peter say, “I do not know the man.” Jesus predicted it, but that may have increased the pain.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · March 10, 2024 · The Road to Redemption
documents.excerpt: Jesus’ words to the church in Ephesus show it isn’t uncommon for believers to lose their first love: “You have forsaken the love you had at first.” Before anyone sends emails, Josh isn’t talking about salvation; he is talking about purpose.
excerpts: Jesus’ words to the church in Ephesus show it isn’t uncommon for believers to lose their first love: “You have forsaken the love you had at first.” Before anyone sends emails, Josh isn’t talking about salvation; he is talking about purpose.

Believers should remain skeptical of themselves. We start out trusting God for life and drift into believing in God and in ourselves, sometimes after a small victory over an addiction or habit. We go from “Jesus, take the wheel” to “You ride shotgun, I got it from here.” Day 30 of sobriety, the Lord is my shield and very great reward; day 100, me and the Lord; day 300, “I don’t even think about it anymore.” That is dangerous.

We have no trouble being skeptical of others. But the wise believer knows the greatest potential for harm comes not from around them but from within, which is why Peter’s story is in all four gospels: Peter loved Jesus and would fight for him, yet self-confidence was his downfall.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · March 10, 2024 · The Road to Redemption
documents.excerpt: Judas betraying Jesus with a kiss was sad, but Judas loved money; we saw it coming. Peter loved the Lord. He was in the inner circle with James and John, who saw Jairus’s daughter healed, the transfiguration, and Jesus praying in Gethsemane.
excerpts: Judas betraying Jesus with a kiss was sad, but Judas loved money; we saw it coming. Peter loved the Lord. He was in the inner circle with James and John, who saw Jairus’s daughter healed, the transfiguration, and Jesus praying in Gethsemane.

It deepens when we recall Peter answering, “Who do you say I am?” He said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” the same confession many make in the waters of baptism, and Jesus said flesh and blood hadn’t revealed it, but the Father in heaven. The higher the position, the greater the fall.

Let this warn anyone seeking to lead in his church: it is a noble pursuit, but the greater the responsibility, the more devastating the sin. But he surrendered to God’s will: he came into the world with nothing and now has a church, wife, kids, job, and food; if God takes it all, so be it. With Peter he says boldly, “I will never stop praising him, never stop preaching the gospel, never turn my back on him.”

But he surrendered to God’s will: he came into the world with nothing and now has a church, wife, kids, job, and food; if God takes it all, so be it. With Peter he says boldly, “I will never stop praising him, never stop preaching the gospel, never turn my back on him.”

Next is his wife: he would rather someone remove his eyes with a spoon than be unfaithful to her. His devotion is to God first and his wife second, and God set it up beautifully: he honors God by submitting to his wife out of reverence for Christ, so long as she doesn’t become an idol. “He almost idol-proofed your wife.”

Then his children (“as much as they look like me, which is not a good thing”): child of God, husband, father, then pastor. He loves this body deeply, but all those commitments come first; we have seen the devastation when men of God place the church above their families. “You are your commitments.”

Picture the setting: a palace courtyard around midnight or 1 a.m., cold, ringed by connected rooms. Jesus is likely in the courtyard being questioned by Caiaphas and the chief priests. Witnesses say he claimed he would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. The high priest charges him under oath to say if he is the Messiah; Jesus says they will see the Son of Man at the right hand of the Mighty One, coming on the clouds. The high priest tears his clothes and cries blasphemy, and they spit in his face and strike him.

Peter moves around the courtyard through each denial, always keeping Jesus in sight as he is beaten. Then: “Man, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” the rooster crows, and the Lord turns and looks straight at Peter. Imagine the memories: “We walked on water together, but I couldn’t walk with him through this.” But as the coming weeks will show, Jesus wasn’t done stretching out his hand to save Peter, and Josh believes he is stretching it out to many today.

Perhaps the scariest verse in Scripture: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?’ Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you. documents.context: Josh Wyatt · March 3, 2024 · Genesis
documents.excerpt: It is the final week of the series in Genesis, picking up in chapter 50. Josh hopes the church has seen that God has been working a plan to save their souls for generations, and that Jesus isn’t Plan B; he was the plan from the beginning and is yes to every promise.
excerpts: It is the final week of the series in Genesis, picking up in chapter 50. Josh hopes the church has seen that God has been working a plan to save their souls for generations, and that Jesus isn’t Plan B; he was the plan from the beginning and is yes to every promise.

Paul proclaimed this to the people in Corinth: no matter how many promises God has made, they are yes in Christ, and through him the amen is spoken to the glory of God. We never grow out of proclaiming that the work is done. We aren’t ashamed or bored of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes. That complicated Greek word “everyone” means all, every kind: everyone.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · March 3, 2024 · Genesis
documents.excerpt: Josh prays the church would see the difference between how God handles those who ignore him and those who take him at his word. Many have made an art form of ignoring God, questioning, challenging, and doubting at every chance.
excerpts: Josh prays the church would see the difference between how God handles those who ignore him and those who take him at his word. Many have made an art form of ignoring God, questioning, challenging, and doubting at every chance.

Believers don’t have an answer for everything; Josh has a lot of questions. The difference is that he doesn’t need the answers, because the fewer he has, the more he places his life in God’s hands: “I don’t know, Lord, but I love you.” Moses had questions, and God didn’t seem to like that very much; Josh prefers the Abraham method: just believe and go. We seek to look like Jesus in Gethsemane: not my will, but your will be done.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · March 3, 2024 · Genesis
documents.excerpt: One phrase grinds Josh’s gears: “I’m just looking to go deeper.” Do you want to dig a hole? Is there something greater than God sending his Son to die for you? What is deeper than daily reflection on the yes to God’s promises, or humbling yourself to obey the one who died to give you everlasting life? If you mean a deeper desire to know him, great, but Josh doesn’t think that is what people mean.
excerpts: One phrase grinds Josh’s gears: “I’m just looking to go deeper.” Do you want to dig a hole? Is there something greater than God sending his Son to die for you? What is deeper than daily reflection on the yes to God’s promises, or humbling yourself to obey the one who died to give you everlasting life? If you mean a deeper desire to know him, great, but Josh doesn’t think that is what people mean.

Nothing in the New Testament teaches that knowledge brings a greater relationship with God; ask the man crucified next to Jesus. Humility, not a well-articulated thesis on the sovereignty of God, is the key to intimacy with God. Peter says, “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand.” The humbled Christian has hit bedrock; you don’t get deeper.
Stop treating God like a genie in a bottle and ask him to humble you, to teach you to do his will rather than grow more comfortable with yours.

excerpts: They are asking about a theme known as God’s providence. You won’t find the word in Genesis 50, but it is an undeniable theme throughout Scripture.

A miracle is an act outside the bounds of natural order, like Jesus walking on water. Josh’s son keeps saying he can run across the water and sinks like a boulder every time; God could let him, though Josh doesn’t see why he would.

Providence is the power of God overseeing his creation and working out his plans within the laws he set. Despite Satan’s efforts to derail the plan, God works through both our good and our bad intentions to bring about his intentions. Josh thinks that is more amazing than miracles.

excerpts: Joseph is awesome. God uses nine words to tell us who created the world, but Joseph gets 13 chapters, 25 percent of Genesis. Today Josh narrows to one moment in Genesis 50:15, but first catches the church up.

In Genesis 37, teenage Joseph dreamed his brothers bowed to him; jealous, they planned to murder him but sold him instead and told Jacob he was dead, a family lie that lasted 22 years. In chapter 39 Potiphar bought him. Joseph was a stud (“unlike me, he probably had hair”), Potiphar’s wife wanted him, and he ran. Quick lesson on handling sexual sin biblically: men, run.

Falsely accused of rape, Joseph was imprisoned, interpreted Pharaoh’s dream, became second in command of Egypt, and saved millions of lives through a seven-year famine. You’d be hard pressed to find a better man in the Old Testament.

excerpts: The brothers make two mistakes: they assume Joseph was dishonest for two decades instead of honest, and instead of talking face to face they send the Egyptian equivalent of a text: “Your father left these instructions before he died.”

Eleven brothers develop the plan around a conference table. They don’t pray, and they don’t go to Joseph and let him smash their assumptions. Josh imagines the text: “Hi Joseph, we forgot to tell you Daddy said on his deathbed he wants you to take good care of us. We know we sold you, and that’s messed up, but Dad’s dying wish was that you let that go.” Verse 17: “I ask you to forgive your brothers the sins and the wrongs they committed.”
Josh pictures them huddled around the iPad: Reuben the firstborn should know better, Simeon and Levi “have so much self-control,” and is Judah, Dan, Asher, or Benjamin going to speak up?

excerpts: Guilt is overwhelming; the wounds sin inflicts on others and ourselves can get out of control if we don’t forgive and forget. The psalmist writes in chapter 38, “My guilt has overwhelmed me like a burden too heavy to bear. My wounds fester and are loathsome because of my sinful folly.”

A guilty conscience needs no accuser; guilt is its own accuser, and no affliction is greater. The natural response to its unbearable weight is to drag others down: misery loves company. Shakespeare said suspicion always haunts the guilty mind. After 40 years, Joseph forgave them, but they never forgave themselves.

excerpts: First, Joseph says, “Get up.” Go fall at the feet of God and worship him, but not me; I’m not worthy.

How do you respond to praise? Josh confesses it is a real temptation in his job. “Great sermon today, Josh” can get “I killed it today; how blessed are you,” or “Thanks for encouraging me, I needed that, but God wrote the letter; I’m just dropping it off at your front door.”

Josh thinks culture has figured out that fame and fortune aren’t the end game; the happiest people aren’t rich and famous. He thinks Taylor Swift isn’t happy, and says just because people want to hear what you have to say doesn’t mean you have something worth saying. How hard must it be to humble yourself before God when your fan base thinks you are a god? Joseph knows there is only one worthy of praise.

excerpts: Think of your life as a timeline. If God gave you a divine eraser that could reach into your past, are there parts you would erase? Ministry comes out of pain, brokenness, and suffering, and the pain is what makes your testimony powerful. Some want to erase a first marriage: he or she intended to harm you, but God intends it for good; who can you help? Some want to erase health problems: that disease intends to harm you, but God intends it for good; who in that waiting room needs to hear about your hope? Some want to erase a childhood with an evil father who hit, hurt, and took advantage of them: God intends it for good.

When the Lord heals our brokenness we may have scars, but we come back stronger, and from that strength we preach and his church is fueled. He gives ministries, platforms, and microphones to tell how he turned evil to good. If you are struggling to find purpose in the church, don’t erase that moment; it is the key. God will use your suffering to help someone else.

excerpts: Genesis is only one book. The Bible is 66 books by 40 authors on three continents in three languages over nearly 2,000 years, and it all points to one person: Jesus.

The story continues: God’s people grow from about 60 to a nation of two to three million, because he said he would. Moses meets the burning bush, leads the people out of Egypt, and receives the Ten Commandments; Joshua leads them into the promised land, where they bury Joseph; judges and kings come and go; Isaiah and John the Baptist say Jesus is coming: repent and be baptized.

Joseph was sent to save millions; Jesus was sent to save everyone and bless all the nations. Hebrews 9 says Christ was sacrificed once to take away the sins of many and will appear a second time to bring salvation to those waiting for him.

excerpts: It is week eight of a nine-week series in Genesis, and the church will be in Genesis 34. Josh’s disclaimer: this chapter is depressing.

From Genesis 28 we read about Jacob starting a family that, as the church heard last week, is pretty dysfunctional. One definition of a dysfunctional family is one in which an individual’s conflict and misbehavior occur continually, leading other members to accommodate them. Everyone is picturing an individual right now, but often our response to that individual deepens the dysfunction rather than relieving it.

Josh’s dad recapped the families of Genesis beautifully last week. Genesis 34 is one of the most important stories in the book, about a woman named Dinah, in three parts: verses 1–5, the rape of Dinah; verses 5–12, the offer; and verses 13–31, revenge.

excerpts: Dinah is Jacob’s only daughter, but first Josh looks at how Jacob leads his home. As husband and father Jacob is extremely passive. If you think your marriage is hard, he was married to two sisters. Josh is a one-woman man until death, though he once broke up with a girl for her sister: “Don’t judge me. I wasn’t being sanctified yet,” and it didn’t go well.

In Genesis 29 and 30 the sister wives compete in the Olympic event of who can have the most children to earn their husband’s affection, and Jacob is completely passive: “Yes, babe. Whatever you want, dear.”

Jacob did reconcile with Esau, but not because of his leadership; Esau was stirred with love and forgiveness. They made plans to meet down the road, and Jacob ghosted him. He plays fast and loose with relationships: if there is nothing in it for him, he won’t even put it on his Google Calendar.

The most shocking part is that now he wants to marry her. Many women still fall for the thinking that since we’ve already been together, we should get married and that will fix it. It won’t. When we sin we feel guilt; when someone sins against us we feel defiled and violated. Almost every time we sin against someone, we prioritize our own guilt over the defilement we caused. The king and his son care more about feeling better than about the one they hurt; they came to negotiate and left Dinah alone in the city instead of returning her.
